settled.claim: Retrieval practice with feedback beats restudy — but the product's chosen format sits in the weakest cell on both axes. Rowland's final-test-format moderator: free recall g≈0.79–0.82, cued recall g≈0.70–0.72, recognition/multiple-choice g≈0.36; and initial RECALL practice produces larger testing effects than initial RECOGNITION practice, independently.
settled.scope: Meta-analytic, mixed lab and educational materials (facts, prose, word pairs), delays from minutes to weeks. Not L2 Chinese, not months.
sources: Rowland, C. A. (2014). The effect of testing versus restudy on retention: A meta-analytic review of the testing effect. Psychological Bulletin, 140(6), 1432–1463. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25150680/

Pan, S. C., & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 144(7), 710–756. https://psycnet.apa.org/manuscript/2018-20773-001.pdf
Adesope, O. O., Trevisan, D. A., & Sundararajan, N. (2017). Rethinking the use of tests: A meta-analysis of practice testing. Review of Educational Research, 87(3), 659–701.
settled.implication: Four-option MC is a pace-and-sociability decision that costs roughly half the available retention benefit. Say that in the design doc rather than claiming the evidence endorses it. Two mitigations are real: competitive distractors (gated — see below), and one meaning-recall beat with the options NOT yet visible, followed by feedback. A recall beat placed after the options are on screen is not a retrieval attempt and buys nothing.

settled.claim: Spacing is the best-evidenced manipulation in L2 vocabulary learning specifically, and a co-located party game is structurally massed. In the closest study, spaced beat massed 26.62% vs 16.87% at a one-week test (1.6×). Expanding and equal schedules perform similarly, so an equal-interval ladder is a defensible v1.
settled.scope: classroom-L2: real L2 words, real learners, 1-week delayed tests (Nakata & Suzuki N=133); Kim & Webb pools 98 effect sizes / 48 experiments / N=3,411 of L2 learning.
sources: Kim, S. K., & Webb, S. (2022). The effects of spaced practice on second language learning: A meta-analysis. Language Learning, 72(2), 269–319. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lang.12479

Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. (2019). Effects of massing and spacing on the learning of semantically related and unrelated words. SSLA, 41(2), 287–311. https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/studies-in-second-language-acquisition/article/effects-of-massing-and-spacing-on-the-learning-of-semantically-related-and-unrelated-words/F58BA8D70385603B9C42E408BFCB8A10
Nakata, T. (2015). Effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language vocabulary learning. SSLA, 37(4), 677–711.
settled.implication: The single largest architectural hole. The whole design optimises one session's encoding; the biggest lever is between sessions. The product needs a reason for the same people to return across days, or its best-evidenced mechanism is simply unavailable to it — a business-model consequence, not only a memory one. Do not spend engineering on expanding-vs-equal tuning.

settled.claim: Spacing gaps must be conditioned on estimated item strength, not on a fixed fraction of the trip horizon. Cepeda's 10–20%-of-retention-interval result is a TWO-SESSION experiment on L1-comprehensible trivia sitting on a deliberately FLAT, asymmetric optimum (too-long gaps cost far less than too-short ones).
settled.scope: lab, L1 trivia facts, one study episode + one restudy. Not defined for the five-to-fifteen encounters an item will get here.
sources: Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T., & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science, 19(11), 1095–1102.
Pavlik, P. I., & Anderson, J. R. (2008). Using a model to compute the optimal schedule of practice. JEP: Applied, 14(2), 101–117.
Settles, B., & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning (Half-Life Regression). ACL.
settled.implication: `gap = 0.15 × (target_date − now)` is a shippable bug: applied to the second-ever exposure of a novel character on a six-week horizon it schedules review ~6 days out, by which point a beginner has lost the item and review becomes relearning. Use the trip date to set the RECALL THRESHOLD (higher as the trip nears), not the gap. First two-to-three encounters get short gaps (one overnight) regardless of trip date.

settled.claim: The second exposure of a newly introduced item should fall after a night, not later the same evening. Lexical integration — the new form starting to compete with similar existing forms — tracks sleep rather than mere elapsed time; and 'recognised in session' and 'integrated' are demonstrably different states.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist, spoken novel words in L1. Never tested on a logographic L2 — applying it to characters is an explicit extrapolation. Complementary-systems is a FRAMEWORK, not an effect; the sleep-dependent competition result has accumulated null results and boundary conditions.
sources: Dumay, N., & Gaskell, M. G. (2007). Sleep-associated changes in the mental representation of spoken words. Psychological Science, 18(1), 35–39. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2007.01845.x

Davis, M. H., & Gaskell, M. G. (2009). A complementary systems account of word learning. Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 364(1536), 3773–3800. https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rstb/article/364/1536/3773/21148/
Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1992). A new theory of disuse and an old theory of stimulus fluctuation (storage vs retrieval strength).
settled.implication: Ship the two-bit item state (acquired / consolidated) — it is cheap and it is what gates the whole confusable policy — but present it as a defensible design bet framed by storage-vs-retrieval strength, NOT as a consequence of established neuroscience. Storage/retrieval strength buys an extra testable prediction the neuro framing does not: a retrieval that succeeds when the item was nearly forgotten is worth far more than an easy one, so do not reward easy repetitions.

settled.claim: Real L2 vocabulary does not decay exponentially to zero — there is a durable plateau — but the plateau's HEIGHT is set by the amount of original training. It is an argument for overlearning, not for early retirement.
settled.scope: classroom-L2, cross-sectional, self-reported rehearsal, decades-long intervals. Absolute retention levels are low (an 8-year figure of ~15%).
sources: Bahrick, H. P. (1984). Semantic memory content in permastore: Fifty years of memory for Spanish learned in school. JEP: General, 113(1), 1–29. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/6242406/
Bahrick, H. P., & Phelps, E. (1987). Retention of Spanish vocabulary over 8 years. JEP: LMC, 13(2), 344–349.
settled.implication: Make the mastery variable cumulative successful cross-day retrievals, not a recency-weighted decay score, and use savings-on-relearning ('this sign took three looks last month, one today') as the progress metric. But do NOT retire an item after four successes — that inverts the finding. Any retirement threshold is an unlabelled product guess; label it and calibrate it from your own attempt log.

settled.claim: Levels of processing survives only as transfer-appropriate processing: what matters is the match between the encoding operation and the retrieval operation, not 'depth'. Semantic encoding beat rhyme encoding on standard recognition, but rhyme encoding BEAT semantic encoding on a rhyme-recognition test — replicated at immediate and delayed test.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist, word lists at minutes-to-a-day delays. The principle is used here to settle a product-defining question on the strength of word-pair experiments — say so.
sources: Morris, C. D., Bransford, J. D., & Franks, J. J. (1977). Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing. JVLVB, 16(5), 519–533. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022537177800169
Craik, F. I. M. (2002). Levels of processing: Past, present... and future? Memory, 10(5/6), 305–318.
settled.implication: Define the criterion task once, at the top of the design document, and settle every argument against it: 'standing in front of a physical sign, in an unfamiliar display typeface, retrieve the meaning.' That is meaning-recall from a rendered form, not four-option discrimination. Never settle a design argument by asking 'is this deeper?'

settled.claim: Encoding specificity licenses the CHARACTER FORM AS IT WILL BE MET as the effective cue — not the surrounding scene. If a learner only ever encodes 出口 as clean black Song on white, then black-Song-on-white is the cue, and a white-on-green backlit station plate is a different stimulus.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist (Tulving & Thomson used word pairs at short delay). The application to typography and substrate is an argument from the principle, not a direct test.
sources: Tulving, E., & Thomson, D. M. (1973). Encoding specificity and retrieval processes in episodic memory. Psychological Review, 80(5), 352–373.
settled.implication: THIS is the correct rationale for Decision 2, and it licenses exactly the fidelity of the sign — typeface, stroke weight, spacing, contrast, substrate, the real colour inversions (white-on-green exit, white-on-red hazard, black-on-yellow price tag) — and nothing about the surrounding environment. Visual consistency across cards is in direct tension with the criterion task, and the criterion task wins.

settled.claim: Environmental context-dependent memory is dead as a design rationale. Pooled d≈0.28 (93 effect sizes / 75 studies); a 2026 meta-analysis gives g=0.32; the effect is reduced or eliminated for RECOGNITION (Godden & Baddeley's own 1980 follow-up found no context effect on recognition); it vanishes for meaningful material at longer study times; and the famous 1975 divers experiment has FAILED a direct replication.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist, environmental (room/underwater) manipulations. Note: the app's rendered sign is not environmental context at all — it is part of the stimulus, present at study and test inside the app and absent in that exact form on the street. Nothing is being reinstated.
sources: Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Environmental context-dependent memory: A review and meta-analysis. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11495110/
Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1980). When does context influence recognition memory? British Journal of Psychology, 71(1), 99–104.

Murre, J. M. J. (2021). The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication. Royal Society Open Science, 8(11), 200724. https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rsos.200724 — plus 2022 addendum, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8728159/
Isarida, T. et al. (2012). Effects of study time and meaningfulness on environmental context-dependent recognition. Memory & Cognition, 40(8), 1225–1235. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22825971/
Context reinstatement effects in younger and older adults' memory: A meta-analysis (2026). https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41525397/
settled.implication: Delete 'context encoded is context retrieved' from the rationale and build no feature that depends on it: no ambient-scene backgrounds, no 'study in the same place' nudge, no geolocation-matched review. A four-option MC test is the maximal-outshining case — it hands the player the target. (Sourcing note: one sweep attributed the recognition null to Smith, Glenberg & Bjork 1978; that paper is the RECALL demonstration. Cite Godden & Baddeley 1980.)

settled.claim: Component decomposition is the app's transfer engine and it has direct CFL experimental support, including transfer to UNTAUGHT characters — demonstrated using precisely a four-option contrastive format holding one component constant and varying the meaning-bearing one. Morphological awareness is the largest single contributor to L2 Chinese reading, far outranking working-memory capacity.
settled.scope: classroom-L2: Nguyen et al. N=54 Vietnamese learners with ~1 year of study, pre/post sentence-cloze, no long-delay posttest; meta-analytic support for radical-based strategies. Small N.
sources: Nguyen, T. P., Zhang, J., Li, H., Wu, X., & Cheng, Y. (2017). Teaching semantic radicals facilitates inferring new character meaning in sentence reading for nonnative Chinese speakers. Frontiers in Psychology, 8, 1846. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01846/full

Investigating the effect of radical-based strategies on improving foreign Chinese learners' radical awareness and character meaning production: a meta-analysis. https://en.front-sci.com/index.php/rerr/article/download/1177/1359
The role of linguistic and cognitive skills in reading Chinese as a second language: A path analysis. Frontiers in Psychology (2023), 14:1131913.
settled.implication: Decision 3 is the best-supported decision in the product and should be the largest block on the reveal. Ship a component-contrast card type that holds one component constant and varies the meaning-bearing one — that is the exact configuration with evidence for generalisable rather than item-specific knowledge, and the 肉 → 月 → 肝/肠/肚/腰/脑 unlock is a textbook instance of it. Reserve it for items already consolidated.

settled.claim: Decompose to COMPONENTS (2–5 per character), never to strokes. Chunking is what makes a character fit in working memory at all; strokes add elements without adding structure. The associated corpus arithmetic (mean ~10.15 strokes, 98% of characters ≤5 chunks, ~2.1 strokes/chunk) is a statistic about the script, not a memory result.
settled.scope: Corpus statistic plus a controlled CFL training study (writing vs visual-chunking vs reading-only) with measurement immediately after training and again at THREE MONTHS — the best retention-interval discipline available in this space.
sources: Cao, F., Rickles, B., Vu, M., Zhu, Z., Chan, D. H. L., Harris, L. N., Stafura, J., Xu, Y., & Perfetti, C. A. (2013). Early stage visual-orthographic processes predict long-term retention of word form and meaning. Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0911604413000043
Gobet, F. et al. (2001). Chunking mechanisms in human learning. Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 5(6), 236–243.
settled.implication: Every item ships with a component decomposition field or it does not ship. Read Cao et al. (2013) in full before finalising the decomposition spec — the arithmetic quoted everywhere in the sweep material is theirs, and the paper also carries the only three-month follow-up in the field.

settled.claim: Compound transparency is decisive and there is NO head-to-head experiment on teaching 出口 whole vs 出 and 口 separately. The nearest evidence says both, conditional on semantic transparency — and radical awareness demonstrably fails for non-transparent compounds.
settled.scope: classroom-L2 processing and instruction studies, not a curriculum RCT. This is the single biggest evidential hole under Decision 3.
sources: Hao, Y., Wu, C., & Duan, X. (2024). Processing Mandarin Chinese Compound Words by Native Speakers and Second Language Learners. SAGE Open. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/21582440241256249
Chen, T., & Feng, Y. (2020). Nontransparent Compound Character Learning in L2 Chinese: Does Radical Awareness Always Work? SAGE Open. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/2158244020969669
Word-meaning inference in L2 Chinese: an interactive effect of learners' linguistic knowledge and words' semantic transparency. Reading and Writing (2020).
settled.implication: Add a required `transparency` enum (transparent | semi | opaque) and branch the reveal on it. Opaque items (东西, 麻烦) must carry an explicit 'this one does not decompose — learn it whole' line. Rendering a bogus decomposition for an opaque word is worse than showing none: it installs an inference rule that will misfire on the street.

settled.claim: Phonetic components predict a character's pronunciation only ~40% of the time, while semantic radicals carry more reliable meaning cues — and semantic radicals themselves vary widely in reliability. The overwhelming majority of Chinese characters are phono-semantic compounds, not pictographs.
settled.scope: Chinese-specific psycholinguistics and sinology. Not an experiment on this app's format.
sources: Perfetti, C. A., Liu, Y., & Tan, L. H. The Lexical Constituency Model. https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8098601_The_Lexical_Constituency_Model
DeFrancis, J. (1984). The Chinese Language: Fact and Fantasy, Ch. 8 'The Ideographic Myth'.
Taft, M., & Zhu, X. (1997). Submorphemic processing in reading Chinese. JEP: LMC.
Feldman, L. B., & Siok, W. W. T. (1999). Semantic radicals contribute to the visual identification of Chinese characters. JML.
settled.implication: Add a per-component `role` (semantic | phonetic | neither) AND a reliability marker; gloss high-reliability semantic components prominently, render low-reliability ones as background structure, and never invite meaning inference from a phonetic component. Mark every gloss `etymological` or `mnemonic-only` against a scholarly reference. Without this, the transfer engine generates confident wrong inferences on unseen characters — the Chineasy failure mode arriving through the front door.

settled.claim: Story/keyword/imagery mnemonics buy nothing for READING. In the best-controlled Chinese test, all strategies were equally effective for reading; the mnemonic advantage appeared only on WRITING and only for the visually-similar-pair group. Tested on Chinese characters directly, imagery mnemonics gave no advantage over rote beyond the immediate test in any instance across two experiments.
settled.scope: classroom-L2 / lab-L2 paired associates: Chang et al. N=66 non-beginners, immediate + 1-week delayed; Wang & Thomas (1992) N=218 undergraduates, delays ≤1 week. Nothing at eight weeks.
sources: Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). The effect of visual mnemonics and the presentation of character pairs on learning visually similar characters for CSL learners. Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.783898/full
Wang, A. Y., & Thomas, M. H. (1992). Effect of keywords on long-term retention of Chinese characters. Language Learning, 42(3), 359–376.
Wang, A. Y., Thomas, M. H., & Ouellette, J. A. (1992). Keyword mnemonic and retention of second-language vocabulary words. JEP, 84(4), 520–528. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ456644
settled.implication: Do not ship a Heisig / Mandarin Blueprint / Chineasy-style invented story per character as the teaching payload. Ship the true component decomposition, the paired confusable, and spaced exposure. Mnemonic flavour is capped at one line, authored (never player-generated), derived from real components, and carries ZERO scheduling weight — the interval comes from the player's outcome, never from whether a mnemonic was shown.

settled.claim: The method of loci is evidenced for immediate SERIAL and free recall of word lists and essentially nothing else; outside serial recall the evidence is graded low to very low quality. Its outcome measure is a capability this product never asks for.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist, immediate ordered/free recall. Note the kill argument is the OUTCOME-MEASURE mismatch, not construction cost — basic MoL benefits appear after minutes of instruction (a five-minute virtual environment works as well as a lifelong familiar one); twenty hours buys memory-athlete list performance.
sources: Ondřej et al. (2025), British Journal of Psychology — method-of-loci meta-analysis. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40457944/
Twomey & Kroneisen (2021), method-of-loci review.
Legge, E. L. G., Madan, C. R., Ng, E. T., & Caplan, J. B. (2012). Building a memory palace in minutes. Acta Psychologica, 141(3), 380–390.
Dresler, M. et al. (2017). Mnemonic training reshapes brain networks to support superior memory. Neuron, 93(5), 1227–1235.
settled.implication: No memory-palace mode, no 'journey' or chain through a set of signs, no spatial layer, no ordered-route item selection. Item pool is random-access. Do not defend this with the cost argument — a stakeholder defeats it by saying 'so make it a two-minute tutorial'. Defend it with the outcome measure: MoL puts N items back in ORDER; 看不懂 needs meaning retrieval from a form.

settled.claim: Self-explanation is the cheapest well-evidenced intervention available: g = 0.55 across 69 effect sizes from 64 reports with 20 coded moderators. Verified exactly by adversarial check.
settled.scope: classroom/instructional — expository text, worked examples, maths and science problems. NOT lab-wordlist (the sweep mislabelled it).
sources: Bisra, K., Liu, Q., Nesbit, J. C., Salimi, F., & Winne, P. H. (2018). Inducing self-explanation: A meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review, 30, 703–725. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-018-9434-x
settled.implication: The co-located format gives this away free. One spoken prompt on the confusable pair at the reveal — 'why isn't it 入口?' — addressed to the highest bettor, ~5 seconds, spoken to the table. Never typed, never scored; typed self-explanation kills party-game pace.

settled.claim: Betting before seeing the item is a PRETEST, and the prequestion benefit is large but strictly item-specific: g = 0.66 for the information the question targeted, and no evidence of any benefit for other material present in the same activity. It requires corrective feedback to exist at all.
settled.scope: classroom/instructional — texts, lectures, videos (the sweep mislabelled it lab-wordlist). Also supported by the unsuccessful-retrieval literature.
sources: The Effect of Prequestions on Learning: A Multilevel Meta-Analysis. Educational Psychology Review (2025). https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-025-10075-7
Pan, S. C., & Carpenter, S. K. (2023). Prequestioning and Pretesting Effects. Educational Psychology Review.
Kornell, N., Hays, M. J., & Bjork, R. A. (2009). Unsuccessful retrieval attempts enhance subsequent learning. JEP: LMC, 35(4), 989–998.
Richland, L. E., Kornell, N., & Kao, L. S. (2009). The pretesting effect. JEP: Applied, 15(3), 243–257.
settled.implication: This is the honest justification for the bet-before-reveal, and it replaces both the 'neural warrant' and the memory-palace 'explicit binding' analogy. Two consequences: (1) narrow the dealt category to prequestion granularity — 'signs on a subway platform', 'weight and price on a market label', not 'Transport' — because the anticipation must target roughly what will be asked; (2) a wrong guess before feedback is PRODUCTIVE, so scoring must keep guessing attractive rather than driving players to hedge, and no round may leave a bet unresolved.

settled.claim: Hypercorrection is real: errors made with high confidence are corrected better and more durably given clear feedback, the effect persists over a week, and a TEST after corrective feedback is what blocks the return of high-confidence errors.
settled.scope: lab/educational general-knowledge material, delays to about a week.
sources: Butler, A. C., Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2011). The hypercorrection effect persists over a week, but high-confidence errors return. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238–1244. — NOTE: the sweep misattributed this paper to Metcalfe & Finn.
Metcalfe, J. (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology, 68, 465–489.
Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Feedback enhances the positive effects and reduces the negative effects of multiple-choice testing. Memory & Cognition, 36(3).
settled.implication: Persist the bet as a confidence value (`bet_tier`, `was_correct`) and route on it: any item missed at the HIGHEST bet tier is re-tested before the session ends via a `high_confidence_miss` queue drained in the final round. Be honest that this is a within-session MASSED repetition — defend it on hypercorrection grounds only, never as good scheduling.

settled.claim: Form similarity is the real hazard; semantic relatedness is weak and, in the direction this app tests, HELPFUL. In a clean factorial with delayed tests, form similarity usually hurt accuracy and ALWAYS increased confusion errors, while semantic relatedness without form similarity IMPROVED accuracy when the first test was L2→L1 and tended to hurt when it was L1→L2.
settled.scope: classroom-L2 / lab-factorial with a delayed test (Kemp); Nakata & Suzuki is real L2 words at 1 week. Ishii (2015), often cited as the decisive form-vs-meaning test, has a 20-MINUTE retention interval and should be weighted as lab, not classroom.
sources: Kemp, J. (2021). Second language vocabulary acquisition: The effects of semantic relatedness, form similarity, and translation direction. Language Learning, 71(3), 730–770. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lang.12449
Ishii, T. (2015). Semantic connection or visual connection: Investigating the true source of confusion. Language Teaching Research, 19(6), 712–722. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1075483
settled.implication: Good news for the concept, and it fixes the pairing rule. The game is sign→meaning (L2→L1 comprehension), the direction in which semantic relatedness HELPS. So: four semantically related MEANINGS among the options is fine; four orthographically near-identical SIGNS during a sign's first appearances is not. And never add a production mode (write/type the Chinese for 'exit') — that is the L1→L2 direction where relatedness turns harmful.

settled.claim: Semantic relatedness can leave overall accuracy unchanged while still installing confusion — the harm shows up in ERROR TYPE, not in score. Related and unrelated items did not differ in posttest scores at one week, but related items produced significantly more interference errors.
settled.scope: classroom-L2, real English–Japanese word pairs, N=133, 1-week test. The strongest material/interval combination in this literature.
sources: Nakata, T., & Suzuki, Y. (2019). Effects of massing and spacing on the learning of semantically related and unrelated words. SSLA, 41(2), 287–311.
settled.implication: The most actionable single item in the whole cluster. Log WHICH distractor was chosen on every wrong answer, not just correct/incorrect, and maintain a per-user confusion matrix keyed on (target_item, chosen_item). A plain accuracy curve will look healthy while a pair is quietly being cross-associated. Sibling-confusion events should lower an item's strength estimate even when the answer was correct.

settled.claim: Retrieving one member of a competing pair suppresses the other by roughly 8.7 percentage points, and the effect is competition-dependent — it appears only when the non-practised item actually competes for retrieval access.
settled.scope: lab-wordlist, mostly category–exemplar materials, intervals of minutes to a day. The phenomenon is not contested; its mechanism is.
sources: Murayama, K., Miyatsu, T., Buchli, D., & Storm, B. C. (2014). Forgetting as a consequence of retrieval: A meta-analytic review of retrieval-induced forgetting. Psychological Bulletin, 140(5), 1383–1409. https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/37052/1/Murayama%20et%20al_2014_PB.pdf
settled.implication: Enforce pair-balanced testing. A deck that repeatedly quizzes 出口 and never 入口 is actively degrading 入口 by roughly the RIF magnitude. When the session builder selects item X, mark every member of X.family_id due-soon rather than letting them drift.

settled.claim: Competitive multiple-choice distractors both help and hurt, and the two effects run in opposite directions for this design. Plausible alternatives can produce test-induced learning of the alternatives and avoid retrieval-induced forgetting — but plausible lures also reliably produce a negative suggestion effect that grows with lure plausibility and number, and it persists in some conditions even with feedback. Crucially, the mechanism that makes competitive MC beneficial (retrieving why each other option is wrong) requires knowledge the learner already has.
settled.scope: Both sides are lab/educational facts and prose at short delays, NOT L2 vocabulary. Neither has been run on Chinese characters.
sources: Little, J. L., Bjork, E. L., Bjork, R. A., & Angello, G. (2012). Multiple-choice tests exonerated, at least of some charges. Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344. https://bjorklab.psych.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/2016/07/Little_EBjork_RBjork_Angello_2012.pdf
Roediger, H. L., III, & Marsh, E. J. (2005). The positive and negative consequences of multiple-choice testing. JEP: LMC, 31(5), 1155–1159.
Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Memory & Cognition, 36(3).
Little, J. L., & Bjork, E. L. (2016). Multiple-choice pretesting potentiates learning of related information. Memory & Cognition, 44, 1085–1101.
settled.implication: Distractor confusability must be a FUNCTION of the item's exposure state, not a constant and not a difficulty dial. First encounters: semantically and visually UNRELATED distractors. Component-sharing / confusable distractors unlock only after the item has been retrieved correctly across at least one night. This makes the consolidation bit load-bearing for distractor policy, and it means 'ban random unrelated distractors' is wrong as a blanket rule — unrelated distractors are correct for a sign's first appearances. Feedback is mandatory, immediate, and corrective rather than verdictive: display the correct answer, and when a lure was chosen, name that lure and mark it wrong.

settled.claim: Simultaneous paired presentation of visually similar Chinese characters improves discrimination of subtle stroke differences in absolute beginners; characters differing by an ADDED stroke are learned more easily than identical-stroke pairs.
settled.scope: One 2025 study, N=183 speakers of non-tonal languages with no prior Chinese, 2×2×2 design, retention interval not established. Converging condition-specific support from Chang et al. (2022). This is thinner evidence than 'best-evidenced element in the whole design' implies — grade it moderate at best and treat it as a hypothesis to instrument.
sources: Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: The Effects of Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages, 10(10), 260.
Chang, L.-Y., Tang, Y.-Y., Lee, C.-Y., & Chen, H.-C. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898.
Carvalho, P. F., & Goldstone, R. L. (2014). Putting category learning in order. Memory & Cognition, 42(3), 481–495. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13421-013-0371-0

Meagher, B. J., Carvalho, P. F., Goldstone, R. L., & Nosofsky, R. M. (2017). Organized simultaneous displays facilitate learning of complex natural science categories. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 24(6), 1987–1994.
settled.implication: Show both members of the pair at the same time, side by side, same size, same baseline, same neutral ink — not sequentially and not one-then-reveal. Prioritise added-stroke pairs early and schedule identical-stroke pairs later. Note the general reconciliation: simultaneous/interleaved presentation helps HIGH-similarity categories, blocking helps LOW-similarity ones.

settled.claim: A silent side-by-side is not enough. Pairing visually similar characters pays off only if the distinguishing component is given MEANING, and learners do not encode a confusable contrast into new items unless attention is explicitly directed to the critical difference during learning. Identification training with feedback beats same/different discrimination training.
settled.scope: classroom-L2 (Chang et al., N=66, immediate + 1-week) plus L2 speech-perception training, which is a different modality and therefore an analogy.
sources: Chang, L.-Y. et al. (2022). Frontiers in Psychology, 13, 783898 — the Pithy-Formulas-with-Key-images advantage over Key-images alone was SPECIFIC to the visually-similar-pair group.
Differential effects of identification and discrimination training tasks on L2 vowel identification and discrimination. SSLA.
From meaning to sound: how word learning shapes non-native speech perception (2025). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12447442/
settled.implication: Budget authoring time for one written, meaning-bearing formula per distinguishing component — required content for any item with a form-confusable sibling, not optional flavour: '出 = feet stepping out of an enclosure; 入 = a wedge entering.' Keep the task as identification ('what does this sign say?') and never add a same/different mode ('are these two the same word?').

settled.claim: Typeface variability during training produces a small generalisation advantage to novel typefaces in a logographic script: variable-typeface training was SLOWER on the familiar typeface and FASTER on a novel one.
settled.scope: lab-logographic, n=190 with no prior Chinese, 24 characters, six exposures each, ALL WITHIN A SINGLE SESSION, no delayed retention test, and the published effects are explicitly small (roughly one-to-two words of accuracy, a few hundred ms of RT).
sources: Pelzl, E. (2025). High variability orthographic training: Learning words in a logographic script through training with multiple typefaces. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32, 2090–2103. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13423-025-02646-0
Variability in training unlocks generalization in visual perceptual learning through invariant representations. Current Biology (2023).
Perceptual variability: Implications for learning and generalization. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review (2020).
settled.implication: Adopt typeface variety as a cheap default because real signage varies — NOT as a validated mechanic with a numeric floor. Drop the 'at least THREE typefaces' requirement; the encoding-specificity argument is doing more work here than the experiment is. The correct schedule rule is 'do not repeat the substrate/typeface this ITEM was last seen on', across its own repeat exposures.

settled.claim: Seductive details measurably harm retention and transfer, and the effect is STRONGER under limited study time — which is exactly the condition a timed, socially pressured card creates.
settled.scope: Meta-analytic across instructional multimedia. The companion Involvement-Load 'evaluation' argument is weaker than it looks: ILH explained 15.0% of variance on immediate post-tests but only 5.1% on DELAYED post-tests, so it is a weak predictor at the interval this product cares about.
sources: Rey, G. D. (2012). A review and meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect. Educational Research Review, 7(3), 216–237.

Sundararajan, N., & Adesope, O. (2020). Keep it Coherent: A Meta-Analysis of the Seductive Details Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 32, 707–734. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10648-020-09522-4
Yanagisawa, A., & Webb, S. (2021). Language Learning, 71(2), 487–536. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/lang.12444
settled.implication: One-line test for every pixel of the sign rendering: does it constrain the meaning of the target? The ¥ and the number on a price label pass (they make 斤 a unit); the station plate's arrow passes. A photographic Chinese street scene behind the card FAILS. Steam curling off a bowl next to 麻辣 FAILS. Keep the heuristic; rest it on the seductive-details leg, not on Involvement Load.

settled.claim: Split attention is a measured cost in Chinese character learning specifically: WHERE the pinyin sits changes the outcome, with a vertical per-character layout beating a horizontal one. Verified by adversarial check.
settled.scope: classroom-L2 presentation-format experiment. Note there appears to be NO controlled experiment on FADING pinyin — the bet ladder itself is an untested design.
sources: Lee, C. H., & Kalyuga, S. (2011). Effectiveness of different pinyin presentation formats in learning Chinese characters: A cognitive load perspective. Language Learning, 61(4).
settled.implication: Render pinyin as per-character syllables directly BELOW each character, baseline-aligned to that character's box — chū under 出, kǒu under 口 — never as 'chūkǒu' beside or beneath the word. Same rule for the gloss: attach it to the whole word under the pinyin row, not off to the side.

settled.claim: Desirable difficulties reverse in two documented ways: for high-element-interactivity material, and with expertise. A difficulty is desirable only if the learner can actually execute the effortful process.
settled.scope: classroom/instructional (high-element-interactivity material is definitionally instructional, not word lists — the sweep mislabelled it).
sources: Chen, O., Castro-Alonso, J. C., Paas, F., & Sweller, J. (2018). Undesirable Difficulty Effects in the Learning of High-Element Interactivity Materials. Frontiers in Psychology, 9:1483. https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.01483/full
Chen, O., Kalyuga, S., & Sweller, J. (2017). The Expertise Reversal Effect is a Variant of the More General Element Interactivity Effect. Educational Psychology Review, 29, 393–405.
settled.implication: Bounds Decision 1. The bet-as-scaffolding-removal is the right SHAPE but must be bounded by competence, not courage: a top-tier bet on a category where the player holds no component knowledge is not a desirable difficulty, it is a coin flip. Also: the reveal card must THIN OUT as an item's accuracy record improves — scaffolding that helps a first-time viewer costs a player who already knows the item.

settled.claim: Learners' judgments about what works are systematically inverted for exactly the manipulations this product depends on — spacing, interleaving, retrieval practice, and difficulty generally.
settled.scope: Broad, well-replicated metacognition literature.
sources: Bjork, R. A., Dunlosky, J., & Kornell, N. (2013). Self-regulated learning: Beliefs, techniques, and illusions. Annual Review of Psychology, 64, 417–444.

Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the 'enemy of induction'? Psychological Science, 19(6), 585–592. https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02127.x
settled.implication: Write this into the experimentation policy at the top of the design doc, not buried in a finding: no learning-relevant feature may be killed or shipped on self-reported difficulty, perceived helpfulness, in-session accuracy, or session satisfaction — all four move the wrong way. The only admissible primary metric is delayed performance at ≥1 week, ideally on TRANSFER items (a sign in a rendering the player has never seen). Expect the confusable panel to feel unpleasant.

settled.claim: Observers gain from watching others retrieve, and collaborative retrieval improves later INDIVIDUAL memory even though the group recalls less in the moment. Separately, seeing another player's wrong answer implants it (social contagion), which is a correctness argument for hiding per-player errors, not merely a comfort argument.
settled.scope: lab collaborative-memory paradigms, not L2 and not co-located games.
sources: Collaborative memory / collaborative inhibition and post-collaborative individual benefit literature (Rajaram and colleagues).
Social contagion of memory (Roediger, Meade & Bergman).
settled.implication: Write an exposure record for EVERY player at the table when an item resolves, flagged role: observer | answerer, and let observer exposures advance scheduling state at a discounted weight — otherwise a player who watched thirty items and answered six is modelled as having seen six. And never show 'what everyone else picked' as a distribution bar; never surface a per-player accuracy leaderboard. Score the table against the item bank; let bets be the only individual number on screen.

settled.claim: Difficulty carries a documented motivational cost that the retention literature routinely omits: learners cannot discover retrieval practice's effectiveness from experience because the in-the-moment signal is opposite to the long-term outcome, and the applied literature on quitting converges on inability to perceive progress.
settled.scope: Mixed applied literature; no RCT quantifying dropout as a function of difficulty in a language app. The practitioner material filling that gap is folklore.
sources: Motivational Strategies to Engage Learners in Desirable Difficulties. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition (2020).
How task difficulty and academic self-efficacy impact retrieval practice guidance. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10698739/
settled.implication: Make progress legible in the product's own currency — signs, not points. End every session with one screen: 'you can now read these 7 signs', rendered as the actual signs at real size in their real typefaces. That directly answers 'what can I do now that I couldn't before?' and costs one screen.

contested.question: Should a confusable be shown beside the target at all — interference theory versus discriminative contrast? (Decision 4)
contested.side_a: INTERFERENCE. Classical transfer theory says maximum damage for exactly this structure: shared cue, different and antagonistic responses. Form similarity ALWAYS increases confusion errors in L2 vocabulary. Multiple-choice lures are later misremembered as correct, and the effect scales with lure plausibility. Learning related items simultaneously produces cross-item confusion from the start, and Chinese characters are unusually susceptible because they share components.
contested.side_b: DISCRIMINATIVE CONTRAST. Juxtaposition is the active ingredient in interleaving benefits — the benefit tracks juxtaposition, not temporal spacing, and temporal separation destroys it. Simultaneous paired presentation of visually similar characters improved discrimination in absolute beginners. Competitive MC distractors avoid retrieval-induced forgetting and can teach the alternatives. Interleaving helps precisely the HIGH-similarity categories.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Four things, and they resolve the apparent contradiction cleanly. (1) WHERE: a post-resolution TEACHING panel with feedback present is not the same manipulation as putting the confusable among the four options at TEST. Panel = supported. Options = hazardous until consolidated. (2) WHEN: the mechanism that makes competitive lures beneficial is retrieving why the others are wrong — unavailable to a beginner who knows none of the four. So confusable options require that the sibling is already consolidated (correct after at least one intervening night). Never introduce both members of a pair as new items in the same session. (3) WHICH KIND: form-confusable (人/入, 斤 inside 公斤) is the real hazard and needs staged introduction; meaning-confusable but visually distinct (麻/辣) can be shown together freely; shared-morpheme two-character pairs (出口/入口, 门口) are a FOURTH category that no cited study covers — the shared 口 is a genuine shared meaning that can be taught, so it plausibly behaves more like the weak semantic case than the strong synform case, but that is a hypothesis. (4) HOW: a silent side-by-side does not work — the discriminating component must be NAMED in words with a meaning-bearing formula, and feedback must name the specific lure the player chose. Also note the direction helps you: the app tests L2→L1 comprehension, the direction in which semantic relatedness among options improves accuracy.
sources: Osgood, C. E. (1949). The similarity paradox in human learning: A resolution. Psychological Review, 56(3), 132–143. — historically important schematic whose specific response-similarity predictions did not survive the 1960s transfer literature; grade WEAK, cite as framing only.
Higa, M. (1963). Interference effects of intralist word relationships in verbal learning. JVLVB, 2(2), 170–175. — direction disputed, see separate entry.
Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Learning painting styles: Spacing is advantageous when it promotes discriminative contrast. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103.

Birnbaum, M. S., Kornell, N., Bjork, E. L., & Bjork, R. A. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
Roediger, H. L., III, & Marsh, E. J. (2005). JEP: LMC, 31(5), 1155–1159.
Little, J. L. et al. (2012). Psychological Science, 23(11), 1337–1344.
Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Languages, 10(10), 260.
Kemp, J. (2021). Language Learning, 71(3), 730–770.

contested.question: Does the interleaving benefit reverse for words, and does that constrain this design?
contested.side_a: REVERSES. The one large meta-analysis of interleaving (59 studies, 238 effect sizes, 158 samples) gives an overall g = 0.42 but a WORDS cell of g = −0.39 — a reliable advantage for blocking — against paintings g = 0.67 and mathematics g = 0.34. Sweeps in two separate clusters built round architecture on this cell.
contested.side_b: DOES NOT APPLY. Interleaving in that literature means alternating exemplars of different CATEGORIES for inductive category learning, over materials like paintings, birds and tastes. The app's question is whether two confusable vocabulary ITEMS should co-occur — a different manipulation with a different literature. Nobody who cited the words cell had read it: its composition, its retention intervals, and whether 'words' means L2 paired associates are all unverified.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether a 看不懂 item is being treated as a visual CATEGORY (the shape of 出 vs 入 — contrast helps) or as a WORD (the 出口 → 'exit' mapping — blocking and spacing help). It is both at once, and the design split follows: contrast the character FORMS freely at the teaching moment; never run two form→meaning MAPPINGS as competing to-be-learned associations in the same acquisition session. Do NOT hang the verdict on the unread moderator cell — rest it on Nakata & Suzuki and Kemp, which are real L2 words, real learners, real intervals, and support the same split independently. Material label for the meta-analysis should be lab-category-learning, not 'both'.
sources: Brunmair, M., & Richter, T. (2019). Similarity matters: A meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin, 145(11), 1029–1052. https://www.psychologie.uni-wuerzburg.de/fileadmin/06020400/2019/Brunmair_Richter_in_press__2019_META-ANALYSIS_OF_INTERLEAVED_LEARNING.pdf
Nakata & Suzuki (2019), SSLA 41(2).
Kemp (2021), Language Learning 71(3).

contested.question: Should confusable siblings be scheduled CLOSE together or deliberately APART in the deal?
contested.side_a: TIGHT. Interleaving works by juxtaposition, so members of a confusion set should sit close together but not adjacent (roughly 5–15 intervening items), alternating — spacing repetitions of the SAME item widely while interleaving DIFFERENT-but-confusable items tightly. On this reading, an anti-adjacency rule prohibits the intervention.
contested.side_b: APART. Crowding a learner with orthographically and semantically similar competitors is a documented source of associative interference (fan effect, RIF). Running simultaneous confusable pairing AND component-family surfacing together guarantees a beginner meets a dense cluster of near-identical forms with related meanings in a short window — the configuration most likely to produce durable confusion.
contested.what_it_turns_on: The item's consolidation state, again, and the separation of the two functions. The defensible synthesis: use simultaneous pairing at the RESOLUTION/teaching moment where the contrast is explained and feedback is present; do not use component-family membership as a reason to schedule siblings close together in the DEAL until both are consolidated; then interleave tightly within the family as declared discrimination training. This is a genuine live disagreement between two adversaries — instrument it rather than deciding it on argument. The scheduler needs both a minimum gap (same item) and, once discrimination training is active, a maximum gap (within confusion set).
sources: Kornell, N., & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Psychological Science, 19(6), 585–592.
Anderson, J. R. (1974). Retrieval of propositional information from long-term memory (fan effect). Cognitive Psychology.
Anderson, M. C., Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (1994). Remembering can cause forgetting. JEP: LMC.
Murayama et al. (2014), Psychological Bulletin 140(5).

contested.question: Should the discriminating component be colour-marked on the resolution panel?
contested.side_a: NO. In the one Chinese-specific study, colour coding SLOWED reaction times, interpreted as visual overload; radical markings have separately been found to interfere with L2 character learning. Two sweeps turned this into a hard prohibition and a general 'never tint any part of a glyph' rule.
contested.side_b: NOT SO FAST. That is an RT main effect at test, not a learning outcome — slower responding is equally consistent with more careful feature-checking. Against it stands a meta-analytically supported signalling/cueing principle: highlighting the critical feature is one of the better-supported multimedia principles and is the standard way to implement 'direct attention to the critical difference', which the same sweeps demand two findings later.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether the outcome measured is RT or delayed discrimination accuracy, and how many simultaneous highlights are on screen. Treat colour as an A/B question tested on delayed discrimination accuracy, not on RT. If visual load is the worry, cap the number of simultaneous highlights rather than prohibiting the affordance. Note this does NOT disturb Decision 5: keeping tone colour off the character and on the pinyin survives on redundancy grounds regardless of how the marking question resolves.
sources: Li, J., Shi, M., & Wang, X. (2025). Languages, 10(10), 260.
Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations on Chinese character learning among L2 learners. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9403612/
Schneider, S., Beege, M., Nebel, S., & Rey, G. D. (2018). A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media. Educational Research Review, 23, 1–24.

contested.question: Should the app ship a finger-trace / handwriting affordance, or ban writing outright?
contested.side_a: SHIP IT (bounded). Handwriting is the best-evidenced Chinese-specific encoding manipulation in the field: 48 adult CFL learners over five consecutive days, handwriting-to-read beat pinyin-typing-to-read on form recognition AND meaning, with a clean dissociation showing pinyin coding strengthened phonology. A companion training study carries a three-month follow-up. A single-component trace on the reveal fits the form factor and directly targets the orthographic representation a four-option tap can be passed without building.
contested.side_b: DO NOT SHIP IT. A newer source in the same literature reports the TYPING group better on character RECOGNITION — which is precisely this app's outcome measure — while handwriting led on meaning recognition. Justifying a feature with a motor-memory narrative on an untested form factor (finger-tracing on a phone during a party game) is the same mechanism-to-UI leap the reviews were commissioned to hunt.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Which outcome you weight. If the criterion is discriminating 人 from 入 on a wall, the orthographic-representation argument is directly on point; if the criterion is the app's own four-option recognition score, the direction is unclear. Resolution: do not write 'never' into the spec and do not ship it as a default. Build it as an explicit experiment — trace only the differing component, only on the resolution screen, only for form-confusable pairs, never on the timed card, never required — with delayed discrimination accuracy as the dependent measure.
sources: Guan, C. Q., Liu, Y., Chan, D. H. L., & Perfetti, C. A. (2011). Writing strengthens orthography and alphabetic-coding strengthens phonology in learning to read Chinese. JEP, 103(3), 509–522. https://sites.pitt.edu/~perfetti/PDF/Writing%20strengthens%20Guan%20JEP.pdf
Cao, F. et al. (2013). Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461.
Shi (2026). Foreign Language Annals, doi:10.1111/flan.70053.
Comparison studies of typing and handwriting in Chinese language learning: A synthetic review. Journal of Second Language Writing (2021).

contested.question: Does the keyword/mnemonic method actively cost long-term retention?
contested.side_a: YES. Keyword-instructed learners forgot roughly twice as many items as rote rehearsers at a TWO-DAY delay (N=218); and with one population, rote outperformed keyword outright.
contested.side_b: CONTESTED. The result is attributed by critics to presentation-rate and initial-learning confounds specific to that paradigm, and there is a published rebuttal. Decisively for the design: in follow-up work, supplying PICTURES of the keyword and the referent at acquisition ELIMINATED the excess forgetting — which collides with the separate recommendation not to add imagery. Also, the 'experienced FL learners are the harmed subgroup' claim rests on a fully confounded between-experiment comparison (different nationality, L1, target language and recruitment), and cannot support a subgroup conclusion.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether imagery accompanies the keyword, and the retention interval (the whole dispute lives at ≤1 week; nothing here speaks to eight weeks). Practically it does not matter much, because the conservative action is the same under both readings: do not schedule an item more leniently because a mnemonic was shown. What must change is the confidence: present it as contested, name the rebuttal, and drop the invented 'suppress the mnemonic from exposure 3' constant — no source specifies any such number.
sources: Wang, A. Y., Thomas, M. H., & Ouellette, J. A. (1992). JEP, 84(4), 520–528. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ456644
Thomas, M. H., & Wang, A. Y. (1996). JEP: Applied, 2(4), 330–342.
Gruneberg, M. M. (1998). A commentary on criticism of the keyword method of learning foreign languages. Applied Cognitive Psychology, 12, 529–532.
van Hell, J. G., & Mahn, A. C. (1997). Language Learning, 47(3), 507–546.

contested.question: Which way does antonym pairing cut — is 入口/出口 the worst case or a facilitated one?
contested.side_a: WORST CASE. Intralist similarity increased learning difficulty with antonyms among the worst; 入口/出口 is literally the antonym-plus-shared-cue configuration.
contested.side_b: POSSIBLY FACILITATIVE. The similarity/difficulty function may be NON-MONOTONIC: strongly pre-associated response sets (antonyms, strong free associates) can be learned relatively easily because the pre-existing association mediates, while MODERATELY similar sets (coordinates, connotative-only similarity) are the damaging ones. If so, 入口/出口 — a canonical strongly-associated antonym pair sharing an L1 semantic frame — falls in the easy cell, and 麻/辣 (a coordinate pair) is the harder one. The same 1963 study is cited with opposite valences in two places in the same brief.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Reading the primary paper. Nobody in this evidence chain has. Until then, do not treat 入口/出口 as the maximal-interference case, and do not treat the staged-introduction rule as a prediction derived from classical transfer theory — it is a precaution. Note the bridge is broken regardless: the classical work describes learning two NEW competing responses to a shared cue in list-to-list transfer, not discriminating one new sign from another in a recognition task with the cue physically present.
sources: Higa, M. (1963). Interference effects of intralist word relationships in verbal learning. JVLVB, 2(2), 170–175. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0022537163800821

contested.question: How much is the production effect ('the whole table says it aloud') worth here?
contested.side_a: HIGH VALUE, ranked third in the build order: it works in pure-list between-subject designs, works for RECOGNITION specifically, is LARGER in a second language, and endures to at least a week.
contested.side_b: MODERATE-TO-WEAK FOR THIS APP. The produced token is pinyin — an alphabetic string — not the target character, and there is no evidence the effect holds when the produced token is not the studied form. The pure-list between-subject variant is the smallest version and has been argued to arise partly from a response-criterion shift rather than improved discriminability, which would not help a four-alternative discrimination between confusable characters. And unison group speech is not the studied manipulation — simultaneous speech degrades self-hearing, and hearing others delivers far less than speaking oneself.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether the character is on screen while the player speaks, and whether the criterion is old/new recognition or forced-choice discrimination among similar lures. Keep the say-it-aloud beat — it is cheap and plausibly positive — but show the CHARACTER during production, not pinyin alone, demote it below the two form-instruction elements in the build order, and instrument it instead of assuming it.
sources: Fawcett, J. M. (2013). The production effect benefits performance in between-subject designs: A meta-analysis. Acta Psychologica, 142(1), 1–5. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23142670/
Fawcett, J. M. et al. (2023). Production improves recognition and reduces intrusions in between-subject designs. Canadian Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77(1), 35–44.
Forrin, N. D., & MacLeod, C. M. (2018). This time it's personal: The memory benefit of hearing oneself. Memory, 26(4), 574–579.
Bodner, G. E., & Taikh, A. — criterion/bias contribution to between-subject production effects.

contested.question: Is excluding pronunciation from the product an evidence-based decision or a scope decision?
contested.side_a: EVIDENCE-BASED, as originally argued: the phonological loop is a mechanism for storing unfamiliar SOUND patterns, and a reading-recognition game largely bypasses it, so pinyin is a meaning aid only.
contested.side_b: SCOPE DECISION, and the evidence runs the other way. Alphabetic (pinyin) coding demonstrably strengthens phonology in adult CFL learners; phonological activation is automatic in Chinese reading; and durable lexical representations require orthography, phonology and semantics bound together. An orthography→semantics-only design builds low-quality lexical representations by construction.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Nothing empirical — the criterion task genuinely is reading a sign, not saying it, and that is a legitimate product choice. What must change is the framing: say plainly 'we are deliberately building a partial lexical representation; the cost is that these representations will be lower quality than a form+sound+meaning learner's and will not support listening or speaking.' Do not dress it as a memory finding. Keep audio optional and unscored, and store pinyin (with tone marks) and audio on every item from day one even if v1 never surfaces them.
sources: Perfetti, C. A., Liu, Y., & Tan, L. H. The Lexical Constituency Model.
The interaction of orthography, phonology and semantics in L2 learners' Chinese character production. Frontiers in Psychology (2023), 14:1076810. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10017467/

myths.myth: 'Context encoded is context retrieved' — rendering the item in a realistic environment reinstates context at retrieval.
myths.why_wrong: Environmental context-dependent memory is a small effect (d≈0.28; g=0.32) that is reduced or eliminated for RECOGNITION tests, vanishes for meaningful material at longer study times, and whose most famous demonstration (Godden & Baddeley 1975, divers) has FAILED a direct replication. Worse, the app's rendered sign is not environmental context at all — it is part of the stimulus, present at both study and test inside the app. Nothing is being reinstated. Build no feature on it: no ambient-scene backgrounds, no 'study in the same place' nudge, no geolocation-matched review.
sources: Murre, J. M. J. (2021). Royal Society Open Science, 8(11), 200724, plus 2022 addendum.
Smith, S. M., & Vela, E. (2001). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 8(2), 203–220.
Godden & Baddeley (1980). British Journal of Psychology, 71(1), 99–104.

myths.myth: The Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, and 'you forget 50% within an hour and 70% within 24 hours'.
myths.why_wrong: Graded folklore for meaningful language material. The original is a single subject — Ebbinghaus on himself — memorising nonsense syllables with savings-in-relearning as the measure, not recall. The modern replication is N=1 and shows substantial variability. Never show the user a forgetting-curve graphic or a 'you'll forget 70% by tomorrow' nudge: it is not true for this material and it makes the product's factual claims indefensible. Any forgetting function in the scheduler must be fitted to the app's own per-item outcome data. Note also that the '24-hour discontinuity' in that N=1 curve does NOT support the overnight-boundary architecture — that rests on the lexical-consolidation work instead.
sources: Murre, J. M. J., & Dros, J. (2015). Replication and analysis of Ebbinghaus' forgetting curve. PLOS ONE, 10(7), e0120644.

myths.myth: A 'direct neural warrant' for the bet-then-reveal structure: curiosity states drive dopaminergic encoding, so put the component breakdown in the high-curiosity anticipation window.
myths.why_wrong: Category error twice over — midbrain BOLD does not measure dopamine, and no imaging result constrains an interface. Strip the fMRI and the behavioural leg that carries the load is curiosity boosting INCIDENTAL memory, which is the weak, inconsistent, underpowered half of that literature — and it has been directly contradicted for the closest analogue: memory was POORER for incidental scholastic facts presented after high-curiosity questions. The original incidental material was unrelated faces; the product would be applying it to instructional content. The '~1.5–2 s anticipation beat' is invented outright; no source specifies any duration. Two better rationales for the same screen already exist: spatial/temporal contiguity with the answer, and feedback timing on a pretest.
sources: Gruber, M. J., Gelman, B. D., & Ranganath, C. (2014). Neuron, 84(2), 486–496.
States of epistemic curiosity interfere with memory for incidental scholastic facts. npj Science of Learning (2024). https://www.nature.com/articles/s41539-024-00234-w

myths.myth: Cowan's ~4-chunk limit (or '~3 for visual') licenses a hard cap on how many elements the resolution screen may show.
myths.why_wrong: Graded folklore as applied. Cowan's limit governs chunks held in the focus of attention IN THE ABSENCE OF THE STIMULUS; a screen whose elements all remain visible imposes essentially no storage demand — the display IS the memory and the eye re-samples it. And the '~3 for visual' figure inherits the discrete-slot model of visual working memory, which is actively contested by continuous-resource accounts, so it derives a hard integer from a model whose integer is the disputed part. Cowan-over-Miller is well supported; this use of it is not. Re-derive the rule from element interactivity: 'one target, one decomposition, one contrast, nothing else on the integration path', with reference material behind a tap.
sources: Cowan, N. (2001). Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24(1), 87–114.
Ma, W. J., Husain, M., & Bays, P. M. (2014). Changing concepts of working memory. Nature Neuroscience.
Failure of self-consistency in the discrete resource model of visual working memory. Cognitive Psychology (2018).

myths.myth: The bet is justified because 'explicit binding' at encoding is what makes the method of loci work, and a wager is an explicit binding act.
myths.why_wrong: RETRACTED. Explicit binding in that study is a SPATIAL operation — attaching an object to a locus in a navigable environment. A wager on a four-option guess shares only the English word 'explicit': no shared mechanism, no shared outcome measure (free recall of 3D objects vs forced-choice recognition of an orthographic form), no study linking them. The bet survives; the citation does not. Justify it as a pretest/prequestion instead.
sources: Reggente, N., Essoe, J. K.-Y., Baek, H. Y., & Rissman, J. (2020). The Method of Loci in Virtual Reality. Journal of Cognitive Enhancement, 4, 12–30.

myths.myth: Picture superiority / dual coding justifies rendering items photorealistically on physical objects.
myths.why_wrong: RETRACTED as applied. Picture superiority compares memory for items STUDIED AS PICTURES against items STUDIED AS WORDS. Here the to-be-remembered item is, in every condition, an orthographic form; photographing that character onto an enamel plate does not convert it into a picture — it changes the surround. It is a stimulus-format effect applied to a presentation-context decision. Separately, Paivio's dual-coding EXPLANATION is not the leading account: picture superiority is eliminated when physical distinctiveness is equated. The rendering survives on transfer-appropriate-processing grounds alone; strike this justification. And do NOT add illustrative clip-art beside characters on dual-coding grounds — an exit-door pictogram beside 出口 adds a cue that will not be on a real Chinese sign and risks the player learning the pictogram.
sources: Higdon, K. F., Neath, I., Surprenant, A. M., & Ensor, T. M. Distinctiveness, not dual coding, explains the picture-superiority effect. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology, 78(1), 180–191.

myths.myth: Force the player to re-tap the visible correct answer after an error — 'the cheapest effect size in the whole product'.
myths.why_wrong: It is a null. Re-tapping a highlighted correct answer that is on screen is COPYING, not retrieval — there is nothing to retrieve. The prompts-beat-recasts result it rests on is about oral, ill-formed learner production in interaction, and there is no ill-formed output in a four-alternative tap. Replace with feedback-then-requeue at a delay, which is the mechanism that actually produces the wanted effect.
sources: Lyster, R., & Saito, K. (2010). Oral feedback in classroom SLA: A meta-analysis. SSLA — cited for 'give feedback', not for 'force an immediate re-tap'.
Butler, A. C., & Roediger, H. L. (2008). Memory & Cognition, 36(3).

myths.myth: Perceptual disfluency as a desirable difficulty — degrade the sign rendering (blur, low contrast, an awkward typeface) to make recognition harder and memory better.
myths.why_wrong: The best-publicised instance failed in large, well-powered replications. A team that has absorbed 'desirable difficulties' will propose this; pre-empt it in the design doc. Distinguish retrieval difficulty (supported: spacing, testing, withholding the answer) from perceptual degradation (unsupported). Varying realistic typefaces is variability, not degradation — the two are different manipulations. Weathered or low-contrast treatments belong in the product only where they reflect signage a player will actually meet.
sources: Diemand-Yauman, C., Oppenheimer, D. M., & Vaughan, E. B. (2011). Fortune favors the bold (and the italicized). Cognition — the original claim.
Taylor, A., Sanson, M., Burnell, R., Wade, K. A., & Garry, M. (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties: The (lack of) effect of Sans Forgetica on memory. Memory, 28(7), 850–857.
Geller, J., Still, M. L., Dark, V. J., & Carpenter, S. K. (2018). Would disfluency by any other name still be beneficial? Memory & Cognition.

myths.myth: Learning styles; the 10,000-hour rule; the bizarreness effect; the method of loci as a product feature.
myths.why_wrong: The field's classic frauds. Notably, none of them appeared in this research — that absence is a decision worth protecting. Put an explicit exclusion list in the design document naming them as banned rationales, so nobody adds a 'visual learner' onboarding question or a memory-palace mode in six months. On bizarreness specifically: it requires mixed lists and within-subject manipulation, is absent in cued recall and unreliable in recognition — which is the app's test — so it should carry NO memory-design load, and the 'cap bizarre glosses at one in five' rule is invented precision policing an effect that does not appear on the outcome measure.
sources: Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D., & Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 9(3), 105–119.
Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science.
McDaniel, M. A., & Einstein, G. O. (1995). The bizarreness effect: It's not surprising, it's complex. JEP: LMC.

myths.myth: 'Study just before bed and you retain 20–30% more', and sleep-audio / targeted memory reactivation as a feature.
myths.why_wrong: The bedtime claim is folklore — the best adolescent study found afternoon training BEAT evening training at 24 hours and no difference at 7 days. TMR works in controlled lab conditions but is fragile, timing-sensitive, and can actively HARM memory in unsupervised home use: a subgroup gets worse, the app cannot detect sleep stage well enough to time cues, and the downside (disturbed sleep) falls on the user. Remove it from the backlog rather than parking it. Build no feature whose value depends on the SIZE of the sleep effect (no sleep score, no consolidation-window countdown, no bedtime-gated content) — the only robust consequence is ordinal: exposures should straddle nights.
sources: Targeted memory reactivation literature, home-use failure modes.
Schimke et al. (2024) — boundary conditions on sleep-dependent lexical competition.

myths.myth: 'PSTM explains ~30% of the variance in uptake.'
myths.why_wrong: Arithmetic error, threefold, in the sentence that spends engineering budget. r = .31 means r² ≈ .096 — roughly 9–10% of variance — and it is scoped to AUDITORY vocabulary acquisition, of unknown magnitude for orthographic learning in a logographic script. The design rule (audio optional, never gating, never scored) survives, but as cheap insurance against a ~10% effect in an adjacent task.
sources: Kurita, K. (2026). Revisiting the effects of phonological short-term memory on second language vocabulary acquisition: A meta-analysis. ITL. https://doi.org/10.1075/itl.25009.kur — 52 effect sizes, 18 studies, r = .31 [.21,.41].

myths.myth: 'The self-reference effect is large (d ≈ 0.65 vs semantic encoding).'
myths.why_wrong: The figure does not match the meta-analysis, which reports a mean weighted d around 0.50 across 129 studies of trait-adjective lists with undergraduates at short intervals — and the effect is SMALLER for self-vs-other than for self-vs-semantic, so the larger number was attached to the comparison that yields the smaller one. The SRE has never been tested on L2 orthographic learning. Grade moderate. The cheap application (frame items as second-person scenarios — 'you're holding a bag of oranges, the label says 5.80/斤') is proportionate and should stand; do not build a personalisation engine on it.
sources: Symons, C. S., & Johnson, B. T. (1997). The self-reference effect in memory: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin, 121(3), 371–394. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9136641/

myths.myth: 'Deliberate vocabulary study is three to four times more efficient than incidental learning.'
myths.why_wrong: The multiplier is manufactured by dividing across two meta-analyses that share no design, no time-on-task control, and no common outcome measure — a ratio of two unrelated denominators. The direction (deliberate beats incidental per unit time) is well supported; the number is not a finding. Also drop the adjacent 'do not build a comprehensible-input mode and expect it to compete' — input-based reading has its own meta-analytic support at small-to-moderate effects and is complementary, not competing. What is genuinely unsupported is the STRONG input hypothesis, which nobody in this evidence base actually asserts.
sources: Webb, Yanagisawa & Uchihara (2020) and the incidental-learning meta-analyses — the two denominators being divided.
Nakanishi, T. (2015). TESOL Quarterly; Jeon & Day (2016).

myths.myth: 'Treat any gamification number below g ≈ 0.4 as noise.'
myths.why_wrong: An invented decision rule with no source, and backwards as a bias heuristic. Effect magnitude is not a bias diagnostic: publication bias inflates estimates regardless of where they land, and small-study effects make LARGE published estimates from small-k literatures the most suspect. A g = 0.30 from a large preregistered trial is stronger evidence than a g = 0.50 from k = 9 underpowered studies. The rule would discard the better evidence and keep the worse. Replace with a provenance rule: weight by design, preregistration, sample size and k.
sources: Sailer, M., & Homner, L. (2020). The gamification of learning: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review — the k=19 cognitive-outcome set from which the 'narrative not points' moderator claim was over-read.

myths.myth: Invented constants that reached spec-level language and must be struck or relabelled as product defaults: a ~1.5–2 s anticipation beat; 'at least THREE typefaces per word'; 'suppress the mnemonic from exposure 3'; 'retire an item after 4 successful retrievals'; '≥3 renderings before an item may be marked consolidated'; 'at most FOUR chunks on the resolution screen'; 'cap bizarre glosses at one in five'; 'you can now read ~40% of what's on the wall'.
myths.why_wrong: No cited source specifies any of these numbers. The last one is wrong twice over: the ~40%/top-100 coverage figure comes from general running text whose top ranks are function morphemes absent from signage (的, 一, 是, 了, 不, 在), and token coverage is not sign comprehension — on a four-character sign, 40% token coverage means essentially zero complete signs readable. Report instead what the user can verify: 'you can read 47 of the 120 signs in the metro set.' The 'retire after 4' rule specifically INVERTS its cited source, whose point is that the durable plateau scales with total training.
sources: Bahrick, H. P. (1984). JEP: General, 113(1), 1–29.
Pelzl, E. (2025). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 32, 2090–2103 — single session, no delay, effects of one-to-two words.

myths.myth: fMRI of expert Chinese readers justifies the layout of the component-breakdown panel; and 'the neuroscience says VARIABILITY is the active ingredient' in the sign rendering.
myths.why_wrong: The second sentence is false as stated: the study invoked is longitudinal fMRI of ten six-year-olds learning an alphabetic script, with no manipulation of training variability, no learning outcome, no L2 learners and no adults. The first is an ALE meta-analysis of where blood flow changes in native readers, which cannot adjudicate between two layouts in a learning app and has a contested interpretive step in the middle. In both cases the RECOMMENDATION survives and the justification should be deleted — which is the healthiest possible outcome, and worth saying plainly: none of these UI decisions was ever derived from neuroscience; they were derived first and decorated afterwards. The behavioural rationale for a spatial breakdown is already available: component POSITION is part of what CSL learners must acquire, and positional regularity is acquired implicitly from distributional exposure.
sources: Dehaene-Lambertz, G., Monzalvo, K., & Dehaene, S. (2018). PLOS Biology, 16(3), e2004103.
Wu, C.-Y., Ho, M.-H. R., & Chen, S.-H. A. (2012). NeuroImage, 63(1), 381–391.
Zhang et al. (2021) on positional regularity in CSL learners — the correct, behavioural citation.
Tamminen, J. et al. (2010). Journal of Neuroscience, 30(43), 14356–14360 — sleep spindles, which justify a logging decision the behavioural dissociation already justifies completely.

myths.myth: Citation and grading defects to fix before this reaches a build spec.
myths.why_wrong: Four that matter. (1) The hypercorrection persistence result at Psychonomic Bulletin & Review 18, 1238–1244 is Butler, Fazio & Marsh (2011), NOT Metcalfe & Finn. (2) The recognition null for environmental context is Godden & Baddeley (1980), NOT Smith, Glenberg & Bjork (1978). (3) Kang & Pashler (2012) is Applied Cognitive Psychology 26(1), 97–103; the DOI prefix used points at Memory & Cognition — a reader following the link verifies a different paper. (4) The chunking arithmetic attributed to an unauthored ResearchGate item is Cao et al. (2013), Journal of Neurolinguistics 26(4), 440–461 — which is also the only Chinese-specific training study in this entire evidence base with a three-month follow-up, cited for its numbers while its result went unread. Also: Osgood's 1949 transfer surface was graded 'strong' from a lecturer's course webpage; it is a historical schematic whose response-similarity predictions did not survive the 1960s transfer literature — grade weak.
sources: Butler, A. C., Fazio, L. K., & Marsh, E. J. (2011). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 18, 1238–1244.
Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1980). British Journal of Psychology, 71(1), 99–104.
Kang, S. H. K., & Pashler, H. (2012). Applied Cognitive Psychology, 26(1), 97–103.
Cao, F. et al. (2013). Journal of Neurolinguistics, 26(4), 440–461.

myths.myth: Material-type honesty: six-plus findings were labelled in ways that flatter their ecological validity, always in the direction of the design decision they carried.
myths.why_wrong: Corrected labels, for propagation: Little et al. (2012) → lab-PROSE with a short filled delay, not lab-wordlist; Bisra et al. (2018) → classroom/instructional; the prequestion meta-analysis → classroom/instructional; Chen et al. (2018) → classroom/instructional, high element interactivity; Gruber et al. (2014) → lab trivia + faces; Pelzl (2025) → lab-logographic, single session; Brunmair & Richter (2019) → lab category learning, NOT 'both'; Ishii (2015) → L2-learner population but a 20-MINUTE lab interval, so lab not classroom; Kemp (2021) → L2-learner, lab-factorial with delayed test; Thomas & Wang (1996), Wang & Thomas (1992), van Hell & Mahn (1997) → lab L2 paired associates with a retention ceiling of ≤1 week, NOT classroom; Macedonia gesture work → artificial constructed corpus, not natural L2; the chunking arithmetic → a corpus statistic, not a memory finding at all. Add a `retention_interval` field per finding: material_type alone cannot carry this. On the reweighting, only a handful of items survive as genuine classroom/real-L2 evidence at real intervals — Bahrick, Nakata & Suzuki, Kemp, Kim & Webb — and the verdicts should be visibly weighted toward those.
sources: Adversarial re-labelling verified against each study's own description in the source material.

verdicts_on_design.decision: Decision 1 — 'The bet is how much scaffolding you give up' (+1/-1 shows pinyin and English options; +5/-3 removes pinyin; +15/-10 makes all four options Chinese signs).
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: As a MEMORY mechanic the wager has no support. Forcing a metacognitive judgement before answering does not reliably improve learning; confidence-weighted / certainty-based marking improves measurement reliability and how learners feel, and nothing else. There is also no controlled experiment on FADING pinyin at all — the scaffolding ladder itself is an untested design.
