As specified the design buys both and budgets neither — the phonology findings mandate an audio table keyed (item_id, talker_id) with several talkers pre-cached for offline play, which at ~900 items × 5 talkers × ~30 KB Opus is roughly 135 MB on top of ~900 photographs at two resolutions, into a PWA cache, offline, in China. If audio ships, make the task identification ('which of these four is it?'), never same-or-different, and treat talker count as an untested parameter (≥2, not '4-6'). Real signage carries no pinyin and no audio.
directives.basis: Storage arithmetic over the design's own stated asset requirements. Roughly a quarter of the L1 sweep's findings are phonology applied to a product it defines as reading-only against signage that carries neither channel.

directives.directive: Put the photograph on the reveal side only, never co-present with the hanzi on the prompt side, and do not mandate one. Co-presenting a highly salient image with an orthographic form risks cue overshadowing — the learner encodes the picture-meaning association and never processes the character form, producing knowledge that fails at a transfer target with no picture, which compounds the documented L2 Chinese tendency to discriminate characters by partial holistic visual features. Add picturable: bool and allow text-only items: a large share of the signage domain is not picturable (禁止, 请勿, 优惠, 注意, 小心, 免费, 营业中, 暂停服务), and for those a photo OF THE SIGN turns the task into photo-to-photo matching, which inflates in-app scores and does not transfer. Also treat in-situ photographs of Chinese menus and shopfronts as third-party copyrighted works frequently containing identifiable people and trademarks — a legal review item BEFORE content authoring, not after.
directives.basis: Cue competition/overshadowing is a hypothesis to instrument, not a settled result for this task. But it directly qualifies the 'image_url non-null' mandate, and the picturable split and the copyright point are cheap and unambiguous either way.

directives.directive: Set answer targets at 48 CSS px minimum with at least 8px spacing — which the 40px-minimum type size for options forces anyway, so the cost is zero — and put the four options in the bottom half of the screen in a 2×2 grid with the hanzi hero element up top where nothing is tapped. The binding constraint for a phone handed around a table under time pressure is the thumb reach arc, not the target minimum. Cite WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (24×24 CSS px, AA) as the floor for non-critical chrome and SC 2.5.5 (44×44, AAA) as the convention; stop repeating '44px' as though it were evidence — the empirical thumb literature points to roughly 9-10 mm. The mini-programme template's deliberately small tap regions violate any target guidance: that is defensible because small targets ARE the difficulty being taught, but document it as a deliberate exception with a non-timed accessible alternative.
directives.basis: The three cited 'standards' disagree by nearly 2× (Apple 44 pt, Material 48 dp, WCAG 24 CSS px AA / 44 AAA), which is itself evidence that none is an empirical result. Mis-taps on confusable-character answers corrupt exactly the telemetry the A/B tests depend on.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 1. The bet is how much scaffolding you give up: +1/-1 shows pinyin and English options; +5/-3 removes pinyin; +15/-10 also makes all four options Chinese signs.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The ladder is upside down as a learning design, and the rungs are wrong in different ways. (a) STRUCTURAL: the +15/-10 tier — four plausible Chinese signs, no pinyin — is the tier that actually teaches. Multiple choice with competitive, plausible alternatives produces retention benefits for the tested item AND for information related to the incorrect alternatives, because the learner must retrieve evidence about why each wrong option is wrong; easy distractors lose this entirely. And under transfer-appropriate processing, reading a sign in the wild IS constrained recognition against the small set of things that sign could plausibly say, so the all-Chinese tier is the criterion task, not a hard mode. The design therefore puts the best learning behind the largest penalty, so players select against it exactly when they need it, and the mechanic will systematically starve them of the format that works. (b) THE LOW RUNG: the +1/-1 tier gives pinyin AND L1 options, which makes it a translation-recognition task, not a reading task — and the specific claim that pinyin actively harms reading is NOT established (that inference rests on a handwriting study that never ran the contrast; see contested #2). So the objection to the pinyin rung is 'it does not build the target representation and there is a better scaffold available', not 'it is harmful'. (c) A confound nobody named: the four-option format has a 25% guess floor, so the score the bet is denominated in overestimates real reading.
verdicts_on_design.change: Decouple the stake from the scaffolding. Keep betting as a social/score mechanic, but make the item format a function of the SCHEDULER (what the player needs), not of the wager. If scaffolding must ladder with the bet, change what each rung buys: low tier = a semantic-component hint (the radical rendered in the accent colour with one line of gloss — '⺼ = body part, so this is something off an animal') plus object context; mid tier = no hint; high tier = all four options in Chinese. Never let pinyin be the thing the bet buys — put pinyin as small secondary text on the REVEAL only, per-character aligned beneath each glyph. Ship the pinyin-to-component scaffold swap as a flagged A/B, graded weak, not as an evidence-backed decision. And guarantee the all-Chinese format appears regardless of betting behaviour — e.g. reserve a fixed share of rounds at that format independent of the wager.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 2. Items render as the physical object they appear on — station plate, printed menu section with prices, shopfront fascia, shelf-edge price label, hazard board — with two treatments deliberately hard to read because real ones are.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Unsupported as a MEMORY intervention, defensible for other reasons, and carrying a documented risk the design does not currently mitigate. The memory case is weak: environmental context-dependent memory is reliable but modest, is attenuated or eliminated by outshining when strong semantic cues exist, and Godden & Baddeley found a substantial context effect for free recall (1975) and essentially none for recognition (1980) — and this product is recognition throughout. The risk is real: Masonheimer, Drum & Ehri (1984, n=102) found that confident environmental-print 'reading' is driven by the whole visual gestalt rather than the letters, and did not predict decontextualised word reading, so a learner who has only met 出口 in enamel-blue metro styling may be recognising the plate and may fail on 出 in 出发, 出租, 出售, 支出. What DOES survive: typeface class is the part that genuinely varies in the wild, CTW's annotation schema needs a dedicated 'wordart' class for decorative lettering because display typography is prevalent in real street-view Chinese text, and the deliberately-hard treatments are honest to that. So the templates earn their place through typographic robustness, motivation and object recognition — not through context reinstatement.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the five CSS-only templates and refuse feature requests for photographic backgrounds, perspective warps and per-city styling variants — spend that budget on correct typeface class per object instead. Then force transfer: contexts: Set<TemplateId> on the mastery record with graduation gated on contexts.size >= 3; a naked probe (character alone, system serif, plain ground) at 10-15% of presentations; a wrong-object probe; and an Xepsi-style foil (a near-identical wrong character in the correct object styling). Surface the diagnostic: if naked-probe accuracy trails in-object accuracy by more than ~20 points, the app is teaching plates. Instrument the object-vs-plain A/B from v1 — this is the most expensive part of the design and the evidence is genuinely contested. Also add MORE typeface variation within the fascia template (including traditional variants), not less.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 3a. The component breakdown is the main teaching surface, promoted to the body of the reveal, advanced only by an explicit tap.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Placing it on the REVEAL, behind a tap, is exactly right and is the resolution of an apparent contradiction in the literature. Explicit radical instruction works as content: a three-week course covering orthographic knowledge plus ≥7 radicals per week produced gains in phonetic-radical awareness, semantic-radical awareness and orthographic knowledge, and learners transferred the strategy to infer meanings of UNTAUGHT characters containing untaught semantic radicals. But decorating the glyph with component cues AT RECOGNITION TIME hurts: radical colour markings increased reaction times and decreased accuracy, and stroke animations decreased accuracy. Teaching the system as content works; annotating the character during a timed recognition round does not. A tap-gated reveal surface is on the right side of that line. For this product's specific bank the component story is also unusually favourable — far better than the general frequency-band statistics suggest — because the survival set is semantically clustered: 火/灬 is the radical of 9 of the 13 core cooking methods, ⺼ carries the organ set, 饣 carries 43 food characters.
verdicts_on_design.change: Two required qualifications. (1) It cannot be the main surface for the EARLY general bank: ~47% of the top 1,000 characters are pictographs or ideographs with no meaning+sound decomposition, and only ~31% of the top 1,000 (13% of the top 100) is both left-right and phonetic. Ship a non-compositional path — pictographic/ideographic origin, or an explicit 'no useful decomposition, learn this whole' state — and an isCompositional flag (出口 yes; 保质期, 时价, 招牌, 方便面 no), with a progress display that reports the split honestly: 'you can work out 61 of these; 44 you have to memorise'. (2) Never colour components inside the glyph on a timed card; keep it to the reveal and the lesson. Also: any decomposition story needs a provenance flag ('etymological' vs 'memory aid only') labelled in the UI — repeating Chineasy-style false etymologies is a known reputational liability.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 3b. The specific worked example: 牛肉 comes apart into 牛 ox + 肉 meat; swap the head for 猪肉/羊肉/鸡肉/鸭肉; then the unlock — 肉 flattens to 月 on the left of a character, so 肝 liver, 肠 intestine, 肚 tripe, 腰 kidney, 脑 brain.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The unlock names the wrong character, and it fails silently. The component in 肝 肠 肚 腰 脑 (and 肺 肾 胗) is ⺼, U+2EBC, Kangxi radical 130 MEAT — not 月, U+6708, the moon character. They are homoglyphs in almost every font and different codepoints. I verified this independently this session against makemeahanzi: all eight organ characters carry radical ⺼ U+2EBC, while 期 and 朋 carry 月 U+6708. So a string match or regex on 月 to apply the accent colour highlights ZERO of the five characters in the example and fires instead on 期 — which sits inside 保质期, a Tier-1 supermarket item. The rule as stated would teach that the shelf-life label contains a body part. The prose gloss is also loose: 肉 does not 'flatten to 月', it has a distinct bound form; and even a correct 'meat' gloss misfires on 期 朗 服 有 望, where the component is the moon or a graphic merger.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the card — it is the best pedagogical idea in the whole corpus and the clearest demonstration that Chinese characters are composed rather than memorised — but fix three things. (1) Teach the component as ⺼ (U+2EBC) and key highlighting off a stored per-item component field or a decomposition database, never off a substring match on 月. (2) Correct the exception list: 血, 皮 and 舌 do NOT carry it; 筋 carries it inside 肋 but takes ⺮ (bamboo) as its Kangxi radical. (3) The 牛肉 → 猪肉/羊肉/鸡肉/鸭肉 head-swap half of the example is clean and should stay as-is. Extend the same pattern to the two other high-yield clusters this bank actually has: 火/灬 across 炒 炸 烤 煮 焖 炖 烧 煎, and 饣 across 饭 饿 馆 饺 饼 饮.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 4. A confusable is shown beside the target on resolution: 入口 beside 出口, 公斤 beside 斤, 麻 beside 辣.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Supported, and it is also mandatory for a different reason the design did not state. Simultaneous PAIRED presentation improved discrimination of subtle stroke differences in absolute beginners with non-tonal L1s (N=183), and characters differing by an added stroke were easier than identical-stroke pairs — so pairing is the right introduction format for visual confusables. Independently, it is the required mitigation for the multiple-choice lure effect: taking a multiple-choice test increases later production of the LURES as answers, and the risk is maximal exactly under a visual-first distractor rule, with immediate corrective feedback the established fix. Showing the confusable beside the target on resolution does both jobs at once.
verdicts_on_design.change: Three scope corrections. (1) The three chosen examples are not the same kind of confusable and the cited mechanism only covers one of them. 入口/出口 is a form-and-meaning antonym pair (the strongest case). 公斤/斤 is an arithmetic/semantic trap with no form similarity — justified by consequence, not by the discrimination literature. 麻/辣 is a semantic contrast with no form similarity at all. Do not present all three as instances of one principle; tag the confusion FAMILY per pair (visual / antonym / arithmetic-trap / same-first-character) so the reveal copy can differ. (2) Pairing pays off only if the distinguishing component is given MEANING — a purely structural breakdown is not enough — so each pair needs a one-clause discriminator, not just adjacency. (3) One confusable is not enough: show ALL FOUR options glossed in a four-row table with hanzi ≥32px, pinyin, English and Dutch, and a note on where you would meet each ('冷冻 = vriezer, staat op diepvriesproducten — niet hetzelfde als 冷藏'), with wrong rows fully legible. The highest-value pairs from this cluster's own content: 出口/入口, 推/拉, 冷藏/冷冻, 生产日期/保质期, 禁止/请勿, 男/女, 素/荤, 硬座/软卧, 去结算/取消, 提交订单/加入购物车, plus the pure visual set 人/入, 日/白, 千/干, 未/末, 出/山, 天/夭, 士/土, 己/已.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 5a. Tone colour never sits on the character.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Correct, and it is the corollary the research never stated out loud even though its own findings force it. Radical colour markings on the glyph increased reaction times and decreased accuracy in L2 character recognition; colour coding independently slowed reaction times in a 2×2×2 study of 183 absolute beginners, interpreted as visual overload. Tone colouring of characters — the default in most competing Mandarin apps — falls squarely on the wrong side of that rule. Making the ban explicit matters, because a designer will otherwise reintroduce it as an industry norm.
verdicts_on_design.change: State the ban explicitly in the design system, not just in the tone section, and extend it: hanzi render as a single solid ink colour on a plain ground during any timed recognition round, with colour reserved for scoring and turn state. Component colour is permitted only in the lesson and the reveal.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 5b. Tone colour sits on the pinyin.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: No controlled trial of Mandarin tone colour coding could be located at all, and the schemes in the wild are mutually incompatible across Pleco, Hanping, Skritter and Dong Chinese — which is itself evidence the practice is convention, not result. It has two further problems specific to this product. Accessibility: the common four-tone palettes are red/green/blue/purple, red-green is the failing pair for ~8% of males, and colour must never be the sole carrier of a distinction (WCAG 1.4.1). Transfer: real signage carries no colour-coded tone, so the cue is guaranteed absent at the criterion task. And for a reading-only product the prior question is whether tone belongs on the card at all — see the unresolved scope call about the audio channel.
verdicts_on_design.change: If tone is displayed, carry it redundantly in shape or number as well as colour, never colour alone — and prefer a contour glyph with the turning point marked over a colour swatch, since the turning point is the cue non-tonal-L1 learners actually fail to use. Do not treat pinyin tone colour as a teaching device; it is at best a lookup convenience. Render surface (post-sandhi) tone whenever audio plays, because 水饺, 米粉, 老板, 一个 and 不要 all display a tone the recording does not contain — showing citation pinyin beside natural audio trains the exact T2/T3 confusion the tone design exists to prevent. The separable segments/tone data model is the genuinely useful half of the original recommendation and should be kept independently of any colour decision.

cluster: interface-social (sweeps: uiux + gbl-multiplayer). ACCESS CAVEAT THAT SCOPES EVERY LINE BELOW: across this cluster's two sweeps and their two critiques, exactly ONE paper was read in full text (Parhi, Karlson & Bederson 2006, via microsoft.com). The uiux sweep read search-engine abstract summaries only; the gbl-multiplayer sweep fetched nothing at all and is entirely recalled from prior knowledge (its own gaps note: "Zero of the required ten distinct searches were performed"). Both adversarial critiques had WebSearch exhausted (200/200) and all scholarly hosts egress-blocked, so neither could verify a single citation; they audited arithmetic, units, internal consistency and Chinese-language content instead — and that found more than a citation sweep would have. No effect size here has been checked against a results section. Treat directions as usable, magnitudes as provisional, and re-verify the top ~10 sources before any number enters a spec.

settled.claim: CSS px do not convert to millimetres at 96/inch on a phone. Phones render ~160 CSS px per physical inch (Android dp = 1/160in; iOS pt ≈ 1/163in), i.e. ~6.3 CSS px/mm. Every physical and angular figure in the original uiux sweep was off by ~1.67x, in the unsafe direction.
settled.scope: Arithmetic/standards fact, recomputed in-session; not an empirical study. Repaired numbers assume a 360 mm viewing distance (Bababekova & Rosenfield mean 36.2 ± 7.1 cm for phone text; Lan 33.95 ± 5.9; Boccardo 36.1 ± 7.2).
sources: CSS Values and Units Level 4 §6.2 (1in = 96px is a fixed ratio, explicitly not physical) | https://www.w3.org/TR/css-values-4/
Android developer docs: 1 dp = 1 px at 160 dpi baseline | no URL captured
Apple iOS HIG: pt anchored to the original 163 ppi display | no URL captured

Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB (2006). Target Size Study for One-Handed Thumb Use on Small Touchscreen Devices. MobileHCI '06 | https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/parhi-mobileHCI06.pdf (the one full-text read in this cluster)
settled.implication: Repaired floors: 42 arcmin preferred size = ~28 CSS px (not 17); tested 12pt running text = ~27 CSS px (not 16-17); Parhi's 9.2 mm discrete-tap floor = 58 CSS px; Conradi's walking-safe 14 mm = 88 CSS px. Never use CSS mm/in/pt for physical sizing. Every hard size in the design doc must be regenerated from 6.3 CSS px/mm.

settled.claim: Positive polarity (dark text on light ground) is more legible than negative, and the advantage grows as characters shrink — but the mechanism is pupil contraction, so it is ambient-light dependent, and the criterion environments here are a dim restaurant and a night metro platform.
settled.scope: Downgraded from 'strong' by the critique: the polarity corpus is bright-office LCD proofreading work with no ambient-illumination moderator. The Chinese-specific arm (Dobres, glance-based legibility) is a different paradigm from the Latin proofreading arm.
sources: Piepenbrock C, Mayr S, Buchner A (2014). Positive Display Polarity Is Particularly Advantageous for Small Character Sizes. Human Factors 56(5) | https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0018720813515509
Piepenbrock, Mayr & Buchner (2013). Ergonomics | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23654206/

Dobres J, Chahine N, Reimer B, Gould D, Zhao N (2016). Effects of Chinese typeface design, stroke weight and contrast polarity on glance-based legibility. Displays 41:42-49 | https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/ffe6fa4b5e0082e6
settled.implication: Ship light as the default but honour prefers-color-scheme rather than forcing it; treat dark as a first-class path (+15% hanzi size, weight 400→500). Do not use the red-tinted dark ground the sweep proposed (#1F0F0F) — it collides with red error feedback; use a neutral/blue-shifted grey and raise the target-character foreground to ≈9:1 (#B8B8B8-class) while leaving chrome dimmer. The 6.11:1 arithmetic for #949494 on #1F0F0F was verified correct but is thin for stroke-level discrimination by a learner.

settled.claim: A Hei/gothic face at bold weight in positive contrast is the most legible on-screen Chinese; Ming/Song is the least. No study exists testing whether any typeface aids acquisition of character FORM by learners.
settled.scope: All typeface evidence is legibility for native readers. The teaching folklore that Kai is better for learners because it shows stroke shape has no controlled test that could be located. One countervailing result: Ming beat Hei on a traditional-Chinese phone study at 10pt only.
sources: Dobres et al. (2016). Displays 41:42-49 | https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/ffe6fa4b5e0082e6
Huang S-M (2019). Effects of font size and font style of Traditional Chinese characters on readability on smartphones. IJIE | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0169814118300416
Text Readability of Smartphone in Dark Mode (HCII 2023, LNCS, n=40) | https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-031-34866-2_2
settled.implication: Hei for the prompt the learner must discriminate. But see the variability finding: legibility and transfer pull apart here, and the resolution is to vary the face across repeated exposures, not to soften the prompt face.

settled.claim: Training every item in one clean typeface under-produces transfer to real signage. Perceptual VARIABILITY (multiple fully legible exemplars) is the supported manipulation; perceptual DISFLUENCY (degrading legibility to add difficulty) is a documented failure.
settled.scope: Variability: the principle is established in category learning generally (Schmidt & Bjork 1992; Gómez 2002; Kornell & Bjork 2008), NOT tested in hanzi acquisition — flagged as a risk-plus-cheap-fix, not a finding. Disfluency: graded folklore/strong-negative by three separate agents across both workflows.
sources: Schmidt RA, Bjork RA (1992). New conceptualizations of practice. Psychological Science | no resolvable URL (unverified)
Kornell N, Bjork RA (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the enemy of induction? Psychological Science 19(6):585-592 | no resolvable URL (unverified)
Taylor A, Sanson M, Burnell R, Wade KA, Garry M (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties (Sans Forgetica, 4 experiments). Memory 28(7) | no resolvable URL (unverified)
Meyer A, Frederick S, et al. (2015). Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems. JEP: General | no resolvable URL (unverified)
settled.implication: Render each item across ≥3 fully legible faces (a Hei, a Song/serif, a display or hand-painted form), rotating across repetitions, plus ≥1 photographed real instance per high-value item; store a render_variant field on the attempt record so variability can be measured. Keep every rendering at WCAG AA contrast. This is the legitimate version of 'make it hard'.

settled.claim: Colour is the wrong channel for linguistic information in this product, on three converging grounds: colour-coding visually similar hanzi slowed learners down; radical markings inside a character raised RT and lowered accuracy; and a cue present in training but absent at test produced the worst retention and transfer of any condition.
settled.scope: Li & Shi (2025): n=183 zero-experience non-tonal-L1 learners, 2x2x2, colour slowed RT (interpreted as visual overload). Hou & Jiang (2022): n=40 alphabetic-L1 L2 learners; effect on character RECOGNITION only, not meaning-matching; stroke-order animations also lowered recognition accuracy. Skulmowski (2022): n=125 and n=107, anatomical visualisation — transfer-by-analogy to hanzi, not a hanzi study.
sources: Li & Shi et al. (2025). Learning Chinese Characters of Visual Similarity: Presentation Style and Color Coding. Languages 10(10):260 | https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/10/10/260

Hou F, Jiang X (2022). Interference effects of radical markings and stroke order animations. Frontiers in Psychology 13:783613 | https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.783613/full
Skulmowski A (2022). When color coding backfires: a guidance reversal effect. Education and Information Technologies 27:3963-3985 | https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-021-10796-6
settled.implication: No tint, highlight, outline or coloured sub-glyph region on any hanzi, ever, anywhere. No stroke-order animation in the answering loop. Colour is reserved for interface chrome (correct/incorrect, player identity, progress). The transfer environment — a metro plate, a menu — carries no cues, so any cue you add in training is the exact configuration that scored worst.

settled.claim: The decisive argument against linguistic colour is legal and accessibility-based, not evidentiary. WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Colour, Level A) prohibits colour as the sole carrier of information; the European Accessibility Act became applicable 28 June 2025 and applies EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA to consumer digital services; congenital red-green CVD affects ~8% of males and ~0.5% of females of Northern European ancestry — i.e. the Dutch user base.
settled.scope: Standards and epidemiology, not experiment. Binding force depends on distribution channel (public-sector/educational distribution makes it hardest), but it settles the argument regardless of how the Godfroid and Skulmowski readings come out.
sources: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act), applicable from 28 June 2025 | no URL captured
EN 301 549 v3.2.1 incorporating WCAG 2.1 AA | no URL captured

Nederlandse overheid: Tijdelijk besluit digitale toegankelijkheid overheid | no URL captured
settled.implication: Four requirements the sweep never mentioned: lang="zh-Hans" on every hanzi (so VoiceOver/TalkBack pick a Mandarin voice) and lang="nl"/"en" on glosses; rem-relative sizing that survives 200% OS text scaling (a single 1.25x in-app toggle does NOT discharge SC 1.4.4); layout tolerant of SC 1.4.12 text-spacing overrides; and an accessible escape from the per-item deadline under SC 2.2.1.

settled.claim: Three options are optimal for multiple choice — more items per unit of time with no loss of score quality — but only if the retained options are the effective ones. Random removal of options reduces difficulty, discrimination and reliability. Independently, MC accuracy falls as the number of alternatives rises, and the negative suggestion effect scales with the number of plausible lures.
settled.scope: Rodriguez (2005): random-effects meta-analysis over 80 years of research, general educational measurement, not L2 or hanzi. The alternatives-count effect on accuracy is from Roediger & Marsh (2005), prose passages, English.
sources: Rodriguez MC (2005). Three Options Are Optimal for Multiple-Choice Items. Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2):3-13 | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1745-3992.2005.00006.x

Roediger HL III, Marsh EJ (2005). The Positive and Negative Consequences of Multiple-Choice Testing. JEP:LMC 31(5):1155-1159 | http://psychnet.wustl.edu/memory/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Roediger-Marsh-2005_JEPLMC.pdf
settled.implication: The inherited four-option format should become three. It buys more items per round, lets each option be a full-width 60-64 CSS px row in the thumb zone, and reduces lure exposure — three benefits from one change. The third option must be a real competitor from the visual-neighbour or situational list, never filler.

settled.claim: The negative suggestion effect is real, small and quantified: MC lures were produced on 5% of questions when not previously tested, rising to 12% a week after testing. Feedback is the fix — both immediate and delayed feedback raise correct responses and cut lure intrusions, and the two timings are equally effective at cutting intrusions.
settled.scope: Roediger & Marsh (2005) and Butler & Roediger (2008): English prose passages, 1-week delay, university samples. Not hanzi, not months. Replicated in Marsh et al. (2007) and Butler & Roediger (2010).
sources: Roediger HL III, Marsh EJ (2005). JEP:LMC 31(5):1155-1159 | http://psychnet.wustl.edu/memory/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Roediger-Marsh-2005_JEPLMC.pdf

Marsh EJ, Roediger HL, Bjork RA, Bjork EL (2007). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review | https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03194051
settled.implication: Budget for ~7 percentage points of lure intrusion as the price of MC; the net effect is still positive. Feedback becomes mandatory on every item — non-negotiable, not a setting. Log every chosen-lure event as {itemId, lureId, timestamp} and force a corrective re-test within 24h. Do NOT adopt the sweep's two other mitigations (see myths).

settled.claim: Distractors that are orthographically or semantically close to the key raise both item difficulty and item discrimination; distractors mined from real learner errors are measurably more competitive than hand-written ones.
settled.scope: Ludewig et al. (2023) is synonym-based vocabulary testing in German schools, not hanzi. The error-mined-distractor work is ACM Learning@Scale 2025 engineering, not a controlled learning study.
sources: Ludewig U, Schwerter J, McElvany N (2023). The Features of Plausible but Incorrect Options. Journal of Psychoeducational Assessment 41(7):711-731 | https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/07342829231167892
Generating Competitive Distractors from Student Error Data. Proc. ACM Learning @ Scale (2025) | https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3698205.3733945
Generating Plausible Distractors via Student Choice Prediction (2025). arXiv:2501.13125 | https://arxiv.org/html/2501.13125v2
settled.implication: Two distinct generators, not one priority list. Priority 1 = visual neighbours from component decomposition / stroke-edit distance (大/太/犬/夫, 人/入/八, 日/白/百/自, 未/末, 己/已/巳, 千/干/于, 我/找, 天/夭). Priority 2 = situational neighbours from the domain corpus for that scene (药店/酒店/饭店/书店, 入口/出口, 男/女). The sweep's flagship example was wrong: 药店 and 酒店 share NO component (艹+约 vs 氵+酉) — they are priority 2, and an implementer following the original spec builds the wrong generator.

settled.claim: 9.2 mm is the empirical minimum comfortable touch target for one-handed thumb use (error rate stops improving above 9.6 mm for discrete taps); 14 mm is needed for use while walking. In CSS px on a phone that is 58, 60 and 88 respectively.
settled.scope: Parhi (2006): n=20 right-handed, 5 target sizes x 9 locations x 5 reps, one-handed — the only full-text-read paper in this cluster. Conradi (2015): 5/8/11/14 mm squares, standing vs walking. Both physical-unit studies; the CSS conversion is this cluster's correction.
sources: Parhi P, Karlson AK, Bederson BB (2006). MobileHCI '06 | https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2006/01/parhi-mobileHCI06.pdf

Conradi J, Busch O, Alexander T (2015). Optimal Touch Button Size for the use of Mobile Devices while Walking. Procedia Manufacturing | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2351978915001833
W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 (AA, 24x24 CSS px) and SC 2.5.5 (AAA, 44x44 CSS px) | https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
settled.implication: Answer rows at 60-64 CSS px height, full content width, 8px gap — this clears Parhi and WCAG AAA simultaneously. Minimum interactive height 56-60 CSS px anywhere. A street/walking mode needs ~88 CSS px. Keep destructive controls (skip, quit, end game) ≥24 px away from any answer option.

settled.claim: The thumb's reachable area is a predictable function of device size and grip, so the bottom ~45% of the viewport is where timed taps belong; the prompt, which is looked at and not tapped, is unconstrained by reach.
settled.scope: Bergstrom-Lehtovirta & Oulasvirta (2014): n=20, model-fitting on thumb kinematics, not an outcome experiment. Refined for arbitrary form factors by CHI 2024 work.
sources: Bergstrom-Lehtovirta J, Oulasvirta A (2014). Modeling the functional area of the thumb on mobile touchscreen surfaces. CHI '14 | https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/2556288.2557354
Grip-Reach-Touch-Repeat. CHI 2024 | https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3613904.3642022
settled.implication: Options stacked full-width in the bottom 45%, sticky to bottom with env(safe-area-inset-bottom); nothing tappable-under-time in the top 25% or the top corners; the hanzi prompt in the upper-middle third.

settled.claim: Visual span for Chinese shrinks as character complexity rises, with the product of span size and complexity roughly invariant (~10 cycles at 1.2 deg). Complexity costs how many characters you take in per fixation — it does not license a per-character font-size formula.
settled.scope: Wang, He & Legge (2014), trigram visual-span method extended to Chinese; replicated across age groups (Vision 2019). The stroke-count-to-size compensation slope the sweep proposed was retracted: it rests on a 6-observer acuity-THRESHOLD study, and threshold-derived compensation does not transfer to suprathreshold display 5-10x above threshold.
sources: Wang H, He X, Legge GE (2014). Effect of pattern complexity on the visual span for Chinese and alphabet characters. Journal of Vision | https://jov.arvojournals.org/article.aspx?articleid=2194058
Aging and Pattern Complexity Effects on the Visual Span (2019). Vision 3(1):11 | https://doi.org/10.3390/vision3010011
Zhang J-Y, Zhang T, Xue F, Liu L, Yu C (2007). IOVS 48:2383-2390 (n=6, acuity threshold) | https://iovs.arvojournals.org/article.aspx?articleid=2164478
settled.implication: Spend the complexity variable on chunking and time budget, not on font-size arithmetic. Cap a single reading target at 6-8 hanzi for low-complexity items and 4-6 when mean stroke count exceeds 12; compute meanStrokes at build time and use it to pick the layout (>12 = one line, larger type, no gloss on the same line). Set one generous size safe for the most complex character in the bank and stop.

settled.claim: Vertical per-character alignment of pinyin (ruby) beats a horizontal row, which imposes split attention and hinders character learning for beginners — and there is an expertise reversal: PARTIAL on-screen pinyin beat both full pinyin and no pinyin for more experienced learners.
settled.scope: Lee & Kalyuga (2011), Language Learning — beginner-level, cognitive-load framing. Wang & Kalyuga (2010, CHB) supplies the expertise reversal. Neither is a phone study; ruby is this cluster's implementation reading of the split-attention result, not a replication.
sources: Lee CH, Kalyuga S (2011). Effectiveness of Different Pinyin Presentation Formats in Learning Chinese Characters. Language Learning 61(4):1099-1118 | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9922.2011.00666.x

Wang & Kalyuga. Effectiveness of on-screen pinyin in learning Chinese: an expertise reversal for multimedia redundancy. Computers in Human Behavior | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0747563210001251
settled.implication: This is the evidence that scaffolding should fade by measured expertise, not by a wager. Where pinyin appears at all: HTML ruby per character; full ruby for the first ~3 exposures, then PARTIAL ruby on only the characters that item's error history flags weak, then none. Store exposureCount and perCharacterErrorRate to drive it.

settled.claim: Competition has essentially no direct effect on performance: the pooled association is near zero because it activates performance-approach goals (which help) and performance-avoidance goals (which hurt), and the two cancel.
settled.scope: Murayama & Elliot (2012), Psychological Bulletin, very large base (~170+ studies). CRITICAL SCOPE, added by the critique: the opposing-processes model was tested by meta-analytic SEM over largely CORRELATIONAL cross-sectional studies in which goal endorsement was measured, not manipulated. The near-zero pooled r also masks high heterogeneity — 'zero on average' is compatible with real harm in identifiable subgroups.
sources: Murayama K, Elliot AJ (2012). The competition-performance relation: a meta-analytic review and test of the opposing processes model. Psychological Bulletin 138(6) | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: This licenses exactly one claim: competition is not automatically harmful, so the mechanic is not disqualified on its face. It does NOT license the product's actual bet — that UI copy can tip the sign. See contested.

settled.claim: Feedback is not reliably beneficial: across ~131 papers and ~607 effect sizes the mean is d ≈ 0.41 but roughly 38% of effect sizes are NEGATIVE, and the moderator is whether attention goes to the task or to the self. A public point loss with no task information attached is close to pure self-level feedback.
settled.scope: Kluger & DeNisi (1996) is organisational/educational, not L2 or games. Hattie & Timperley (2007) reach the same four-level conclusion but are the same research programme, not independent corroboration.
sources: Kluger AN, DeNisi A (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance. Psychological Bulletin 119(2):254-284 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Hattie J, Timperley H (2007). The power of feedback. Review of Educational Research 77(1):81-112 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: This is the single most damning result against 'the table watches you lose points'. Invert the emphasis: on a wrong answer the SHARED view carries the correct character and the correction at full size; the score change is a small, brief, uncoloured tick. Public task information, private self information.

settled.claim: Elaborated feedback > knowledge-of-correct-response > bare verification in computer-based learning (roughly d ≈ 0.49 / 0.32 / 0.05) — but the elaborated-feedback advantage is concentrated in HIGHER-ORDER outcomes and narrows sharply for the low-order recognition this product is scoped to.
settled.scope: Van der Kleij, Feskens & Eggen (2015), ~40 studies / ~70 effects, computer-based environments. The critique corrected two over-reads: d ≈ 0.05 is a between-feedback-TYPE contrast, not 'verification is worthless versus nothing' (retrieval-practice meta-analyses find the testing effect is LARGER with feedback, and most of that feedback is verification + correct answer); and the sweep quoted the pooled estimate while the moderator that most weakens its recommendation was available.
sources: Van der Kleij FM, Feskens RCW, Eggen TJHM (2015). Effects of feedback in a computer-based learning environment. Review of Educational Research | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Rowland CA (2014). Psychological Bulletin 140(6):1432-1463 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Always show the correct answer — KCR is cheap and well-supported. Make elaboration mandatory only where a discriminating cue genuinely exists (confusables, shared radicals, compound semantics). A universal fixed-length explanation on every item is an unvalidated product bet to A/B test, not an evidence-mandated requirement.

settled.claim: Errors followed by corrective feedback produce better retention than error-free study, and errors made with HIGH confidence are the most likely of all to be corrected — but both effects require the learner to have related knowledge to recruit.
settled.scope: Metcalfe (2017) review; Butterfield & Metcalfe (2001) hypercorrection. Critical scope added by the critique: for genuinely unknown, arbitrary cue-target pairs the errorful-generation evidence is mixed and can be neutral or harmful. A beginner shown an unseen hanzi has no generative basis — that is a blind guess, not a productive error.
sources: Metcalfe J (2017). Learning from errors. Annual Review of Psychology 68:465-489 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Butterfield B, Metcalfe J (2001). Errors committed with high confidence are hypercorrected. JEP:LMC 27 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: This is what rescues the public-failure mechanic — conditionally. The condition is a competence bound on what an opponent may deal, plus immediate unmissable task-focused correction. It also means the confusable-pair item type must be gated behind demonstrated familiarity with BOTH members of the pair, or a hypercorrection opportunity becomes a coin flip.

settled.claim: Being watched impairs accuracy on complex/novel tasks and slightly facilitates simple well-learned ones, but the average is tiny (0.3-3% of variance) — and that number describes a PASSIVE audience, not a stake-holding opponent who chose your item. The small average also hides opposite-signed subgroups.
settled.scope: Bond & Titus (1983): 241 studies, ~24,000 participants, passive audience or co-actors. Uziel (2007): direction flips by trait — high neuroticism / low self-esteem impaired, extraverts facilitated. The critique's correction is the load-bearing part: evaluation apprehension plus outcome interdependence is a different and plausibly larger manipulation, and hanzi recognition for a beginner is by definition a non-dominant response — the impairment side.
sources: Bond CF, Titus LJ (1983). Social facilitation: a meta-analysis of 241 studies. Psychological Bulletin 94(2):265-292 | https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/b0c7e392f24446279a65f30f8fb
Uziel L (2007). Individual differences in the social facilitation effect. Journal of Research in Personality 41(3):579-601 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)

Killing with Kindness: Spectator Presence and Tone in Competitive Video Games (2025). Proc. ACM HCI / CSCW, lab experiment n=85, racing game — SUPPORTIVE spectatorship was MORE detrimental than critical | https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3748598
settled.implication: Private input, public resolution is a v1 REQUIREMENT, not a nicety — the correction moves it up in priority, not down. Answers are entered on the answering player's own device; the shared view shows 'Player 2 is answering' plus a progress bar, never the live selection; no 'X got it right in 2.1s' banner. Never require a player to speak an answer aloud or hold up their screen. Reading, not speaking, is the target skill, so privacy costs nothing competitively.

settled.claim: It is LOSING, not competing, that undermines intrinsic motivation — and giving losers explicit competence feedback restores their motivation to levels comparable with winners. Pressure to win undermines motivation even among winners.
settled.scope: Reeve & Deci (1996) n≈100 and Vansteenkiste & Deci (2003): lab studies, ~100 undergraduates, non-language tasks. The SDT reward-undermining backdrop (Deci, Koestner & Ryan 1999) is genuinely contested — see contested — so justify by these two studies, not by treating undermining as established.
sources: Reeve J, Deci EL (1996). Elements of the competitive situation that affect intrinsic motivation. PSPB 22(1):24-33 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Vansteenkiste M, Deci EL (2003). Competitively contingent rewards and intrinsic motivation: can losers remain motivated? Motivation and Emotion 27:273-299 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: The end-of-match screen for EVERY player leads with an absolute competence statement before any relative one ('You read 23 characters correctly tonight. 6 were new'). Win/loss appears second and smaller. Award the same streak/credit for retrievals attempted regardless of match outcome — competence-contingent, never competition-contingent.

settled.claim: Competitive, publicly evaluated goal structures make ABILITY the salient explanation for the outcome, which harms low performers specifically; and bottom-position players on absolute whole-cohort leaderboards fare measurably worse on motivation and engagement than on near-peer relative ones.
settled.scope: Ames (1992) is seminal and theoretically central but its causal experiments are older, smaller and with children. Bai, Hew, Sailer & Jia (2021) is fully-online higher education, not co-located play. Hanus & Fox (2015) is small (n≈80) and confounded by section — a caution, not a result.
sources: Ames C (1992). Classrooms: goals, structures, and student motivation. Journal of Educational Psychology 84(3):261-271 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)

Bai S, Hew KF, Sailer M, Jia C (2021). From top to bottom: how positions on different types of leaderboard may affect learning performance. Computers & Education | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Hanus MD, Fox J (2015). Assessing the effects of gamification in the classroom: a longitudinal study. Computers & Education 80:152-161 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Ban from the shared interface: any per-player accuracy percentage visible to others, any persistent cross-match ranking of individuals, any 'weakest player' label, any live who-is-losing ordering during play. Show team totals only; the individual breakdown is private, on the player's own device, after the match. The only comparison a player sees about themselves is against their own prior state.

settled.claim: Foreign-language anxiety correlates about r = −0.34 to −0.39 with L2 achievement across three large independent syntheses (~97 samples, N ≈ 23,000 in the largest) — one of the most robust individual-difference findings in SLA. Enjoyment and anxiety are distinguishable dimensions (r ≈ −0.36), not opposite ends of one.
settled.scope: Correlational, overwhelmingly cross-sectional self-report with course grades as the outcome, so common-method variance inflates the pooled r. Causal direction is disputed (see contested). The magnitude is not in serious doubt.
sources: Teimouri Y, Goetze J, Plonsky L (2019). Second language anxiety and achievement: a meta-analysis. SSLA 41(2):363-387 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Botes E, Dewaele J-M, Greiff S (2020). The FLCAS and academic achievement. JPLL | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Dewaele J-M, MacIntyre PD (2014). The two faces of Janus? Anxiety and enjoyment in the foreign language classroom. SSLLT, n≈1,746 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Two hard consequences. (1) An anxiety-inducing mechanic is not a neutral design choice in a LANGUAGE product specifically — it operates on the largest measured affective moderator in the field. (2) 'Players report they had fun' is NOT evidence the mechanic is safe: enjoyment and anxiety are only moderately negatively correlated, so a session can be both. Never accept enjoyment or NPS as the safety signal.

settled.claim: Team scoring without identifiable individual contribution produces social loafing — and hiding contributions to protect against ability attributions is in DIRECT tension with the accountability condition that cooperative-learning benefits depend on. The tension is resolvable.
settled.scope: Karau & Williams (1993) Collective Effort Model, ~78 studies, general social psychology — not games, not L2. The resolution proposed (presence-of-contribution as an effort cue vs magnitude as an ability cue) is a reasoned synthesis with Ames, not a tested design.
sources: Karau SJ, Williams KD (1993). Social loafing: a meta-analytic review and theoretical integration. JPSP 65(4):681-706 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Latané B, Williams K, Harkins S (1979). Many hands make light the work. JPSP 37(6):822-832 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Make contribution identifiable in real time in a form that carries no ability implication: a filled dot per player per round showing THAT they contributed, never how much or how accurately. Presence-of-contribution is the effort cue Ames wants salient; magnitude-of-contribution is the ability cue to suppress. That resolves the tension instead of trading one harm for the other.

settled.claim: Downtime while another player answers is not dead time — but the benefit attaches specifically to PAIRED, DIALOGIC observation of the other learner's reasoning. Solo observers did substantially worse.
settled.scope: Chi, Roy & Hausmann (2008): tens per condition, physics tutoring dialogues, not L2 reading. Replicated in classrooms by Craig, Chi & VanLehn (2009). The critique's correction is decisive: the sweep's proposed private shadow item implements the arm that FAILED while citing the arm that succeeded.
sources: Chi MTH, Roy M, Hausmann RGM (2008). Observing tutorial dialogues collaboratively. Cognitive Science 32(2):301-341 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Craig SD, Chi MTH, VanLehn K (2009). Improving classroom learning by collaboratively observing human tutoring videos. Journal of Educational Psychology | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: If you want this benefit, downtime must be filled with paired talk ABOUT THE ACTIVE PLAYER'S ITEM — two non-active players confer aloud on a prediction plus one discriminating cue. If you instead give each observer a private parallel item, that is defensible on retrieval-practice grounds (more attempts per minute) but must be justified by Rowland/Yang, NOT by Chi, and it forecloses the vicarious benefit rather than capturing it.

settled.claim: Time pressure costs accuracy (d ≈ 0.35) over and above making people faster, and it hits difficult items and high-ability/high-WM participants hardest. Performance pressure consumes the same working memory the effortful strategy depends on. Speed scoring in quiz games shows no learning advantage over accuracy scoring.
settled.scope: The d ≈ 0.35 is Raven's Matrices (Journal of Intelligence 2023), not L2 reading. Beilock & Carr (2005) is modest-n lab maths. The Kahoot speed-scoring point comes from a literature review of ~93 mostly weak-design studies. The mechanism (worry as concurrent WM load) is well established more broadly.
sources: Should Intelligence Tests Be Speeded or Unspeeded? (2023). Journal of Intelligence 11(6):120 | https://www.mdpi.com/2079-3200/11/6/120
Beilock SL, Carr TH (2005). When high-powered people fail: working memory and choking under pressure in math. Psychological Science 16(2):101-105 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Wang AI, Tahir R (2020). The effect of using Kahoot! for learning. Computers & Education 149 | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131520300208
Time on Their Side: How Visual Timers Affect Anticipatory Anxiety (visual timers cut anticipatory anxiety without changing performance) | https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12731990/
settled.implication: Never award points for speed; score correctness only and break ties on total round time. Do not stack pressures: observation is inherent to a co-located game, so the visible countdown is the cheapest pressure to remove. Use a silent generous window with a subtle desaturation in the final fifth rather than counting digits, and no timeout penalty on an item's first exposure.

settled.claim: Task resumption after interruption costs time that grows with the interruption's duration and demand, and the cost is mitigated by cues that reinstate the suspended goal. Working-memory capacity strongly predicts resumption lag.
settled.scope: Monk, Trafton & Boehm-Davis (2008), three experiments, interleaved-tasks paradigm; Altmann & Trafton memory-for-goals model. Lab paradigms, not phones — but a phone learning app is interrupted constantly, so the transfer is the obvious one.
sources: Monk CA, Trafton JG, Boehm-Davis DA (2008). The effect of interruption duration and demand on resuming suspended goals. JEP: Applied | https://www.interruptions.net/literature/Monk-JEPA08.pdf
Altmann EM, Trafton JG (2004). Task Interruption: Resumption Lag and the Role of Cues. Proc. CogSci | https://www.interruptions.net/literature/Altmann-CogSci04.pdf
Individual differences in WM capacity and task resumption following interruptions (2016). JEP:LMC | https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26882286/
settled.implication: Persist full item state (itemId, options in shown order, elapsedMs, selection-in-progress) to IndexedDB on every visibilitychange and every option focus, not at item boundaries. On resume, never drop the player into a running timer: show a ~2s reinstatement card redisplaying the target and the round context, then restart the item timer from full.

settled.claim: Push reminders raise studying on the days they fire but produce no net increase in study frequency versus a never-reminded control — they appear to substitute for self-initiated study rather than add to it.
settled.scope: Nobbe et al. (2024), npj Science of Learning: n=85 CHILDREN aged 10-12, 36-day vocabulary-app intervention. Generalisation to adult Dutch/English learners is an inference. The 'converging' MALL RCT percentages the sweep quoted came from a non-indexed outlet and have been struck.
sources: Nobbe L, Breitwieser J, Biedermann D, Brod G (2024). Smartphone-based study reminders can be a double-edged sword. npj Science of Learning | https://www.nature.com/articles/s41539-024-00253-7
settled.implication: One notification per day maximum, self-scheduled by the user at onboarding rather than algorithmically timed. Build an explicit wean (after 21 consecutive self-initiated on-time opens, offer to turn reminders off and say why). Never a second same-day 'you're about to lose your streak' notification — that is the dependency pattern. Track selfInitiatedOpens vs notificationOpens separately so substitution is visible.

settled.claim: Gamification's cognitive effect clusters around g ≈ 0.45-0.50, but the elements that moderate BEHAVIOURAL outcomes are game fiction and competition-combined-with-collaboration — not points and leaderboards. Badges, leaderboards, competitions and points are the elements most often reported as causing negative effects, with lower performers specifically demotivated by leaderboards.
settled.scope: Downgraded from strong and reclassified as contested-magnitude (see contested): the three 'converging' meta-analyses draw on a heavily overlapping primary pool with short durations, novelty confounds and researcher-made post-tests. Sailer & Homner's own motivational and behavioural effects did NOT survive their high-rigour subsplit.
sources: Sailer M, Homner L (2020). The Gamification of Learning: a Meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review 32:77-112 (cognitive g=0.49 k=19 N=1686; motivational 0.36; behavioural 0.25) | https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1245270
Almeida C, Kalinowski M, Uchôa A, Feijó B (2023). Negative effects of gamification in education software. Information and Software Technology | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.08346
Hanus MD, Fox J (2015). Computers & Education 80:152-161 (16 weeks: gamified condition showed LOWER intrinsic motivation, effort and exam performance over time) | no resolvable URL
settled.implication: Invest in fiction and in competition-plus-collaboration; ship no global leaderboard and no points economy. Frame each round as a place ('the noodle shop', 'Line 2 to the airport'). Rank the end-of-session screen by 'characters you can now read', so the bottom player still sees a positive number. And expect decay: instrument retention at 8+ weeks rather than assuming the effect persists past novelty.

settled.claim: There is NO controlled study of whether public failure in a language-learning game suppresses subsequent participation. Both the sweep and its adversary state this independently. Any claim that it does — or that it doesn't — is currently an inference from adjacent literatures.
settled.scope: This is a statement about the absence of evidence, and it is the single most product-critical question in this cluster. The supporting chain (FL anxiety → achievement; whole-class contexts produce the lowest willingness to communicate; Kahoot reviews report recurring anxiety/embarrassment themes in weak self-report designs) is adjacent, not a test.
sources: Wang AI, Tahir R (2020). The effect of using Kahoot! for learning — a literature review of ~93 studies. Computers & Education 149 | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360131520300208
Cao Y, Philp J (2006). Interactional context and willingness to communicate. System 34(4) | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
MacIntyre PD, Dörnyei Z, Clément R, Noels KA (1998). Conceptualizing willingness to communicate in a L2. Modern Language Journal | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: The product must answer this in-house, and can, cheaply. Store 'turns since last public failure' as a field so the analysis is a query, not a data-collection project. Log per player: turns voluntarily initiated, next-turn response latency, abandonment, and next-session return, each keyed to whether the PREVIOUS turn was a public failure. A within-player pre/post comparison is a real experiment at n≈200 players.

settled.claim: Anxiety degrades processing EFFICIENCY (effort and time) before it degrades effectiveness (accuracy) — so latency inflates before accuracy drops. That gives the product a measurable early-warning signal for harm.
settled.scope: Attentional Control Theory (Eysenck et al. 2007) is a general cognitive account, not a game or L2 study. Offered by the critique explicitly as the falsifiable replacement for Krashen's Affective Filter, which is unfalsifiable and should be kept out of the design document.
sources: Eysenck MW, Derakshan N, Santos R, Calvo MG (2007). Anxiety and cognitive performance: attentional control theory. Emotion 7(2):336-353 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Gregg KR (1984). Krashen's monitor and Occam's razor. Applied Linguistics 5(2):79-100 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Response latency is the harm tripwire, and it is already in the logging schema. Set an alert on within-player latency inflation on opponent-dealt items relative to self-dealt ones. Never write 'affective filter' in the design document — a reviewer with SLA training will discount the surrounding argument.

settled.claim: Adaptive item difficulty targeting roughly a 75% success rate is the standard, production-proven way to run a mixed-ability practice game, using an Elo rating on players AND items updated after every response.
settled.scope: Klinkenberg et al. (2011) Math Garden — arithmetic, Dutch schoolchildren, national scale; a user-selectable difficulty corresponding to roughly 60/75/90% success. Not L2, not co-located. But it is a real production system with published evidence, which is more than the sweep's invented exposure gate had.
sources: Klinkenberg S, Straatemeier M, van der Maas HLJ (2011). Computer adaptive practice of maths ability using a new item response model. Computers & Education | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
van der Maas HLJ, Nyamsuren E (2017). Cognitive analysis of educational games: the number game. Topics in Cognitive Science 9(2) | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: This makes the opponent-dealing mechanic safe BY CONSTRUCTION and replaces the invented '≥5 prior exposures' gate. Opponents choose the CATEGORY; the engine chooses the ITEM within a rating band of the target player. Elo is a few lines of code, needs no training data, and works from the first match. It also supplies the item difficulties that make improvement-based team scoring fair.

settled.claim: Equal-opportunity / improvement scoring — contributing to the team based on performance relative to your OWN rolling baseline — is the best-evidenced fix for competition among mixed-proficiency players, and it is absent from both the sweep and the current design.
settled.scope: Slavin's Student Teams-Achievement Divisions, decades of school-based cooperative-learning research inside the Johnson/Slavin tradition, which carries the allegiance-bias problem noted in contested. Not tested in a co-located phone game.
sources: Slavin RE (1980). Cooperative learning. Review of Educational Research 50(2):315-342 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Slavin RE (1995). Cooperative Learning: Theory, Research, and Practice (2nd ed.) | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Replace 'team score = sum of correct × proportion of members contributing' with contribution = f(correct_this_round − personal_rolling_baseline), clipped, baseline recomputed after each match. The proportion formula still rewards raw correctness and therefore still makes the beginner a liability — which is precisely the condition under which competitive structures do their documented damage. This also delivers Ames's mastery framing as a scoring rule rather than a UI afterthought.

settled.claim: Interleaving confusable exemplars is unusually well-supported for exactly this material: it helps most for inductive learning of visually similar categories and least for expository text, and the mechanism is discriminative contrast.
settled.scope: Brunmair & Richter (2019) similarity-moderator meta-analysis; Kornell & Bjork (2008) paintings; Rohrer et al. (2015) mathematics. Not hanzi — but visually confusable hanzi are the paradigm case of the moderator that makes interleaving work. Learners reliably believe blocking works better; the better schedule feels worse.
sources: Brunmair M, Richter T (2019). Similarity matters: a meta-analysis of interleaved learning and its moderators. Psychological Bulletin 145(11):1029-1052 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Kornell N, Bjork RA (2008). Psychological Science 19(6):585-592 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Birnbaum MS, Kornell N, Bjork EL, Bjork RA (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning. Memory & Cognition 41:392-402 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: Two different scheduling constraints, not one: space repetitions of the SAME item widely (≥24h between correct repetitions), but interleave DIFFERENT-but-confusable items TIGHTLY (alternating, 5-15 intervening items, never separated across sessions). The schema needs a confusion_set_id distinct from any isomorph_group_id, and the scheduler needs both a minimum gap (same item) and a maximum gap (within confusion set). Warn the team in advance: interleaving lowers self-rated session satisfaction, and an A/B on satisfaction will kill it wrongly.

settled.claim: Co-located play produces the highest enjoyment and perceived social presence of any play configuration, exceeding merely knowing a human opponent exists — and serious games work better when played in groups than alone. This is the honest evidential basis for the co-located format.
settled.scope: Gajadhar et al. (2008) measures enjoyment and social presence, NOT learning. Wouters et al. (2013) supplies the group-play moderator inside a meta-analysis whose headline motivational effect was itself non-significant (learning d≈0.29, retention d≈0.36, motivation d≈0.26 n.s.). The CHI/CHI PLAY co-located literature is qualitative with no learning-outcome study anywhere.
sources: Gajadhar BJ, de Kort YAW, IJsselsteijn WA (2008). Shared fun is doubled fun: player enjoyment as a function of social setting. Fun and Games 2008, LNCS | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)

Wouters P, van Nimwegen C, van Oostendorp H, van der Spek ED (2013). A meta-analysis of the cognitive and motivational effects of serious games. Journal of Educational Psychology | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Emmerich K, Masuch M (2017). The Impact of Game Patterns on Player Experience and Social Interaction in Co-Located Multiplayer Games. CHI PLAY '17 | https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/3116595.3116606
settled.implication: Claim engagement, never learning, for the co-located format. Competition earns its place as an attendance/retention mechanism: put competitive salience high at match setup and at the single end-of-match screen, and near zero during the retrievals in between. The item loop itself should be as neutral and task-focused as a flashcard.

settled.claim: Retrieval practice with feedback is the mechanism that actually produces learning in a quiz game (g ≈ 0.50-0.61, ~222 studies in authentic classrooms in the largest, robust to publication-bias diagnostics) — and it dwarfs every social and game-shell effect this cluster examined.
settled.scope: Yang et al. (2021) is classroom-based and bias-tested — one of the few literatures here where diagnostics were both performed and passed. Rowland (2014) and Adesope et al. (2017) are the other anchors. Not hanzi-specific.
sources: Yang C, Luo L, Vadillo MA, Yu R, Shanks DR (2021). Testing (quizzing) boosts classroom learning. Psychological Bulletin | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Rowland CA (2014). Psychological Bulletin 140(6):1432-1463 | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
Adesope OO, Trevisan DA, Sundararajan N (2017). Rethinking the Use of Tests. Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701 | https://www.researchgate.net/publication/315706448
settled.implication: Priority order that should settle internal arguments: retrieval-with-feedback (≈0.5, strong) > self-explanation with domain-proposition prompts (≈0.55, strong, but see myths on the chip version) > gamification wrapper (≈0.5, contested) > game-vs-nongame (≈0.33, weak controls) > competition (≈0, null). No 'browse the character' or 'study the list' screens in the main loop; any study/preview mode is a separate, non-default surface.

settled.claim: Spacing beats massing for L2 learning (g = 0.40 on delayed tests for long vs short gaps), expanding and equal schedules are statistically equivalent, and cross-DAY scheduling is the largest and cheapest lever available to a character-recognition app. The gbl sweep never cites it once.
settled.scope: Kim & Webb (2022): 98 effect sizes, 48 experiments, N=3,411, L2 specifically; delayed = ≥1 day. Cepeda et al. (2006), 317 experiments, is the general base. This is a cross-cluster import, but it collides head-on with this cluster's architecture recommendation and therefore has to be ruled on here.
sources: Kim SK, Webb S (2022). The Effects of Spaced Practice on Second Language Learning: A Meta-Analysis. Language Learning 72(1):269-319 | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lang.12479
Cepeda NJ, Pashler H, Vul E, Wixted JT, Rohrer D (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks. Psychological Bulletin | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)
settled.implication: THE ARCHITECTURE INVERSION. An app played when friends happen to meet cannot schedule across days, and 're-queue at 5 and 15 intervening items' is within-session massing dressed as spacing. So the solo daily surface is LOAD-BEARING, not 'a degenerate case of multiplayer' as the gbl sweep concluded. The scheduling layer, not the match engine, is the product: nextDueAt must persist across matches and devices, and the match engine must draw from a due-queue rather than a per-match item list.

contested.question: In the co-located round, should feedback be immediate and adjacent to the answer, or batched to the end of a 5-item round so opponents cannot read your answer off your face?
contested.side_a: IMMEDIATE, ADJACENT. The bet is a commitment-before-feedback (generation/pretesting) structure, and the association-learning benefit is the contested part — delayed feedback removes what support there is (Potts & Shanks 2014 vs the Seabrooke et al. 2019 non-replication). Applied, motivationally-loaded, low-prior-knowledge, item-level associative material is exactly the cell where immediate feedback wins (Kulik & Kulik 1988's applied/laboratory dissociation). And socially you cannot leave a public error uncorrected in front of a table of people; hypercorrection requires the correction to land at the moment of surprise.
contested.side_b: BATCHED, END-OF-ROUND. Butler & Roediger (2008) found immediate and delayed feedback EQUALLY effective at cutting lure intrusions, and delayed feedback showed an advantage for retention of correct answers — so batching costs nothing on the negative-suggestion axis and may gain on retention. Butler, Karpicke & Roediger (2007) found delayed feedback better on a delayed test with MC materials. Batching also removes the live-monitoring channel that the social-facilitation correction says matters more than the sweep assumed.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether the mechanism you are protecting is the ERROR-CORRECTION moment (needs immediacy, needs adjacency of chosen option and correct option in one visual frame) or the SPACED RE-EXPOSURE that a delay incidentally creates (recoverable separately, by re-queueing the missed item later in the match and again the next day). If you can recover the spacing benefit through the lapse queue — and you can — immediacy wins, because the pretesting and hypercorrection benefits are not recoverable any other way. Recommended resolution: immediate correction at the item, spacing recovered via the lapse queue, and the social protection delivered by the private-input/public-resolution split rather than by delaying the reveal. Note this reverses the uiux sweep's own recommendation ('pick end-of-round batch reveal for the multiplayer mode').
sources: Butler AC, Roediger HL III (2008). Memory & Cognition 36(3):604-616 | https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/MC.36.3.604
Kulik JA, Kulik C-LC (1988). Timing of feedback and verbal learning. Review of Educational Research 58(1):79-97 | no resolvable URL

Potts R, Shanks DR (2014). The benefit of generating errors during learning. JEP: General 143(2):644-667 — LAB WORD-LIST material (rare English words, Euskara nouns), short intervals; Seabrooke et al. (2019) failed to replicate on a cued-recall test, concluding the benefit does not extend to the cue-target ASSOCIATION
Metcalfe J, Kornell N, Finn B (2009). Memory & Cognition 37(8):1077-1087 — direction of the age interaction flagged by the sweep itself as unverified and not to be relied on

contested.question: Can approach-framing (UI copy, score presentation) actually tip competition from harmful to beneficial, as the design's whole social licence assumes?
contested.side_a: YES, IN PRINCIPLE. Murayama & Elliot's opposing-processes model localises the harm in performance-AVOIDANCE goals and the benefit in performance-APPROACH goals. If a design can shift which goal is salient — gain framing, no large red negative numbers, no live losing-ordering — the null total effect should resolve positively.
contested.side_b: UNTESTED, AND THE PAPER DOES NOT SUPPORT THE STEP. The model was fitted by meta-analytic SEM over correlational cross-sectional studies in which goal endorsement was MEASURED, not manipulated. Nothing in it demonstrates that a copy change shifts goal adoption, still less that shifted adoption shifts performance causally. The paths also come from different study sets (the standard MASEM objection).
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether 'we can tip the sign with framing' is treated as a finding or as the product's central untested hypothesis. It is the latter. Make it the FIRST thing the product A/B tests (gain-framed vs neutral-framed score presentation, outcome = next-turn latency and next-session return), not the assumption the product is built on. The design decisions it motivates — no red negative numbers, no live losing order, gain-framed copy — are cheap and harmless either way, so ship them; just do not book the benefit.
sources: Murayama K, Elliot AJ (2012). Psychological Bulletin 138(6) | no resolvable URL (recalled, unverified)

contested.question: Does reducing anxiety improve learning, or does improving decoding skill reduce anxiety?
contested.side_a: ANXIETY → ACHIEVEMENT. Three independent meta-analyses land in a 0.05 band (r ≈ −0.34 to −0.39), and the mechanism (worry as concurrent working-memory load) is independently established in the cognitive-load and test-anxiety literatures.
contested.side_b: ACHIEVEMENT → ANXIETY. Sparks & Ganschow's Linguistic Coding Differences Hypothesis argues the correlation is substantially a CONSEQUENCE of underlying aptitude and L1 literacy differences — anxious learners are anxious largely because they are struggling. This has run as an explicit decades-long exchange with MacIntyre in the Modern Language Journal and is unresolved. The studies are overwhelmingly cross-sectional self-report with course grades as outcome, so common-method variance inflates r.
contested.what_it_turns_on: What you are allowed to PROMISE from the mitigations. Under the LCDH reading, anxiety-reduction alone buys little learning. Keep the instrumentation, but justify every anxiety mitigation by RETENTION AND ATTENDANCE — anxious players quit, and the product can measure that directly — not by a promised learning gain. This is the defensible framing regardless of which side wins.
sources: Teimouri Y, Goetze J, Plonsky L (2019). SSLA 41(2):363-387 | no resolvable URL
Sparks & Ganschow, LCDH; the Sparks–MacIntyre exchange in the Modern Language Journal | no resolvable URL

contested.question: Should confusable distractors (入口 beside 出口, 麻 beside 辣) be in the four options at test time, or reserved for the post-answer panel?
contested.side_a: IN THE OPTIONS. Competitive MC with plausible alternatives can produce test-induced learning of the alternatives themselves — the player retrieves why the others are wrong, which strengthens rather than damages them (Little, Bjork, Bjork & Angello 2012). Interleaving's discriminative-contrast mechanism says the same: juxtapose confusables to make the difference salient. Weak filler options also destroy Rodriguez's three-option result.
contested.side_b: NOT DURING ACQUISITION. The negative suggestion effect scales with lure plausibility, and Little et al.'s mechanism REQUIRES that the learner can reject the distractors on knowledge they already hold. General-knowledge facts at short delay is not a beginner facing four Chinese signs none of which they know — the mechanism the benefit depends on is absent at exactly the moment you want to deploy it. Harm from relatedness also shows up as interference errors while accuracy looks fine, so it is easy to miss.
contested.what_it_turns_on: The item's consolidation state, which makes this a scheduler question, not a content-authoring question. Rule: unrelated (but domain-plausible) distractors for a sign's FIRST appearances; competitive confusable distractors once BOTH members of the pair are consolidated. This makes 'ban random unrelated distractors' wrong as a blanket rule and makes the consolidation gate load-bearing for the distractor policy as well as for the dealing policy.
sources: Little JL, Bjork EL, Bjork RA, Angello G (2012). Psychological Science 23(11):1337-1344 — LAB, general-knowledge facts, short delay | no resolvable URL
Roediger HL III, Marsh EJ (2005). JEP:LMC 31(5):1155-1159 | http://psychnet.wustl.edu/memory/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Roediger-Marsh-2005_JEPLMC.pdf
Brunmair M, Richter T (2019). Psychological Bulletin 145(11):1029-1052 | no resolvable URL

contested.question: How large is the cooperation-over-competition achievement advantage, and can it be used as a planning number?
contested.side_a: ROUGHLY HALF A STANDARD DEVIATION, HOLDING FOR FOUR DECADES. Roseth, Johnson & Johnson (2008): 148 studies, ~17,000 early adolescents, cooperative > competitive ES ≈ 0.46, cooperative > individualistic ≈ 0.55, plus better peer relationships. Qin et al. (1995): d ≈ 0.55 on problem solving. Kyndt et al. (2013), k ≈ 65: d ≈ 0.54.
contested.side_b: THE POINT ESTIMATES ARE ALLEGIANCE-CONTAMINATED. Cotton & Cook (1982) and McGlynn (1982) argued in Psychological Bulletin that study inclusion and the coding of 'cooperative' vs 'competitive' were not independent of the authors' theoretical commitment, and that re-analysis gives a much smaller advantage. The Johnsons replied; the field never converged, and later syntheses were still largely conducted inside the same tradition.
contested.what_it_turns_on: The sign is safe; the magnitude is not. Use it as a prior, never as a planning number, and never present 'cooperation beats competition' internally as settled fact justifying a design. Architecturally, make the dealing rule a swappable strategy object (opponent-deals / random-deals / self-selects) configurable per match, so testing this costs a config flag rather than a rewrite. Note also that these studies manipulated genuine positive interdependence PLUS individual accountability — a lone player answering for a team score with no teammate involvement is competition wearing a team costume and gets none of this evidence's support.
sources: Roseth CJ, Johnson DW, Johnson RT (2008). Psychological Bulletin | no resolvable URL
Cotton JL, Cook MS (1982). Psychological Bulletin 92(1) | no resolvable URL
Kyndt E et al. (2013). Educational Research Review | no resolvable URL
Springer L, Stanne ME, Donovan SS (1999). Review of Educational Research, k≈39 undergraduate STEM, d≈0.51 | no resolvable URL

contested.question: Should the app ship word-spaced Chinese to help learners parse, given that real signage has no spaces?
contested.side_a: SPACING HELPS L2 READERS. Eye-tracking with CSL learners: word-spaced text produced least disruption, unspaced produced longer reading times than character-spaced, nonword-spaced was worst; adding spacing facilitated comprehension, speed and vocabulary learning.
contested.side_b: IT IS THE EXACT GUIDANCE-REVERSAL CONFIGURATION THE DESIGN BANS ELSEWHERE. Word spacing is a training-only cue absent from the transfer environment — structurally identical to the tone colour and radical highlighting the design correctly bans on Skulmowski grounds, and defended with a weaker literature. It is also largely moot: signage and menu targets are 1-4 characters (出口, 火车站, 牛肉面), where segmentation carries almost no information, and the eye-tracking benefit was measured on running prose this app does not contain.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Applying the design's own transfer rule consistently. Resolution: do NOT ship word spacing in the answering loop. Confine it, if used at all, to a post-answer explanation screen where nothing is being tested, or to a long-form reading mode added later — with unspaced as the default there too. The sweep's own gap note ('no evidence found on whether word-spacing during training transfers to unspaced real-world reading') is the reason to withhold, not to ship with a toggle.
sources: Eye movements of second language learners when reading spaced and unspaced Chinese texts (2023). Frontiers in Psychology 14:783960 | https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.783960/full
Skulmowski A (2022). Education and Information Technologies 27:3963-3985 | https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10639-021-10796-6

contested.question: Does an image on the reveal card help or hurt, given the product is teaching the written FORM?
