contested.side_a: MULTIMODAL GLOSSES BEAT TEXT-ONLY. Abraham (2008), Yun (2011) g≈0.46, and a 2024 System meta-analysis all report text+visual glossing outperforming text-only, with the largest benefit for beginners.
contested.side_b: PICTURE OVERSHADOWING. When a picture accompanies a written word, learners attend to the picture — the easier, more informative cue — and encode the orthography less well. Solman & Wu found the effect even when the picture appeared as FEEDBACK after the response, which is precisely the proposed configuration. The gloss meta-analyses measure MEANING acquisition for words the learner can already decode; here the written form is the thing being learned, which flips the prediction.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Whether the outcome you care about is meaning or orthography. For this product it is orthography, which favours side B. Cheap resolution that satisfies both: on the reveal, show the hanzi ALONE first (~800 ms, large, nothing else), then the gloss text, then the image — so the glyph gets an unshared encoding window. Then A/B image-on-reveal against text-only against a delayed recognition test; the literature predicts the image condition loses.
sources: Samuels SJ (1967). Attentional process in reading: the effect of pictures on the acquisition of reading responses. JEP 58(6):337-342 | no resolvable URL
Solman RT, Wu HM (1995). Pictures as feedback in single word learning. Educational Psychology 15(3):227-244 | no resolvable URL
Torcasio S, Sweller J (2010). Applied Cognitive Psychology 24(5):659-672 | no resolvable URL
Multimedia glosses and second language vocabulary learning: a second-round meta-analysis (2024). System | https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S000169182400218X

myths.myth: Deliberately hard-to-read rendering aids memory ('desirable difficulty'), so two of the sign treatments should be hard to read on purpose.
myths.why_wrong: Perceptual disfluency is the most UI-tempting member of the desirable-difficulties family and the one that failed. Taylor, Sanson et al. (2020) ran four experiments on Sans Forgetica and found it rated harder to read but producing equivalent or IMPAIRED memory; Wetzler, Pyke & Werner (2021) replicated the null; Meyer, Frederick et al. (2015) found large-sample nulls on disfluent fonts for problem solving. Three separate agents across both workflows independently graded this folklore. Difficulty must come from RETRIEVAL demands (longer gap, more competitive distractors, meaning→form direction), never from degrading the pixels. A hard-to-read treatment is permissible ONLY when it faithfully reproduces signage the player will actually meet — realism, not a difficulty manipulation — and the target glyph must still clear WCAG AA contrast.
sources: Taylor A, Sanson M, Burnell R, Wade KA, Garry M (2020). Disfluent difficulties are not desirable difficulties. Memory 28(7)
Wetzler, Pyke & Werner (2021). SAGE Open
Meyer A, Frederick S, et al. (2015). Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems. JEP: General
Geller J, Still ML, Dark VJ, Carpenter SK (2018). Would disfluency by any other name still be beneficial? Memory & Cognition

myths.myth: Multiple choice beats recall: MC practice produced a larger testing effect than short answer (g = 0.70 vs 0.48), overturning the prediction that recall must beat recognition.
myths.why_wrong: Dead twice over. (1) The 0.70 vs 0.48 contrast in Adesope et al. is a BETWEEN-STUDY moderator, confounded with final-test format — MC-practice studies disproportionately used MC final tests, and the same meta-analysis separately reports format match inflating the effect (0.63 vs 0.53). The within-subject literature points the other way: Kang, McDermott & Roediger (2007) found short-answer practice WITH corrective feedback produced better long-term retention than MC. (2) Rowland's final-test-format moderator puts recognition/MC at g ≈ 0.36 against free recall 0.79-0.82 and cued recall 0.70-0.72 — the product's mechanic sits in the weakest cell on BOTH axes. The honest statement: MC is a PACE-AND-SOCIABILITY decision that costs roughly half the retention benefit, partly recovered by competitive distractors and by transfer-appropriate processing (the criterion task really is recognition — 'is that shopfront 药店 or 酒店'). Keep MC; delete the justification.
sources: Adesope OO, Trevisan DA, Sundararajan N (2017). Review of Educational Research 87(3):659-701
Kang SHK, McDermott KB, Roediger HL III (2007). European Journal of Cognitive Psychology 19(4-5):528-558
Rowland CA (2014). Psychological Bulletin 140(6):1432-1463
Pan SC, Rickard TC (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning. Psychological Bulletin 144(7):710-756

myths.myth: The Duolingo efficacy study gives an hours anchor: ~112-141 hours to functional reading, so plan the bank and the roadmap copy against ~100-140 hours.
myths.why_wrong: RETRACTED. Jiang, Rollinson, Plonsky, Gustafson & Pajak (2021) evaluated learners of SPANISH AND FRENCH by English-speaking US adults. It contains no Mandarin data. Transferring hours-to-proficiency from two shallow-orthography Romance languages — where the learner already knows the script and shares thousands of cognates — to a logographic script with zero orthographic transfer is invalid and under-budgets badly. It was the sweep's ONLY quantitative planning anchor, so the error is load-bearing. The relevant comparator is the FSI Category IV classification (~2,200 class hours for Mandarin vs ~600-750 for Spanish/French), and even that is a whole-language classroom figure. For a narrow reading-only scope, project bank size and review load from the spacing ladder — which you can compute — and project no total-hours figure at all.
sources: Jiang X, Rollinson J, Plonsky L, Gustafson E, Pajak B (2021). Foreign Language Annals 54(4) | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/flan.12600
US Foreign Service Institute language difficulty categories (Mandarin: Category IV)

myths.myth: The specific product numbers are evidence-backed: ≥5 prior exposures before an opponent may deal a category; ≤20-word explanations; ≤14px score delta and ≥17px explanation text; correction within 300ms; no screen idle >2s; 8-12 minute matches; ≥40 scored retrievals per 10-minute session; a 60/40 content-vs-game-feel budget split; re-queue at 5 and 15 intervening items; 1-match-in-5 anxiety sampling; a 3-row leaderboard.
myths.why_wrong: GRADED FOLKLORE by the adversary. None of these appears in, or is derivable from, any cited source. Every one is an invented product decision wearing a citation, and this is the pattern most likely to do downstream damage — '≥5 exposures, per Horwitz et al.' will be in the codebase within a week. Only the 20-word cap is honestly labelled as an arithmetic heuristic, and even it combines a NATIVE-ENGLISH silent reading rate (Brysbaert 2019, ~238 wpm) with an invented on-screen degradation factor and an invented window length. Fix: split the spec into two registers — (1) findings, with a source and an effect size; (2) decisions, with an owner, a rationale and a planned test — and label every line. The px values additionally need restating in rem with a contrast ratio, or they will fail WCAG 1.4.4 and 1.4.3.
sources: Brysbaert M (2019). How many words do we read per minute? Journal of Memory and Language 109:104047
Adversary verdict on the gbl-multiplayer sweep, correction 13 (graded folklore)

myths.myth: Fear of negative evaluation is one of the three constitutive factors of foreign-language classroom anxiety, so the mechanic is close to a laboratory operationalisation of it.
myths.why_wrong: Standard textbook misreading. Horwitz, Horwitz & Cope (1986) drew an ANALOGY to communication apprehension, test anxiety and fear of negative evaluation to motivate the construct, and were explicit that FL anxiety is a distinct situation-specific construct not reducible to their sum. Factor-analytic replications over three decades recover anywhere from two to five factors, most commonly collapsing communication apprehension and fear of negative evaluation, and Horwitz herself has objected to the three-component reading and to scoring FLCAS subscales. Fear of negative evaluation remains a well-motivated concern for a publicly-observed answering mechanic — but if the product's post-match check-in is meant to measure it, the items must come from a validated FNE instrument (Leary's Brief FNE), not from a nonexistent FLCAS subscale.
sources: Horwitz EK, Horwitz MB, Cope J (1986). Foreign language classroom anxiety. Modern Language Journal 70(2):125-132

myths.myth: A private 'shadow item' on every observer's phone during another player's turn captures the vicarious-learning benefit.
myths.why_wrong: It implements the arm of the study that FAILED. In Chi, Roy & Hausmann (2008) the benefit attaches to PAIRED, DIALOGIC observation — collaborative observers discussed the observed reasoning with a partner and learned comparably to tutees; solo observers did substantially worse. A private parallel item answered alone and silently is the solo condition, and worse, it removes the observation entirely, because a player answering their own item is not attending to anyone's reasoning. Parallel private retrievals may still be worth shipping — on retrieval-practice grounds, more attempts per minute — but they must be justified by Rowland/Yang and they FORECLOSE the vicarious benefit rather than capturing it.
sources: Chi MTH, Roy M, Hausmann RGM (2008). Cognitive Science 32(2):301-341
Craig SD, Chi MTH, VanLehn K (2009). Journal of Educational Psychology

myths.myth: Two or three tappable 'reason chips' after the answer ('I knew the radical' / 'I guessed from context' / 'I confused it with another character') is a self-explanation prompt worth g = 0.55.
myths.why_wrong: That mechanic is not self-explanation. Every study in Bisra et al.'s pool prompts learners to GENERATE an explanation — spoken, typed, or selected from a structured domain menu that names a principle. Tapping a post-hoc label about HOW you answered is a strategy attribution, closer to a judgment of learning or a confidence rating, and produces no new inference. Menu-based self-explanation CAN work, but only when the options are DOMAIN PROPOSITIONS: 'which part told you? [semantic radical] [phonetic component] [the character it is NOT: 未]'. Keep the strategy chip if you want the confidence signal for hypercorrection scheduling — but bill it as instrumentation, not as a 0.55-effect learning mechanic. Also note Rittle-Johnson et al. (2017): self-explanation costs TIME, and the advantage shrinks when time-on-task is equated, so it must DISPLACE something rather than be added on top.
sources: Bisra K, Liu Q, Nesbit JC, Salimi F, Winne PH (2018). Inducing self-explanation: a meta-analysis. Educational Psychology Review 30:703-725
Rittle-Johnson B, Loehr AM, Durkin K (2017). ZDM

myths.myth: Wisniewski, Zierer & Hattie (2020) — '~435 studies, ~994 effect sizes, N ≈ 61,000' — independently corroborates the feedback effect sizes.
myths.why_wrong: Unit-of-analysis error plus false independence. It is a meta-analysis OF META-ANALYSES: ~435 meta-analyses, on the order of 61,000 primary studies and ~7 million students. The sweep relabelled 'meta-analyses' as 'studies' and 'studies' as 'N', understating participants by orders of magnitude and making an umbrella review look like a primary synthesis. Worse for the argument: it re-pools the very primary studies Van der Kleij, Hattie & Timperley, and Kluger & DeNisi already pooled — it double-counts. And Hattie authors both 'converging' sources, so this is one research programme cited twice, not two teams agreeing. The feedback story rests on one substantially shared evidence pool.
sources: Wisniewski B, Zierer K, Hattie J (2020). The power of feedback revisited. Frontiers in Psychology 10:3087
Hattie J, Timperley H (2007). Review of Educational Research 77(1):81-112

myths.myth: Wait-time research (extend the pause to ~3 seconds) sets the response window for a phone recognition item; hence a 5-second minimum and a 10-second soft window.
myths.why_wrong: Over-graded and transferred across an unbridged gap. The wait-time corpus is 1970s-80s classroom observation of TEACHER pause duration after an oral question in whole-class discourse — small samples, no randomisation, unblinded observers, and outcomes that are properties of student TALK (response length, number of speculative responses) rather than learning. There is no oral discourse, no teacher and no turn-taking norm in a silent tap on a phone. The specific 5s and 10s numbers have no source at all. The right basis for a response window is the product's own data: set a generous default, measure the latency distribution of its correct responses, and set the window near the 90th percentile.
sources: Rowe MB (1986). Wait time: slowing down may be a way of speeding up. Journal of Teacher Education 37(1):43-50
Tobin K (1987). Review of Educational Research 57(1):69-95

myths.myth: Digital game-based L2 vocabulary learning delivers g ≈ 0.87, so plan against a large effect.
myths.why_wrong: A pooled g near 0.87 for a vocabulary intervention should be disbelieved on sight — it exceeds nearly every well-controlled educational effect in this cluster, including retrieval practice. With k ≈ 26, short interventions and predominantly passive controls, it is far better explained by small-study effects plus control-group weakness, which is the explicit contribution of Tsai & Tsai's own moderator analysis ('conditions of research designs'). Plan against the active-control subgroup estimate; if that cannot be recovered from the paper, plan against the general game-vs-nongame figure (g ≈ 0.33). Related: Chiu, Kao & Reynolds (2012) is a four-page BJET Colloquium note (E104-E107), not a full meta-analysis, and should not sit alongside Review-of-Educational-Research-grade syntheses unflagged.
sources: Tsai Y-L, Tsai C-C (2018). Computers & Education
Chiu Y-H, Kao C-W, Reynolds BL (2012). BJET (Colloquium note)
Clark DB, Tanner-Smith EE, Killingsworth SS (2016). Review of Educational Research — g ≈ 0.33 game vs non-game, and g ≈ 0.34 for redesigned-vs-standard SAME game

myths.myth: Being watched is a small effect (0.3-3% of variance), so do not over-engineer against the observation part of the mechanic.
myths.why_wrong: The reassuring number describes the wrong manipulation. Bond & Titus pooled studies of a PASSIVE audience or co-actors. This mechanic has an opponent who SELECTED your item, holds a competitive stake in your failure, and observes the outcome — evaluation apprehension plus outcome interdependence, the conditions under which the Cottrell account and the test-anxiety literature predict substantially larger impairment on non-dominant responses. Hanzi recognition for a beginner is by definition non-dominant. The sweep used the weakest operationalisation of observation to license the strongest one. This correction cuts AGAINST the sweep's own conclusion: private input becomes MORE necessary, not less, and is a v1 requirement.
sources: Bond CF, Titus LJ (1983). Psychological Bulletin 94(2):265-292
Uziel L (2007). Journal of Research in Personality 41(3):579-601

myths.myth: After a wrong answer, immediately re-present the same item with the chosen lure removed; and never reuse a wrong option as the correct answer for a different item in the same session.
myths.why_wrong: Both mitigations are wrong for this bank. Immediate re-presentation with the lure removed is massed repetition of a now-trivial two-option item — a correct response with almost no retrieval difficulty and therefore almost no durable benefit; Butler & Roediger attribute the repair to CORRECTIVE FEEDBACK, not to immediate re-testing. And the no-reuse rule is unworkable: in a menu domain the confusable set IS the syllabus (牛肉 is the correct answer for one item and the ideal distractor for 羊肉 and 猪肉), so forbidding reuse either forces weak filler distractors — which destroys Rodriguez's three-option result — or fragments the confusable set across sessions, which is the opposite of what discrimination learning needs. It also directly prohibits interleaving, the best-evidenced intervention for this product's core problem. Keep only the third mitigation: log {itemId, lureId, timestamp}.
sources: Butler AC, Roediger HL III (2008). Memory & Cognition 36(3):604-616
Rodriguez MC (2005). Educational Measurement: Issues and Practice 24(2):3-13
Brunmair M, Richter T (2019). Psychological Bulletin 145(11):1029-1052

myths.myth: Tone colour-coding is an established learner aid; and conversely, Godfroid et al. (2017) proves colour coding is harmful.
myths.why_wrong: Both halves are wrong. Colour-coding tones on CHARACTERS (the Pleco/Hanping convention) has no controlled evidence of benefit or of transfer to uncoloured text — unsupported folklore, with an untested dependency risk. But Godfroid does not show harm either: colour training WORKED (~11% item-learning and ~12% system-learning gains), just slightly behind pitch contours and numbers, with dual cues adding nothing over single cues. 'Slightly worse than the best alternative' is not 'do not do it', and the study trained tone PERCEPTION via colour, not glyph tinting in a reading interface. Keep the no-colour rule; change the justification to WCAG 1.4.1 plus ~8% male CVD plus the guidance-reversal transfer argument. And for a reading-only product the prior question is whether to surface tone at all — probably only in the audio, never as a visual system to be learned.
sources: Godfroid A, Lin C-H, Ryu C (2017). Hearing and Seeing Tone Through Color. Language Learning 67(4):819-857 | https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/lang.12246
W3C WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A)
Wang Y, Spence MM, Jongman A, Sereno JA (1999). Training American listeners to perceive Mandarin tones. JASA 106(6) — high-variability phonetic training is the supported route if tone is ever added

myths.myth: Hand-authored Chinese examples and physical-size figures in the original sweep can be reused: 18-stroke exemplars 蔬/齿/警; the '2-stroke high-frequency' set 出/入/男/女; 药店 vs 酒店 as component-sharing visual neighbours; '44px is folklore with no experiment behind it'; and a MALL adherence RCT reporting 82%/67%/49%.
myths.why_wrong: Every one is wrong. Stroke counts: 蔬 is 15, 警 is 19, 齿 is 8 (the 15-stroke form is TRADITIONAL 齒 — a traditional count leaked into a Simplified-only product as its worked example of maximum complexity); of the 'easiest 2-stroke' set only 入 is 2 (出 is 5, 女 is 3, 男 is 7). 药店/酒店 share no component at all (艹+约 vs 氵+酉) — they are situational, not visual, neighbours, and this was the single worked example for the top-priority distractor rule. '44px folklore' is half-true and misleading: 44x44 CSS px is NORMATIVE as WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.5 (AAA) and 24x24 is normative at AA under SC 2.5.8. The 82/67/49 adherence percentages come from a KMAN Publications journal not indexed in Scopus, Web of Science or PubMed — strike them, along with the internally inconsistent '100 ms ≈ 9% faster' stroke-latency figure (100 ÷ 0.09 implies an 1,111 ms baseline, well above typical single-character lexical-decision latencies). Rule for the spec: derive strokeCount programmatically from Unihan kTotalStrokes and assert at build time; derive components from Unihan IDS / CHISE; no non-indexed outlet supplies a number.
sources: Unicode Han Database (Unihan), kTotalStrokes and IDS data
通用规范汉字表 (Table of General Standard Chinese Characters), 2013
W3C WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.5 and SC 2.5.8 | https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
Source-quality assessment: journals.kmanpub.com not indexed in Scopus/WoS/PubMed

myths.myth: Ship Simplified only, because the target is mainland China.
myths.why_wrong: Wrong for the specific criterion task chosen. Mainland law (国家通用语言文字法, 2001) mandates simplified for public signage but carves out calligraphy, seal carving, handwritten inscriptions and heritage contexts — and commercial shopfront and restaurant signage exploits those exceptions constantly. Traditional forms, seal script and calligraphic 行书/隶书 renderings are pervasive on exactly the shopfronts, tea houses and noodle shops the product targets. Only transit signage is cleanly standardised Hei. Compounding this, simplification MERGES land directly on menu vocabulary: 面 covers both 面 and 麵 (牛肉面 is 牛肉麵 in Taipei); 干 covers 干/乾/幹, so 干炒 is 乾 'dry', and a naive gloss of 干 as 'to do' on a menu is simply wrong. Also 里/裡, 后/後, 发/發 vs 髮. Fix: ship Simplified as the learning target but give the schema separate simplified, traditional and sense_id fields — one simplified form can map to two traditional forms with different meanings, so a one-to-one mapping table WILL generate wrong content. Surface the traditional counterpart on the reveal for high-divergence signage characters (门/門, 车/車, 面/麵, 药/藥, 饭/飯, 银/銀), and segment the bank by environment.
sources: 中华人民共和国国家通用语言文字法 (2001), Articles 13-17
Unicode Han Database (Unihan), kTraditionalVariant / kSimplifiedVariant

verdicts_on_design.decision: THE HARD ONE (inherited mechanic, not in the numbered list): the game makes you fail publicly, in front of opponents who chose your category. Is it defensible, for whom is it harmful, and what mitigations does the evidence support?
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: RULING: defensible in two of its three components, indefensible in the third as currently framed. Roughly two-thirds survives; one specific element must be inverted. (1) OPPONENT-CHOSEN CATEGORY — defensible, conditionally. Errors followed by corrective feedback beat error-free study, and high-confidence errors hypercorrect (Metcalfe 2017; Butterfield & Metcalfe 2001, strong). But both effects REQUIRE the learner to have related knowledge to recruit: a blind guess at an unseen character is not a productive error, it is a coin flip. So dealing must be bounded by competence — and the evidence-grounded bound is an Elo band targeting ~75% success (Klinkenberg et al., moderate, production-proven at national scale), not the invented '≥5 prior exposures' gate, which is folklore. (2) BEING WATCHED — small on average but the average is the wrong statistic. Bond & Titus's reassuring 0.3-3% of variance is about a PASSIVE audience; this is a stake-holding opponent who picked your item, i.e. evaluation apprehension plus outcome interdependence, and hanzi recognition for a beginner is a non-dominant response — the impairment side of Zajonc's account. Uziel (2007): the small average hides opposite-signed subgroups. A 2025 CSCW experiment (n=85) found SUPPORTIVE spectatorship more detrimental than critical — so 'my friends will be nice about it' is not a mitigation. (3) PUBLIC POINT LOSS — NOT DEFENSIBLE as framed. Kluger & DeNisi (1996, strong): ~38% of feedback effect sizes are negative, and the moderator is task-level versus self-level attention; a public point loss carrying no task information is close to pure self-level feedback. Ames (1992, moderate): competitive public evaluation makes ability the salient attribution, harming low performers most. Bai et al. (2021, moderate): bottom-position players fare worse on absolute rankings. WHO IS HARMED: not the average player — the harm is concentrated in anxious, low-self-esteem and lower-proficiency players, and a co-located game among friends has heterogeneous proficiency BY CONSTRUCTION, which is exactly the condition under which outcome and ability become confounded. In a language product specifically this is not a neutral choice: anxiety is the largest measured affective moderator in SLA (r ≈ −0.36 across ~97 samples). HONESTY REQUIREMENT: there is NO controlled study showing public failure in a language game suppresses subsequent participation — the sweep and its adversary say so independently. The claim that it harms is an inference; the claim that it is harmless is equally unsupported. And 'players report they had fun' is not evidence of safety: enjoyment and anxiety are distinguishable dimensions (r ≈ −0.36, Dewaele & MacIntyre 2014), so a session can be both.
verdicts_on_design.change: Ship it with these changes, as v1 acceptance criteria rather than backlog. (a) KEEP opponent-dealt CATEGORIES; the engine picks the ITEM within an Elo band of the target player (~75% success target). The mechanic becomes 'pick their weak spot among things they can plausibly get', never 'ambush them'. (b) PRIVATE INPUT, PUBLIC RESOLUTION as a requirement, not an option — answers entered on the player's own device, shared view shows only 'answering' plus a progress bar, never the live selection; no spoken-answer item type in v1 (reading, not speaking, is the target skill, so privacy is free). (c) REPLACE the public point loss with a public CORRECTION: on a wrong answer the shared view carries the character and the correction at full size; the score delta is small, uncoloured, unanimated, no sound. Point GAINS may stay salient; point LOSSES must not. (d) A wrong answer currently costs points AND passes the turn — two visible consequences attached to one person's error. Separate them: keep the turn consequence, minimise the score consequence, or pass the turn on a rotation rather than on error. (e) Competence feedback before result on the end-of-match screen, for every player. (f) Improvement-based team scoring (Slavin) so the beginner can contribute the maximum. (g) Instrument the unanswered question: log turns voluntarily initiated, next-turn latency, abandonment and next-session return, keyed to whether the previous turn was a public failure — latency inflates before accuracy drops, so it is the early-warning metric. Justify all of it by retention and attendance, which you can measure, not by a promised learning gain, which the LCDH dispute makes unsafe to promise.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 1. The bet is how much scaffolding you give up: +1/-1 shows pinyin and English options; +5/-3 removes pinyin; +15/-10 also makes all four options Chinese signs.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The SHAPE is defensible; the CONTROL VARIABLE is not. Committing to an answer before feedback is a pretesting/generation structure with real (if contested) support, and it has strong game value — keep it. But scaffolding fading is an expertise-reversal phenomenon: Wang & Kalyuga found PARTIAL on-screen pinyin beat both full pinyin and no pinyin for more experienced learners, i.e. what should be faded is determined by measured competence on THIS learner and THIS character, not by how brave they feel at the moment of betting. A wager is a courage dial keyed to a points economy; the evidence keys the dial to per-item error history. Worse, the tiers are inverted relative to the transfer argument: the LOW bet (pinyin shown) is the guidance-reversal configuration — a training-only cue absent from every real menu and metro plate, which is the exact structure the design correctly bans for tone colour and radical highlighting. So the 'safe' tier is the one carrying the transfer risk, and the design does not acknowledge it. Finally, betting before seeing the item is an uninformed decision that adds an extraneous element to the card and stacks a stake on top of a timer on top of observation (do not stack pressures).
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the bet as a stake on POINTS only, and decouple it from scaffolding. Drive pinyin fading by measured competence: full ruby for an item's first ~3 exposures, then PARTIAL ruby on only the characters that item's error history flags weak, then none — store exposureCount and perCharacterErrorRate. If the wager must gate scaffolding for game reasons, gate the top tier by competence rather than courage (a player may bet it only in a category where they already hold component knowledge), and never let the harder tier carry the shorter timer — time pressure costs accuracy d ≈ 0.35 and hits difficult items and high-ability players hardest.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 1b. At +15/-10, all four options are rendered as Chinese signs.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: This silently changes the criterion task. The only surviving justification for multiple choice in this product is transfer-appropriate processing: the real-world task is 'see hanzi in the world, know what it means or what to do', and MC mirrors it when the stem is hanzi and the options are meanings in Dutch or English. Make all four options Chinese and the task becomes hanzi-to-hanzi visual matching, which a player can solve by glyph pattern-matching without ever accessing meaning — the shallow-processing failure mode that competitive distractors are supposed to prevent. It also maximises lure exposure at the tier where the learner is least equipped to reject the lures, which is precisely where the negative suggestion effect is largest and where Little et al.'s exculpatory mechanism is absent. The top tier therefore removes the one mechanism that makes MC defensible while amplifying its documented cost.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the meaning-side options in Dutch/English at every tier so the criterion task is constant across tiers. Escalate difficulty by removing pinyin, by raising distractor competitiveness within the visual-neighbour and situational-neighbour sets, by using harder real substrates, and by dropping from three options to a two-option forced discrimination against the single best confusable — all of which raise retrieval demand without changing what is being retrieved.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 2. Items render as the physical object they appear on — a station plate, a printed menu section with prices, a shopfront fascia, a shelf-edge price label, a hazard board.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Well-founded, and the strongest of the five hypotheses. The cue the encoding-specificity literature licenses is the character form AS IT WILL BE MET, and the transfer risk that runs through this whole cluster — every colour, spacing and highlight cue banned on guidance-reversal grounds — is the same argument pointing the same way. It is also the answer to the single-typeface transfer risk: mainland shopfronts, menus and packaging use 楷体, 隶书, 行书, 宋/明, condensed and expanded Hei, neon and hand-painted forms freely, and only transit and road signage is standardised, so a Simplified-only bank in one clean Hei face trains a form the learner will frequently not encounter. Real substrates deliver the variability for free.
verdicts_on_design.change: Extend it: render each item across ≥3 fully legible faces rotating across repetitions, plus ≥1 photographed real instance per high-value item, with a render_variant field on the attempt record so variability-trained items can be compared against single-face items on a photographed-signage transfer test. Store the traditional counterpart for characters whose forms diverge visibly and surface it on the reveal for shopfront/food items. Two signage facts absent from both sweeps: vertical setting is still common on shopfronts and banners, and metro signage is systematically bilingual and romanised — so subway should be the SMALLEST of the four content pillars, not an equal quarter, because a learner who cannot read 换乘 will read 'Transfer' printed underneath it.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 2b. Two of those treatments are deliberately hard to read, because real ones are.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The stated reason ('because real ones are') is fine. The word 'deliberately' is not, and the two readings have opposite evidential status. Perceptual disfluency as a learning aid is folklore: the Sans Forgetica result failed in four experiments plus independent replications, and large-sample nulls exist for disfluent fonts generally — three separate agents in this research programme flagged it unprompted, which tells you how reliably a team that has absorbed 'desirable difficulties' proposes it. Difficulty that helps comes from retrieval demand; difficulty that comes from degrading the pixels does not. Note also the accessibility exposure: a deliberately low-contrast or degraded target glyph fails WCAG 1.4.3, which under the EAA is not a style debate.
verdicts_on_design.change: Rewrite the rule as: a hard-to-read treatment ships ONLY when it faithfully reproduces signage the player will actually encounter — a weathered fascia, a grimy label, a low-contrast neon — and never as a difficulty manipulation. The target glyph must clear WCAG AA contrast in every treatment. If someone wants more difficulty, take it from the distractor set, the retrieval interval, or the removal of pinyin. Put 'perceptual disfluency' on the design document's explicit banned-rationales list so it cannot be reintroduced in six months.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 3. The component breakdown is the main teaching surface, promoted to the body of the reveal, advanced only by an explicit tap (牛肉 → 牛 ox + 肉 meat; swap the head for 猪肉/羊肉/鸡肉/鸭肉; then 肉 flattens to 月 on the left, so 肝 肠 肚 腰 脑).
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The PLACEMENT is exactly right and is the correction the evidence demands. Radical markings inside a character raise reaction time and lower recognition accuracy for L2 learners, and stroke-order animations lower accuracy too — so components must never decorate the glyph in the answering loop. Showing them as separate glyphs BESIDE the character, on a post-answer screen the user taps to open, is precisely the repair, and the explicit tap correctly gates reference material behind an interaction instead of forcing integration. Teaching semantic radicals as first-class content also genuinely works and transfers to untaught characters (Nguyen et al. 2017, n=54, quasi-experimental). BUT 'main teaching surface' over-claims in two ways. First, the elaborated-feedback advantage that would justify a heavyweight reveal is concentrated in higher-order outcomes and narrows sharply for the paired-associate recognition this product is scoped to — so mandatory elaboration on every item is a product bet, not an evidence mandate. Second, the reveal card is heading for overload: component tree plus confusable plus image plus pinyin plus audio plus score delta plus a say-it-aloud prompt is seven competing elements in a few seconds of party-game reveal.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the tap-gated post-answer breakdown; demote 'main teaching surface' to 'the reveal's primary optional layer'. Impose an element budget by integration load rather than by a chunk-count constant: one target, one decomposition, one contrast — everything else behind the tap. Make the discriminating-cue field TYPED (semantic_radical | contrast_character | position_in_compound | phonetic_hint) with phonetic_hint optional and hand-verified, never auto-generated: the phonetic component gives the exact syllable-plus-tone for only a minority of compounds, and a wrong hint delivered as 'elaborated feedback' in the protected resolution moment is worse than no elaboration. Add a per-component reliability marker — the 肉→月 unlock is a good example precisely because it needs one (肝肠肚腰脑 are flesh-月; 明朋期 are moon-月, and a learner told '月 means flesh' will mis-generalise). Finally, do NOT let the radical layer gate the scheduler: alphabetic-L1 learners process hanzi holistically at first and radical awareness develops with exposure, so front-loading 40-60 radicals teaches meaningless shapes. Allow whole-character recognition from item one for high-frequency signage targets and introduce the component layer as a second pass after ~50-100 characters of whole-form exposure; store the radical fields from the start (they cost nothing), just do not let them block presentation.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 4. A confusable is shown beside the target on resolution: 入口 beside 出口, 公斤 beside 斤, 麻 beside 辣.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Directly supported, and by an unusually on-point study: simultaneous PAIRED presentation of visually similar characters improved discrimination of subtle stroke differences relative to serial presentation, in n=183 zero-experience non-tonal-L1 learners — the same experiment that found colour coding slowed them down. Interleaving supplies the mechanism and the meta-analytic weight: interleaving helps most for inductive learning of visually similar categories, via discriminative contrast, which is the paradigm case here. The specific pairs chosen are also domain-correct, which matters: 入口/出口 is core signage vocabulary, and the adversary explicitly nominated it as one of the confusions that actually causes failure on real signage (unlike the classic teaching-list pairs 夭 and 巳, which never appear on consumer signage and should be dropped). Two qualifications. First, PLACEMENT: for consolidated items the confusable belongs in the OPTIONS at test time, not only in a post-hoc panel — that is where the discriminative work happens. Second, TIMING: competitive confusable distractors are actively risky during acquisition, because the exculpatory mechanism (retrieving why the alternatives are wrong) requires knowledge the beginner does not yet have, while the negative suggestion effect scales with lure plausibility.
verdicts_on_design.change: Make it conditional on consolidation state, which turns this into a scheduler rule rather than a content rule. First appearances of a sign: domain-plausible but non-confusable distractors, with the confusable shown only on the resolution panel. Once BOTH members of a pair are consolidated: the confusable moves into the options, and the pair is scheduled tight and alternating (a maximum gap within confusion_set_id), while repetitions of the same item stay widely spaced (a minimum gap ≥24h). Tag pairs as identical-stroke versus added-stroke and schedule identical-stroke pairs later — they were the harder condition. Every resolution card must name one feature that is TRUE of this item and FALSE of its paired lure. And warn the team that interleaving feels worse than blocking: do not let a satisfaction A/B kill it.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 5. Tone colour sits on the pinyin, never on the character.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The 'never on the character' half is doubly supported and should be stated even more strongly: colour-coding visually similar hanzi slowed learners' reaction times (visual overload), and radical markings inside a character raised RT and lowered recognition accuracy. No part of a hanzi glyph should ever be tinted, highlighted or outlined, for any reason. That is the strong half of this decision and it is correct.
verdicts_on_design.change: Tighten the rule to: no colour carries linguistic information anywhere in the product, including on pinyin. Reserve colour for interface chrome only. Justify it by WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Colour, Level A) plus the European Accessibility Act plus ~8% male / ~0.5% female CVD prevalence in a Dutch user base — legal and accessibility grounds that hold regardless of how the learning evidence reads. Add an explicit note for the future: if tone is ever added, do not default to colouring — the supported route is high-variability phonetic training, and tone colour on characters is unsupported folklore with an untested dependency risk.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 5b. The colour half specifically: does putting tone colour on the pinyin help?
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: No demonstrated benefit in this configuration, and a documented cost structure. Godfroid et al. (2017, n=303, three-week randomised training with delayed posttest — the reference study) found colour-mediated tone training WORKED but was slightly behind pitch contours and tone numbers, and crucially that DUAL-cue methods did not beat single-cue methods. Pinyin already carries tone in its diacritic, so tone colour on pinyin is exactly the dual-cue configuration that bought nothing — an added channel with added cost and no measured gain. Two further problems: the study trained auditory tone PERCEPTION, not glyph tinting in a reading interface, so the transfer is not direct; and for a silent visual signage-recognition product, tone is close to irrelevant to the criterion task. Note also that 'Godfroid proves colour is harmful' is an over-read in the other direction — it shows colour is not NECESSARY, not that it hurts.
verdicts_on_design.change: Do not ship tone colour on pinyin by default. If it ships at all, make it an off-by-default preference that never combines with a contour glyph (dual cues add cost with no gain) and that is fadeable. Spend the pinyin budget instead on rendering quality, which is the real risk the sweep missed: at a 48 px hanzi with 0.45em ruby, the information-bearing tone diacritic is a 2-3 px mark, and many system CJK fallback faces render Latin-with-diacritics from a different poorly-hinted fallback with ü frequently substituted or mis-stacked. Specify a diacritic-complete Latin face for pinyin (Noto Sans, Source Sans or Inter), ruby at ≥0.5em with a ≥20 CSS px absolute floor, and a build-time render test asserting ā á ǎ à / ē é ě è / ī í ǐ ì / ō ó ǒ ò / ū ú ǔ ù / ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ all render from the intended face. Verify ruby positioning in Safari.

directives.directive: Convert all physical sizing at ~160 CSS px per inch (6.3 CSS px/mm), never at 96, and never use CSS mm/in/pt units. Regenerate every size in the spec from this constant.
directives.basis: Android dp = 1/160in, iOS pt ≈ 1/163in; CSS Values L4 §6.2 fixes 1in=96px as nominal. The original sweep's mm and arcmin figures were all ~1.67x wrong, in the unsafe direction.

directives.directive: Hanzi type scale, at a 360 mm design viewing distance: absolute floor 28 CSS px for any glyph the learner must discriminate; answer-option hanzi 40-48 CSS px (60-73 arcmin); prompt hanzi 64-80 CSS px (97-121 arcmin); running-text hanzi ~27 CSS px with line-height 1.6-1.8, capped at 2-3 lines per card. Two independent type scales in custom properties: --latin-base 16px, --hanzi-base ~2-3x that.
directives.basis: 42 arcmin preferred-size finding (Ergonomics 2011; proofreading accuracy 73.3% at preferred vs 65.4% at minimum acceptable) plus Zhu/Su/Dong 2021 (n=115) 12pt-with-generous-line-spacing optimum, both re-derived at the corrected px/mm ratio. Chinese readers need ~1.7-2.0x the ETDRS acuity size Latin readers need.

directives.directive: Drop the stroke-count-driven font-size formula entirely. Set one generous size safe for the most complex character in the bank. Spend the complexity variable on chunking instead: cap a reading target at 6-8 hanzi (low complexity) or 4-6 when mean stroke count exceeds 12, computed at build time.
directives.basis: The +0.25 arcmin/stroke slope was unverifiable, the multiplicative formula did not implement it (+12% vs +20%), and it is a category error — acuity-threshold compensation does not transfer to a display running 5-10x above threshold. Wang, He & Legge's visual-span invariance is the defensible complexity finding.

directives.directive: Answer rows: 60-64 CSS px height, full content width, 8px gap, in the bottom 45% of the viewport, sticky to bottom with env(safe-area-inset-bottom). Minimum interactive height anywhere 56-60 CSS px. Street/walking mode raises every target to ~88 CSS px. Keep skip/quit/end-game ≥24 px from any answer option.
directives.basis: Parhi 9.2 mm = 58 CSS px (the one full-text-read study in this cluster); Conradi 14 mm = 88 CSS px; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 24x24 AA floor and SC 2.5.5 44x44 AAA; Bergstrom-Lehtovirta & Oulasvirta thumb-reach model.

directives.directive: Three options per item, not four. The third option must be a real competitor from the visual-neighbour or situational-neighbour list, never filler.
directives.basis: Rodriguez (2005) meta-analysis: three options optimal, more items per unit time with no psychometric loss — but only if retained options are the effective ones. Roediger & Marsh: MC accuracy falls as alternatives rise, and negative suggestion scales with the number of plausible lures. Also frees the width for 60-64px rows.

directives.directive: Build two separate distractor generators. Priority 1, visual neighbours from Unihan IDS / CHISE component decomposition and stroke-edit distance. Priority 2, situational neighbours from the domain corpus for that scene. Never a random unrelated character except on an item's first appearances (see the consolidation gate).
directives.basis: Ludewig et al. 2023 (close distractors raise difficulty AND discrimination); the corrected worked examples — 药店/酒店 share no component and are priority 2, while 大/太/犬/夫, 人/入/八, 日/白/百/自, 未/末, 己/已/巳, 千/干/于, 我/找 are genuine priority 1.

directives.directive: Gate confusable distractors on consolidation state: non-confusable domain-plausible distractors on a sign's first appearances, competitive confusables only once BOTH members of the pair are consolidated. Schedule confusion-set members tight and alternating (5-15 intervening items) while keeping ≥24h between correct repetitions of the same item. Schema: confusion_set_id, plus a min-gap (same item) and a max-gap (within set).
directives.basis: Brunmair & Richter interleaving-similarity moderator (tight juxtaposition) versus Roediger & Marsh negative suggestion (lure plausibility) and Little et al.'s requirement that the learner can already reject the alternatives.

directives.directive: Feedback is mandatory on every item and must be immediate and adjacent: the chosen option and the correct option in the same visual frame, with the correct hanzi, its meaning, and audio. Log every {itemId, lureId, timestamp}. Do NOT immediately re-present the item with the lure removed; re-queue it later in the same match and again the next day. Do NOT forbid reusing a lure as another item's correct answer.
directives.basis: Butler & Roediger 2008 (feedback cuts lure intrusions; the repair is corrective feedback, not re-testing); the confusable set IS the syllabus in a menu domain, so the no-reuse rule would force filler distractors and prohibit interleaving.

directives.directive: On a wrong answer the SHARED view carries the correct character and the correction at full size; the score delta is small, uncoloured, unanimated, silent. Point gains may be salient; point losses must not. Specify these sizes in rem with a stated contrast ratio, not in fixed px, and never as 'muted colour at 14px'.
directives.basis: Kluger & DeNisi task-level vs self-level moderator (~38% of feedback effects negative); the original 14px/17px numbers are invented and would fail WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.4.

directives.directive: Private input, public resolution, as a v1 requirement. Answers on the player's own device; the shared view shows only 'X is answering' plus a progress bar, never the live selection; no mid-round 'got it right in 2.1s' banner. No spoken-answer item type in v1 — state the modality as recognition-and-selection only.
directives.basis: Bond & Titus / Uziel plus the correction that a stake-holding opponent is a stronger manipulation than a passive audience; the sweep's own 'select/say the meaning' phrasing quietly admitted a spoken modality that collapses this mitigation.

directives.directive: Opponents choose the CATEGORY; the engine chooses the ITEM within an Elo band of the target player, targeting ~75% success. Run Elo on players AND items, updated after every response. Delete the '≥5 prior exposures' gate.
directives.basis: Klinkenberg et al. Math Garden — production-proven at national scale, a few lines of code, no training data, works from the first match. It makes the dealing mechanic safe by construction and supplies the item difficulties that improvement-based scoring needs.

directives.directive: Team scoring by improvement: contribution = f(correct_this_round − personal_rolling_baseline), clipped, baseline recomputed after each match. Replace the 'sum of correct × proportion of members contributing' formula.
directives.basis: Slavin's STAD equal-opportunity scoring. The proportion formula still rewards raw correctness, so the beginner remains a liability — the exact condition under which competitive structures do their documented damage among mixed-proficiency friends.

directives.directive: Show a filled dot per player per round indicating THAT they contributed — never how much, never how accurately. Contribution magnitude stays private, on the player's own device, after the match.
directives.basis: Karau & Williams Collective Effort Model requires identifiability to prevent loafing; Ames requires suppressing ability cues. Presence-of-contribution is an effort cue; magnitude is an ability cue. This resolves the tension rather than trading one harm for the other.

directives.directive: Ban from the shared interface: per-player accuracy visible to others, persistent cross-match individual ranking, any 'weakest player' label, any live losing-order during play, and any global leaderboard. Ship a per-session result screen only, ranked by 'characters you can now read' so the bottom player still sees a positive number.
directives.basis: Ames 1992 (ability attributions under public normative evaluation); Bai et al. 2021 (bottom-position players on absolute leaderboards); Almeida et al. 2023 (leaderboards/points/badges are the elements most often reported as causing negative effects).

directives.directive: End-of-match screen leads with an absolute competence statement for EVERY player ('You read 23 characters correctly tonight. 6 were new'); win/loss appears second and smaller. Award the same credit for retrievals attempted regardless of match outcome.
directives.basis: Vansteenkiste & Deci 2003 (losers given competence feedback retained motivation comparable to winners); Reeve & Deci 1996 (pressure to win undermines even winners). Lab studies, ~100 undergraduates, non-language tasks.

directives.directive: Separate the two consequences of a wrong answer. Currently it costs points AND passes the turn — two visible penalties attached to one person's error in front of the table. Keep the turn consequence and minimise the score consequence, or pass the turn on rotation rather than on error.
directives.basis: Kluger & DeNisi self-level feedback plus Ames ability attribution: minimise the number of publicly visible consequences that attach to a person rather than to the task.

directives.directive: Score correctness only; never award points for speed; break ties on total round time. Use a silent generous window with a subtle desaturation in its final fifth — no ticking digits, no shrinking bar until then. No timeout penalty on an item's first exposure. Provide an accessible way to turn off, adjust or extend the limit.
directives.basis: Time pressure d ≈ 0.35 accuracy cost hitting difficult items and high-ability players hardest; Kahoot review finds no learning advantage from speed scoring; visual timers reduce anticipatory anxiety without changing performance; WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable is a requirement, not a nicety.

directives.directive: Do not stack pressures: allow at most one of {visible countdown, live opponent monitoring, public score change} to be salient on any item. Since observation is inherent to a co-located game, the visible countdown is the one to remove. Whatever the bet-to-timer mapping, the harder tier must never carry the shorter timer.
directives.basis: Beilock & Carr choking-under-pressure (worry occupies the same WM the effortful strategy needs), plus the time-pressure finding that difficult items suffer most.

directives.directive: Set the response window from the product's own data: ship a generous default (the inherited 45/75/120s are already far above the 10-15s the general literature suggests, which is fine), then measure the latency distribution of correct responses and set the window near the 90th percentile. Delete the 5s/10s wait-time-derived numbers.
directives.basis: The wait-time corpus is 1970s-80s oral classroom discourse observation, graded weak and non-transferable to phone taps; no study exists on response-deadline length for L2 character recognition.

directives.directive: Log per attempt: itemId, presented_at, response latency (ms), correctness, chosen lure id, whether the item was opponent-dealt, is_active_turn, render_variant, the player's score position at that moment, and turns_since_last_public_failure as a stored field. Store locally in IndexedDB with opt-in sync; the PWA must work fully offline.
directives.basis: This is the minimum schema needed to answer in-house the question the field has not answered (does public failure suppress participation) as a query rather than a data-collection project. Latency inflates before accuracy drops under anxiety (Attentional Control Theory), so it is the tripwire.

directives.directive: If you sample anxiety, draw the items from a validated fear-of-negative-evaluation instrument (Leary's Brief FNE), not from FLCAS subscales — those subscales do not exist as validated factors. Justify every anxiety mitigation by retention and attendance, never by a promised learning gain.
directives.basis: Horwitz et al. defined FL anxiety as a situation-specific construct not composed of three subscales, and has objected publicly to subscale scoring; the anxiety→achievement causal direction is disputed (LCDH).

directives.directive: Downtime: if you want the vicarious-learning benefit, fill it with PAIRED talk about the ACTIVE player's item (two non-active players confer aloud on a prediction plus one discriminating cue). If instead you ship parallel private shadow items, justify them by retrieval practice, not by Chi et al., and accept that they forfeit the vicarious benefit.
directives.basis: Chi, Roy & Hausmann: the benefit attaches to paired dialogic observation; solo observers did substantially worse. The sweep's shadow-item design implements the failed arm.

directives.directive: Peer-instruction turn shape where the format allows: private individual answer on own phone → brief team confer → team commits → reveal + explanation → then ONE isomorphic item answered individually with no discussion. Schema needs isomorph_group_id.
directives.basis: Smith et al. 2009 (Science) showed improvement on a second isomorphic question answered alone, ruling out copying — but it is a single genetics-classroom study (~350 students), downgraded from strong to moderate by the critique. Freeman et al. 2014 supports the general active-learning direction.

directives.directive: If you build a 'say why' teammate slot, require selection of the discriminating cue (radical / contrast character / position), never free restatement of the answer, and expect g ≈ 0.3 at best. Score it small as a team bonus.
directives.basis: Kobayashi 2019 learning-by-teaching pooled ~0.3 (flagged by the sweep itself as one of its least reliable numbers); Roscoe & Chi showed tutors default to shallow knowledge-telling and only knowledge-building produces tutor learning. The Betty's Brain protégé result is a single n≈62 agent-specific study.

directives.directive: If you ship a post-answer prompt, make the options DOMAIN PROPOSITIONS ('which part told you? [semantic radical] [phonetic component] [the character it is NOT: 未]'), not strategy labels. Keep strategy chips only as instrumentation for confidence-based scheduling, and bill them as such.
directives.basis: Bisra et al.'s self-explanation pool requires generation or a structured domain menu naming a principle; a post-hoc strategy label is a judgment of learning, not an explanation, and cannot claim g = 0.55.

directives.directive: Always show the correct answer (KCR). Make elaboration mandatory only on items where a genuine discriminating cue exists. Type the cue field: semantic_radical | contrast_character | position_in_compound | phonetic_hint, with phonetic_hint optional and individually hand-verified, never auto-generated from a component table. Add a per-component reliability marker.
directives.basis: Van der Kleij's elaborated-feedback advantage is smallest for low-order recognition; the phonetic component gives the exact syllable-plus-tone for only a minority of compounds, so an auto-generated hint teaches errors inside the protected resolution moment.

directives.directive: Reveal-card element budget by integration load, not by a chunk constant: one target, one decomposition, one contrast. Everything else behind the explicit tap. On reveal, show the hanzi ALONE first (~800 ms, large, nothing else), then the gloss, then any image. Autoplay the correct answer's audio at reveal (post-answer, never simultaneous with the item).
directives.basis: Split attention and redundancy effects plus the picture-overshadowing literature (Samuels 1967; Torcasio & Sweller 2010; Solman & Wu 1995 tested pictures specifically as post-response feedback). Reading-while-listening benefits are largest for the most orthographically distant L2 (Koh 2024), but as a feedback event, not a simultaneous presentation.

directives.directive: One item per screen, no peek or preview of the next item. Drop the 10-20% paging time penalty adjustment — it is a survey-form artifact (page loads, navigation taps) that does not apply to a timed game where per-item time is set by the deadline. Size the round from the deadline directly.
directives.basis: Coherence/extraneous-material removal (at the corrected independent estimate g ≈ 0.3, not 1.00) plus the retrieval-support argument: adjacent on-screen items reduce the difficulty of the retrieval attempt. Mavletova & Couper is survey research and a weak analogue.

directives.directive: Persist full item state (itemId, options in shown order, elapsedMs, selection-in-progress) to IndexedDB on every visibilitychange and every option focus. On resume, show a ~2s reinstatement card (target hanzi + round context) before restarting the item timer from full — never drop the player into a running clock.
directives.basis: Monk, Trafton & Boehm-Davis: resumption lag grows with interruption duration and demand and is mitigated by goal-reinstating cues; WM capacity strongly predicts the lag, so the cost falls hardest on the players already most loaded.

directives.directive: Make the solo daily surface load-bearing, not a degenerate case of multiplayer. Persist nextDueAt per item across matches and devices; the match engine draws from a due-queue rather than a per-match item list. State the risk explicitly in the design doc: an app played when friends happen to meet cannot deliver spacing, which is the effect that actually drives hanzi retention.
directives.basis: Kim & Webb (98 effect sizes, N=3,411, L2-specific, g=0.40 for longer gaps on delayed tests); Cepeda et al. 317 experiments. This inverts the gbl sweep's recommendation that multiplayer be the primary code path — keep the transport-agnostic reducer, but the scheduling layer is the product.

directives.directive: Modelling stack: Elo on players and items, plus Settles & Meeder-style half-life regression. Do not build a neural knowledge tracer. Prefer per-item difficulty (Leitner/SM-2-style intervals) over a fixed 1/3/7/21/60-day ladder applied identically to 出口 and to 蒜蓉.
directives.basis: Gervet et al., Khajah et al., Wilson et al., Xiong et al.: DKT's advantage evaporates against simple models given equivalent features and reverses on small datasets, and part of its original reported advantage traced to duplicated benchmark records. This is a better basis for 'keep it simple' than the spacing-schedule-shape argument, and it degrades gracefully at n=20 users.

directives.directive: One notification per day maximum, self-scheduled by the user at onboarding. Build an explicit wean after 21 consecutive self-initiated on-time opens. Never a second same-day streak-loss notification. Track selfInitiatedOpens vs notificationOpens separately.
directives.basis: Nobbe et al. 2024 (n=85 children, 36 days) found reminders raised study on reminder days but produced no net increase versus a never-reminded control — substitution, not addition. The corroborating adherence percentages came from a non-indexed outlet and are struck.

directives.directive: Accessibility as build gates, not backlog: lang="zh-Hans" on every hanzi and lang="nl"/"en" on every gloss; rem-relative sizing verified at 200% OS text scaling; layout tolerant of text-spacing overrides; a diacritic-complete Latin face for pinyin with a build-time render test for ā á ǎ à / ē é ě è / ī í ǐ ì / ō ó ǒ ò / ū ú ǔ ù / ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ; ruby ≥0.5em with a ≥20 CSS px floor; Safari ruby-position verification.
directives.basis: European Accessibility Act applicable 28 June 2025, EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA; WCAG SC 1.4.1, 1.4.4, 1.4.12, 2.2.1, 2.5.8. The pinyin diacritic is a 2-3 px mark at typical ruby sizes and is frequently mis-rendered by system CJK fallback faces.

directives.directive: Split the design document into two labelled registers: (1) findings — source plus effect size; (2) decisions — owner, rationale, planned test. Every invented number goes in register 2. Add an explicit banned-rationales list: perceptual disfluency, Krashen's affective filter, tone colour on characters, and 'MC beats recall'.
directives.basis: The adversary graded the sweep's entire hard-number layer folklore precisely because it was indistinguishable from its findings layer. A design doc that cannot separate 'the literature says' from 'we decided' will not survive its first disagreement, and '≥5 exposures, per Horwitz et al.' will be in the codebase within a week.

directives.directive: Before any number here enters a build spec, re-fetch and read the results sections of: Godfroid et al. 2017, Skulmowski 2022, Rodriguez 2005, Li & Shi 2025, Hou & Jiang 2022, Zhu/Su/Dong 2021, Kluger & DeNisi 1996, Van der Kleij et al. 2015, Murayama & Elliot 2012, Bond & Titus 1983, Rowland 2014, and Klinkenberg et al. 2011. Regenerate every stroke count from Unihan kTotalStrokes and every decomposition from Unihan IDS/CHISE, asserted at build time.
directives.basis: One paper was read in full text across this entire cluster. Both adversarial critiques had zero scholarly egress and verified nothing. The Chinese-language errors found by pure arithmetic and domain checking (every hand-authored stroke count wrong, the flagship distractor example wrong) are the evidence that hand-authoring does not survive contact with a build.

cluster: systems — scheduling, adaptivity, measurement instruments, and content/asset licensing (sweep topics: srs-adaptivity; landscape-licensing)

settled.claim: FSRS massively outperforms the scheduler a team would otherwise hand-roll. On the identical corpus (9,999 Anki collections, 349,923,850 evaluation reviews), Log Loss: SM-2 0.722±0.017, SM-2-short 0.653±0.015, Anki-SM-2 0.616±0.011, SM-2-trainable (6 params) 0.581±0.012 — against FSRS-6 (21 params) 0.3456±0.0042 and the constant baseline AVG 0.3945±0.0051.
settled.scope: Recall-prediction calibration on Anki review logs that were themselves generated under Anki's SM-2-derived scheduling (selection bias: intervals are not randomised). Measures prediction, not learning outcome. The SM-2 rows are absent from the current README and were recovered from git history at commit 45f61b2 (2025-07-24).
sources: Open Spaced Repetition, srs-benchmark README, current — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark/main/README.md
Open Spaced Repetition, srs-benchmark README @45f61b2182c27da83839383ec3b044fa5ae27b47, 'Unweighted' table — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
settled.implication: Never hand-roll an SM-2/Leitner interval-doubling scheme. Take ts-fsrs as a dependency. The gap to a hand-rolled scheduler is ~0.38 log loss, roughly twenty times the 0.019 that per-user optimisation buys.

settled.claim: Default-parameter FSRS is benchmarked BELOW a zero-parameter moving average on calibration, and there is a documented four-parameter middle path that recovers most of the optimisation gain without an optimiser dependency.
settled.scope: Same benchmark, no-same-day split. FSRS-7 default param. (0 optimizable) Log Loss 0.3629±0.0044 / RMSE(bins) 0.0910±0.0014; FSRS-6 default param. 0.3661 / 0.0927; MOVING-AVG (0 params) 0.3369 / 0.05915. FSRS-6 pretrain (4 optimizable params, initial stability per grade) 0.3548±0.0042 / 0.0790±0.0012 / AUC 0.6999±0.0022; FSRS-6 full 21-param 0.3456.
sources: srs-benchmark README, current and @45f61b2 — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
settled.implication: Ship FSRS-6 pretrain-4, not defaults. Fit only the four initial-stability parameters once a player has a few hundred reviews — closed-form, no WASM optimiser, no model file. Shipping stock defaults means shipping the exact configuration whose numbers argue FSRS is unnecessary.

settled.claim: FSRS-6 forgetting-curve constants, read from two reference implementations. decay_param w[20] = 0.1542; the exponent is −w[20]; FACTOR = 0.9^(1/−w[20]) − 1 = 0.980346. R(t,S) = (1 + 0.980346·t/S)^(−0.1542), giving R = 0.9 at t = S. Inverse: I(r,S) = S·(r^(1/−0.1542) − 1)/0.980346.
settled.scope: Verified numerically against both fsrs-rs and ts-fsrs. FACTOR = 19/81 = 0.234568 belongs to decay 0.5 (FSRS-4.5/5) only; pairing 19/81 with 0.1542 gives a curve wrong at every t, and writing the exponent as +DECAY yields R(10S) = 1.443, a probability above 1. ts-fsrs's own docstring writes t/(9·S) while its code uses t/S — copy the code, not the docstring.
sources: fsrs-rs src/inference.rs, DEFAULT_PARAMETERS (21 values, w20 = FSRS6_DEFAULT_DECAY = 0.1542) and current_retrievability() — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs-rs/main/src/inference.rs
ts-fsrs packages/fsrs/src/algorithm.ts, computeDecayFactor / forgetting_curve / next_interval — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/ts-fsrs
settled.implication: Paste these four lines into the spec verbatim. Per-(player,item) state is exactly (stability f32, difficulty f32, last_review) = 16 bytes; compute R(t,S) inline at selection time and never persist a due-date, so a device asleep three weeks needs no catch-up job on wake.

settled.claim: ts-fsrs is one algorithm generation behind the benchmark table people quote: npm latest 5.4.1 = FSRS-6.0 (engines node>=20; 6.0.0-beta.7 on the beta tag), while the benchmark's best FSRS is FSRS-7.
settled.scope: npm registry metadata and ts-fsrs constant.ts read 2026-08-22.
sources: npm registry metadata for ts-fsrs — https://registry.npmjs.org/ts-fsrs
ts-fsrs packages/fsrs/src/constant.ts, FSRSVersion = 'using FSRS-6.0' — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/ts-fsrs
settled.implication: Do not quote FSRS-7 numbers in a document that specifies ts-fsrs. Quote FSRS-6 rows (full 0.3456, pretrain 0.3548, default 0.3661).

settled.claim: Half-Life Regression — the most-cited scheduler in the language-learning literature — is one of the worst performers on independent data, worse-calibrated than predicting the user's own constant average retention.
settled.scope: srs-benchmark, 9,999 collections. HLR Log Loss 0.4694±0.0073, RMSE(bins) 0.1275±0.0019, AUC 0.6369±0.0026; HLR-short 0.4929±0.0078 / 0.1397 / 0.6115; Ebisu v2 0.4989±0.0078; AVG (a 0-parameter constant) 0.3945±0.0051. HLR retains above-chance ranking (AUC 0.637) but its absolute probabilities are badly wrong — exactly what matters if predicted recall drives item selection.
sources: srs-benchmark README, HLR / HLR-short / Ebisu rows — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016), A Trainable Spaced Repetition Model for Language Learning, ACL 2016, 1848–1858 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf
settled.implication: Do not implement half-life regression despite its convenient closed form p = 2^(−t/h). If you want a cheap closed-form retrievability for the group-selection scoring function, use FSRS-6's R(t,S) — same cost, far better calibrated, and it ships with the library you already installed.

settled.claim: The famous '+12% Duolingo engagement' is NOT HLR beating Leitner. Head-to-head, HLR versus Leitner produced no significant engagement gain and a significant 7.3% DROP in practice sessions; the +12% came from making the model SIMPLER.
settled.scope: Settles & Meeder 2016, Table 4, read from the paper PDF; * = p<0.001. Experiment I, HLR vs Leitner, 6 weeks, just under 1M randomised students: Any activity +0.3 (n.s.), New lesson +0.3 (n.s.), Practice −7.3*. Experiment II, HLR-lex (lexeme-tag features REMOVED) vs HLR, 2 weeks, 3.3M students: +12.0* / +1.7* / +9.5*. The outcome measured throughout is next-day retention — no vocabulary gain was measured in either experiment.
sources: Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016, §4.3–4.4 and Table 4 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf
ACL Anthology record P16-1174 — https://aclanthology.org/P16-1174/
settled.implication: Never justify a design decision — internally or in app copy — on the grounds that a smarter scheduler drives engagement. The largest industry experiment on exactly that question found the opposite. Do not instrument the PWA to optimise next-day return; treat session-return as a guardrail only.

settled.claim: No published spaced-repetition model discriminates item-level recall much above chance in a real language-learning product, and in Duolingo's own evaluation the crude Leitner box had the highest AUC of any model tested.
settled.scope: Settles & Meeder 2016 Table 2, 12.9M student-word traces over two weeks of production logs. MAE↓ / AUC↑ / Spearman: HLR 0.128 / 0.538 / 0.201; HLR-lex 0.128 / 0.537 / 0.160; Leitner 0.235 / 0.542 / −0.098; Pimsleur 0.445 / 0.510 / −0.132; Logistic Regression 0.211 / 0.513. Every model within 0.04 of chance. HLR's celebrated '45% error reduction' is MAE only. Flashcard data is easier: srs-benchmark AUC reaches FSRS-7 0.7069±0.0023 and RWKV-P 0.8329±0.0017.
sources: Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016, Table 2 and §4.1 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf
srs-benchmark AUC column — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
settled.implication: Never show a player a numeric strength or mastery percentage for an item — the model cannot support that precision and a wrong number is a visible, trust-destroying lie. Three coarse states per item, distinguished by shape and fill (NEW outline / LEARNING half / SOLID filled). Aggregate progress at deck level only, where averaging over ~100 items makes the estimate defensible.

settled.claim: Rich per-item difficulty features overfit, produced user-visible unfairness, and broke cold start in production — and the documented industrial fix was to delete them.
settled.scope: Settles & Meeder 2016 §4.4, an industrial post-mortem at one company, not a controlled test of the mechanism. Users reported that particular words 'would decay rapidly, regardless of how often they practiced'; traced to lexeme-tag features with highly negative weights despite L2 regularisation. Simultaneously new courses had no training data for those weights. The two top variants were 'virtually tied' on offline metrics — offline evaluation gave no signal the feature-rich model was harmful.
sources: Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016, §4.4 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf
settled.implication: Cold-start item difficulty as a heavily shrunken, hard-clamped prior: predicted_initial_difficulty = global_mean + 0.3 × (feature_prediction − global_mean), features limited to stroke count, character count, frequency band and whether all component characters are introduced; clamp the resulting initial interval to [0.5×, 1.5×] the global new-item interval; empirical-Bayes weight n/(n+5) so observed responses fully override after 5. Store prior_difficulty and observed_difficulty as separate columns so the prior can be switched off in one line.

settled.claim: Deep knowledge tracing does not reliably beat logistic regression over hand-built count features: across eight standard datasets Best-LR and DKT split the wins 4–4 with gaps of 0.01–0.06 AUC — and sequence length does NOT explain which wins.
settled.scope: Gervet, Koedinger, Schneider & Mitchell (2020), JEDM 12(3), results table read in full. Best-LR wins: assist09 0.77 v 0.75, bridge_algebra06 0.80 v 0.79, algebra05 0.83 v 0.82, spanish 0.86 v 0.83. DKT wins: assist12 0.77 v 0.75, assist15 0.73 v 0.70, assist17 0.77 v 0.71, statics 0.83 v 0.82. The two LONGEST-sequence datasets (spanish median 1,924; bridge_algebra06 median 1,362) both go to logistic regression; the SHORTEST (assistments15, median 20) goes to DKT. IRT-only is clearly worse everywhere (0.64–0.79); PFA is erratic (0.62–0.85).
sources: Gervet, Koedinger, Schneider & Mitchell (2020), When is Deep Learning the Best Approach to Knowledge Tracing?, JEDM 12(3) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theophilee/learner-performance-prediction/master/README.md
Liu, Z. et al. (2022), pyKT, NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks — https://github.com/pykt-team/pykt-toolkit
settled.implication: Ship a logistic regression over six integers per (player, item-skill): total attempts, total correct, attempts on this character/word, correct on this character/word, log1p(days since last attempt), item difficulty. ~24 bytes per player-item, SGD in milliseconds on a phone, no ML dependency. Write 'no neural knowledge tracing' into the architecture doc with these citations — but justify it by gap size and engineering cost, NOT by a sequence-length rule the evidence contradicts.

settled.claim: Bayesian Knowledge Tracing with forgetting is a standard, implemented variant — the reason not to ship BKT is its binary latent state, not an inability to forget.
settled.scope: pyBKT exposes `forgets` as a first-class model option (model.fit(..., forgets=True), cross-validated in the README's own examples) and documents it as 'the probability of transitioning to the "not knowing" state given "known"'; the transition matrix contains both learns and forgets. The no-forget premise is true of Corbett & Anderson's 1995 canonical formulation only.
sources: pyBKT README, model variants and parameter documentation, incl. Badrinath et al. (EDM 2021, 468–474) and Bulut et al. (Psych 5(3), 770–786) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CAHLR/pyBKT/master/README.md
settled.implication: Keep the recommendation (no BKT), drop the stated reason. Retrievability in a reading task is continuous and time-dependent, and the logistic-over-counts model is cheaper and at least as accurate. The UI consequence is independent and stands: no permanent 'mastered' badge, no achievement that certifies a character forever. SOLID must be able to fall back to LEARNING when R decays below ~0.7, surfaced as '3 characters need a refresh', not as a demotion.

settled.claim: Randomised field experiments on algorithmic item selection and scheduling DO exist, with public code and released trial data — the closest published work to the group-selection problem is single-learner session-level selection.
settled.scope: Repository existence, design and code confirmed; the papers themselves were not retrievable this session. Upadhyay, Lancashire, Moser & Gomez-Rodriguez (2021), npj Science of Learning 6:26, doi 10.1038/s41539-021-00105-8 — a randomised trial in a live commercial app (Swift driving-theory) of which items to serve in a session the learner initiated, evaluated against competitive baselines, trial data released. Tabibian et al. (2019), PNAS 116(10):3988–3993 — reviewing intensity as stochastic optimal control. Nioche, Murena, de la Torre-Ortiz & Oulasvirta (2021), IUI '21, 445–453.
sources: Networks-Learning/spaced-selection — 'a method for optimally selecting the items which the user should revise during a given session'; randomised trial; data released — https://github.com/Networks-Learning/spaced-selection
Networks-Learning/memorize — code and data for Tabibian et al. PNAS 2019 — https://github.com/Networks-Learning/memorize
Open Spaced Repetition wiki, Research-resources — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/awesome-fsrs/wiki/Research-resources
settled.implication: Read both before writing pickItem — their single-learner objective is what any hand-rolled squared-deviation heuristic is a substitute for. And never write 'no experimental evidence exists' in the design document; it is false and would be embarrassing.

settled.claim: There is a de-facto standard review-log schema, and adopting it costs nothing.
settled.scope: FSRS Optimizer specification, explicitly intended as 'a ubiquitous standard for spaced repetition review logs'.
sources: Open Spaced Repetition, FSRS Optimizer review_logs schema — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs-optimizer
settled.implication: Required: card_id, review_time (timestamp in MILLISECONDS, UTC), review_rating ∈ {1 Again, 2 Hard, 3 Good, 4 Easy}. Recommended: review_state ∈ {0 New, 1 Learning, 2 Review, 3 Relearning}, review_duration (ms). Per-user: timezone (IANA) and day_start = 4 (04:00 local, so a late-night session counts as one day). Add product columns: player_id, mode (solo|group), role (answered|co_committed|observed|exposure), format_tier, n_alternatives, eligible_for. review_duration is free to record and is your only signal for 'was this player actually looking at the screen'.

settled.claim: The k-alternative guessing correction inverts any controller that targets a fixed observed accuracy across different response formats.
settled.scope: Arithmetic identity, solved numerically: P(correct) = R + (1−R)/k. Holding observed accuracy at 0.85 gives true R = 0.700 in 2AFC, 0.800 in 4AFC, 0.850 in free recall — so the weakest players, on the easiest format, sit at the LOWEST true retrievability, the opposite of the intent. At that operating point roughly half of all 2AFC 'correct' responses are guesses. A post-hoc grade discount does not fix it: it changes what is recorded, not what the controller targets.
sources: Standard k-AFC guessing correction, solved numerically 2026-08-22
settled.implication: Set the target in retrievability, never in observed accuracy. To hit a common true R of 0.85: target observed 0.925 in 2AFC, 0.8875 in 4AFC, 0.85 in free entry. Better: do not feed 2-choice outcomes into stability updates at all — log them role: exposure. Store format_tier and n_alternatives on every row so the correction can be re-derived later.

settled.claim: HSK 3.0 exact structure, twice independently parsed from the official lists: 3,000 reading characters = 300 at each of levels 1–6 plus 1,200 at 七—九级, zero duplicates; 11,092 words across nine levels = 500 / 772 / 973 / 1,000 / 1,071 / 1,140 / 5,636; separate handwriting sub-lists 初等 300 / 中等 400 / 高等 500 = 1,200.
settled.scope: Source is 《国际中文教育中文水平等级标准》 GF 0025-2021 via Pleco's OCR (elkmovie/hsk30). The files carry the header "OCR'ed but not extensively proofread (yet)" — the aggregate structure checks out exactly, individual entries are unproofread OCR. Cumulative words through level 6 = 5,456, within ~9% of HSK 2.0's ~5,000 at level 6; the apparent 'doubling' at the top end is entirely the newly created 7–9 band sitting above the old ceiling.
sources: elkmovie/hsk30, charlist.txt and wordlist.txt, parsed independently by two agents 2026-08-22 — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30
settled.implication: What HSK certifies is asymmetric and it is the single best onboarding line available: the official standard demands 3,000 characters READ against only 1,200 written. A reading-only product is aligned with the standard, not a shortcut around it. Say so once and the 'shouldn't I learn to write?' objection is gone.

settled.claim: HSK character-to-word coverage recomputed from the official lists, correcting both endpoints of the original sweep.
