settled.claim: A serverless co-located multiplayer PWA is not achievable on iPhones as stated: there is no browser API for local peer discovery, and the default STUN server everyone inherits is blocked in the country the product exists for.
settled.scope: caniuse feature data read 2026-08-22: rtcpeerconnection 'y' in ios_saf, safari, chrome, and_chr; web-bluetooth 'n' in ios_saf through 26.5 and safari through 27/TP, marked non-standard. WebRTC data channels are universally supported but require out-of-band signalling — an exchange of SDP offers/answers over something. Separately: the default in nearly every WebRTC tutorial and library is stun.l.google.com:19302, a Google host blocked in mainland China (inferred, not verifiable from this sandbox). Screen Wake Lock is supported everywhere per the same dataset and is never mentioned in the design.
sources: caniuse features-json: web-bluetooth and rtcpeerconnection, read 2026-08-22 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Fyrd/caniuse/main/features-json/web-bluetooth.json
settled.implication: For a CO-LOCATED game this is fortunate rather than fatal, because you need no NAT traversal: all phones are on the same LAN or hotspot. Configure an EMPTY iceServers array explicitly (never inherit a library default), host candidates only, star topology with one session host sharing a join code by QR. Ship a same-device pass-and-play fallback — it is the only genuinely zero-dependency option. Make the game state machine transport-agnostic: a pure reducer over {playerId, itemId, choice, elapsedMs} with the transport (same-device handoff, BroadcastChannel, WebRTC datachannel) swapped underneath. Test in aeroplane mode plus hotspot. Take a Screen Wake Lock for the session. Before ship, enumerate every external host the PWA touches at runtime and confirm each is reachable from inside China; fonts and STUN are the two that were missed.

settled.claim: iOS Safari evicts script-writable storage — IndexedDB, Cache API and service-worker caches — after roughly seven days of non-use for sites not installed to the home screen.
settled.scope: Cited from WebKit platform documentation and ITP storage-eviction announcements; not re-verified against a live source this session. This destroys exactly the returning-user history that a fortnightly-play product depends on.
sources: WebKit storage policy, seven-day cap on script-writable storage for non-installed web apps (WebKit blog / ITP announcements) — cited from platform documentation, not re-verified
settled.implication: Prompt Add to Home Screen on the first successful session. Make an explicit JSON export/import (or sync) the durable store with local as cache, not the reverse — this is in direct tension with 'no server, no account', and the tension must be resolved in the spec rather than discovered in production. Test the seven-day eviction case explicitly in QA; it is the failure mode that silently deletes a returning user's entire history.

settled.claim: The photographed-signage corpus carries copyright, trademark and privacy exposure in two jurisdictions, and the proposed marketing line makes it worse by advertising the provenance.
settled.scope: Legal analysis from first principles, flagged for counsel, not asserted as settled — no case law was reachable. The TEXT and the IMAGE have completely different risk profiles. Dish names and station names are short factual phrases with thin-to-no copyright, and a frequency count over them is your own work. Photographs are not: menu layout and typography, dish photography, package artwork and shopfront logos are protected expression, and a photographed fascia carries a live trademark. A Dutch controller photographing on private premises engages GDPR the instant a person is in frame; PRC PIPL applies at collection; the PRC Surveying and Mapping Law restricts geographic data collection by foreign nationals, and photographing certain installations is restricted.
sources: Legal analysis from first principles; PRC PIPL (2021) and Surveying and Mapping Law; GDPR Art. 9 and Art. 44–49 — Chinese government sources 403-blocked, routed to counsel rather than asserted
settled.implication: Ship transcribed text set in your own licensed font; never ship the source photograph. Photographs are internal reference material, kept out of the repo and the bundle. If capture ships at all: strictly on-device, no GPS, no peer sync of images, no server-side pooling — store only the extracted character list. Drop the 'we photographed 200 real menus in Chengdu' line; it converts a private research practice into a public admission for no benefit that 'built from real-world signage' does not also deliver.

settled.claim: The proposed 60-item yes/no check-in cannot function as a learning-outcome metric: its minimum detectable change between two sittings is about 27 percentage points.
settled.scope: Arithmetic from the instrument's own specification (40 real items + 20 pseudowords, corrected score = hits/40 − false_alarms/20). At hit rate 0.75 and false-alarm rate 0.10, SE ≈ 0.096, so a single score carries a 95% interval of roughly ±19 points and the difference between two sittings has SE ≈ 0.136, i.e. MDC ≈ 0.27. Even at a flattering 0.90/0.05 the MDC is ≈0.19. Resolving a 10-point change needs ~284 real + 142 pseudowords (~10 minutes); 5 points needs ~1,700 items.
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 from binomial sampling error over the instrument's own specification
settled.implication: Running it every ten sessions produces a number that moves mostly at random, which is worse than no number because the team will read the noise. Demote it to a PLACEMENT instrument at onboarding — which also supplies the cold-start calibration a mixed-ability table needs — and a coarse band estimate. If a discrete hero number is wanted, run ONE long test (400+ items) twice a season, not a short one ten times.

settled.claim: The yes/no format imports an assumption about wordhood that Chinese does not supply, and the standard pseudoword recipe is wrong.
settled.scope: Graded weak-to-moderate; the Chinese lexical-decision and segmentation literature could not be reached, and the foundational yes/no validation work (Meara & Buxton 1987, Language Testing 4(2); Mochida & Harrington 2006, Language Testing 23(1); Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt 2012, Language Testing 29(4)) was likewise unretrievable. Two problems stand on their own. (1) Pseudo-CHARACTERS are rejected on sight, collapsing the false-alarm rate the correction divides by. Pseudo-WORDS are the valid stimulus — but the worked example 票冷 is a noun+adjective juxtaposition with no licit compound structure and fails the same way. (2) Chinese has no word delimiters and 'is this a word?' is a judgement on which native readers and competing segmentation standards disagree substantially.
sources: Meara & Buxton (1987), Language Testing 4(2), 142–154 — NOT RETRIEVED — https://doi.org/10.1177/026553228700400202
Mochida & Harrington (2006), Language Testing 23(1), 73–98 — NOT RETRIEVED — https://doi.org/10.1191/0265532206lt321oa
Pellicer-Sánchez & Schmitt (2012), Language Testing 29(4), 489–509 — NOT RETRIEVED — https://doi.org/10.1177/0265532211430367
settled.implication: Build pseudowords by substituting one character of an attested two-character compound with a frequency-matched character sharing the semantic radical, so the string is morphologically well-formed but non-existent. Better still for a READING product: keep the yes/no format but ask about readability of a real string in context ('can you read this sign?') over cropped real signage, with distractor strings drawn from a domain the player has not unlocked. That measures what the product promises and sidesteps wordhood entirely.

settled.claim: The documented failure modes of adaptive selection are over-short intervals on a feature-defined slice, superlinear review-volume growth from raising retention, and — reasoned rather than located — massed-practice inflation and sustained-failure demotivation.
settled.scope: Directly evidenced: the Duolingo post-mortem (Settles & Meeder §4.4) is a documented production instance of an adaptive system driving a subset of items to punishing intervals, with user complaints, invisible in offline metrics because the two variants were 'virtually tied'. Also evidenced: FSRS's own retention analysis frames scheduling as minimising workload/knowledge, which makes explicit that raising retention drives review volume up superlinearly. Massed-practice inflation and the demotivation path were NOT located in the literature this session. Note the massed-practice point is not hypothetical here: in a party game the same item may legitimately recur within an evening.
sources: Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016 §4.4 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf

Open Spaced Repetition, The-Optimal-Retention wiki (min workload/knowledge, Brent's method, 0.70–0.97 range, 0.90 default) — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs4anki/wiki/The-Optimal-Retention
settled.implication: Four HARD constraints in the selection function, none tunable by the difficulty controller: (1) no item is scored twice in one session — if it recurs, log role: exposure and do not update stability; (2) an item may not advance out of LEARNING on same-session corrects, require one correct in a later session; (3) cap consecutive incorrect answers per player at 2 — on the third, force-inject an item where that player's R > 0.95 regardless of what the group objective wants; (4) cap any item's per-player minimum interval at 1 day. Plus one monitoring query you actually look at: the per-item distribution of mean interval, so a slice of the bank collapsing to the floor is visible before players complain.

settled.claim: Co-located group retrieval suppresses individual recall — 'collaborative inhibition' — and the compensating benefit lives in re-exposure after the retrieval, not during it.
settled.scope: Groups recalling together retrieve less than the pooled total of the same people recalling alone, because exposure to others' retrievals disrupts each individual's own retrieval organisation; post-collaborative individual recall is often improved via re-exposure. Well-replicated, textbook-level, but CITED FROM KNOWLEDGE — every scholarly host was 403-blocked and the classic sources could not be re-verified. Scope note: the classic paradigm is free recall of word lists in the lab, not L2 orthographic recognition in a game, so the mechanism transfers by argument, not by demonstration.
sources: Weldon, M. S. & Bellinger, K. D. (1997), JEP:LMC 23(5) — NOT VERIFIED
Basden, B. H., Basden, D. R., Bryner, S. & Thomas, R. L. (1997), JEP:LMC 23(5) — NOT VERIFIED
Rajaram, S. & Pereira-Pasarin, L. P. (2010), Perspectives on Psychological Science 5(6) — NOT VERIFIED
settled.implication: This is the central design constraint for a co-located multiplayer LEARNING game. Every player must produce their own answer privately on their own phone before any answer is revealed to the room: simultaneous blind commit → reveal → social scoring. Never a buzzer, never turn-taking where three players watch one player retrieve. The social layer belongs in reveal and scoring, where the re-exposure benefit lives, not in retrieval, where the inhibition lives. This is also what makes per-player scheduling coherent: every player has actually retrieved every item.

settled.claim: The closest well-developed prior art for one-item-many-learners is the classroom-response-system (clicker) literature, and its central result is a transfer result, not a copying artefact.
settled.scope: Smith, Wood, Adams, Wieman, Knight, Guild & Su (2009), Science 323(5910), 122–124, n≈350 in a genetics course. Design: individual clicker answer → peer discussion → re-answer → then a SECOND, isomorphic question answered ALONE with no further discussion. Performance on the second, independently-answered question improved, ruling out 'they just copied'. Sits inside the broader active-learning result (Freeman et al. 2014, PNAS, k=225: exam performance d ≈ 0.47). Scope limit: undergraduate STEM concept questions, not L2 orthographic recognition, and not a spaced-repetition context.
sources: Smith, M. K. et al. (2009), Why peer discussion improves student performance on in-class concept questions, Science 323(5910), 122–124
Freeman, S. et al. (2014), Active learning increases student performance in STEM, PNAS 111(23), 8410–8415
settled.implication: This is the nearest thing to a validated turn shape for a shared-stimulus multi-learner round, and it is a four-beat sequence, not two: (1) private individual answer on own phone, (2) brief confer, (3) commit, (4) reveal + explanation — then immediately ONE isomorphic item answered individually with no discussion. That last beat is the load-bearing part and it requires an isomorph_group_id field on the item bank. Note the tension with collaborative inhibition: beat (2) must never precede beat (1).

settled.claim: The European Accessibility Act converts several discretionary UI recommendations into legal requirements for a Dutch-published consumer app.
settled.scope: Directive (EU) 2019/882 applicable since 28 June 2025 to consumer digital services, via EN 301 549 v3.2.1 incorporating WCAG 2.1 Level AA. Bites specifically: SC 1.4.1 Use of Colour (colour never the sole carrier); SC 1.4.3 / 1.4.6 contrast (4.5:1 AA, 7:1 AAA); SC 1.4.4 Resize Text (functional at 200%); SC 1.4.12 Text Spacing (must tolerate user overrides); SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable (the user can turn off, adjust or extend a time limit); SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) 24×24 CSS px at AA, with 44×44 being SC 2.5.5 at AAA; and lang attributes — lang="zh-Hans" on every hanzi and lang="nl"/"en" on every gloss, without which the app is unusable with a screen reader and non-conformant.
sources: Directive (EU) 2019/882 (European Accessibility Act), applicable from 28 June 2025
EN 301 549 v3.2.1, incorporating WCAG 2.1 Level AA
settled.implication: Two of the product's stated mechanics engage this directly. The 45s/75s/120s bet timers and any minimum reveal dwell engage SC 2.2.1 — ship a 'no timers' setting. And SC 1.4.1 settles the tone-colour question on legal grounds regardless of how the pedagogy reads.

contested.question: Is FSRS actually better than a zero-parameter moving average?
contested.side_a: On the no-same-day split (9,999 collections, 349,923,850 reviews) MOVING-AVG wins on both calibration metrics: Log Loss 0.3369±0.0042 and RMSE(bins) 0.05915 versus FSRS-7 recency 0.3414 / 0.0627 and FSRS-7 0.3437 / 0.0655. FSRS leads only on AUC (0.7069 vs 0.7001).
contested.side_b: On the same-day split (10,000 collections, 519,296,315 reviews) the ordering flips: FSRS-7 recency 0.3236±0.0041 LL and 0.06339±0.00088 RMSE(bins) versus MOVING-AVG 0.3301±0.0044 and 0.0789±0.0010. FSRS-7, FSRS-7 preset and FSRS-7 sched. penalties all beat MOVING-AVG there on both calibration metrics.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Which split you consider representative. A co-located party game legitimately re-shows the same card within one evening, so the SAME-DAY table is the more relevant one — which favours FSRS. But the honest headline in either direction is 'FSRS and a moving average are within ~0.007 log loss of each other', not 'FSRS wins' and not 'a moving average wins'. Independently: MOVING-AVG cannot produce an interval and the benchmark README itself says it 'has no practical applications', so it is not an alternative scheduler in any case.
sources: srs-benchmark README, both result tables — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark/main/README.md

contested.question: Should a scheduler be implemented at all, given the play frequency this product will actually see?
contested.side_a: NO. A co-located party game at a restaurant table generates almost no longitudinal per-item review history. The only regime it will reach is default-parameter FSRS, which is benchmarked at Log Loss 0.3629 — worse than a zero-parameter moving average and worse than every optimised variant. Storing a full timestamped review log is real architectural complexity buying a benefit that cannot materialise at fortnightly play. Store (n_seen, n_correct, last_seen, last_outcome) and select with a recency-weighted difficulty estimate; revisit FSRS only if telemetry shows several-times-a-week play.
contested.side_b: YES, but as pretrain-4, not defaults. FSRS-6 pretrain (4 optimizable parameters, initial stability per grade) scores 0.3548 — beating both the moving average on the same-day split and default-parameter FSRS everywhere — and it is a closed-form fit over a handful of first-review outcomes, not an optimiser dependency. And the review log is free to store now and impossible to reconstruct later.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Median inter-session gap, which is measurable from the first cohort. This is the same falsification test as the biggest product risk: instrument sessions_per_week and days_between_sessions split by mode from day one. If median multiplayer gap exceeds ~7 days while solo sits under ~3, the solo daily surface is the product and the scheduler earns its keep there, not in the party game.
sources: srs-benchmark README, current and @45f61b2 — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark

contested.question: Is Half-Life Regression the right reference implementation for a cold-start language PWA?
contested.side_a: Two separate critiques recommend it: HLR is a spaced-repetition model trained on exactly this data shape (item features + lag + outcome), it is a few dozen lines, it runs client-side, its half-life output is directly interpretable as next_due_at, and it 'beat Leitner and Pimsleur in production at Duolingo'.
contested.side_b: HLR is one of the worst-calibrated models on independent data — Log Loss 0.4694±0.0073 against the constant baseline's 0.3945 — and the production claim is false: HLR versus Leitner produced no significant engagement gain and a significant −7.3% drop in practice sessions, while Leitner had the nominally HIGHEST AUC in Duolingo's own Table 2 (0.542 vs HLR's 0.538).
contested.what_it_turns_on: Nothing, once the sources are opened — this resolves. Side A is graded 'memory-sourced, NOT verified this session' in both critiques that assert it. Side B was read from the benchmark table and the paper PDF directly. DO NOT IMPLEMENT HLR. The reason it keeps being recommended is that its reputation propagated faster than its numbers, which is exactly the failure mode this digest exists to stop.
sources: srs-benchmark README, HLR rows — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark
Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016, Tables 2 and 4 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf

contested.question: Subset the font from the item bank, or ship the whole 1.09 MB chinese-simplified file?
contested.side_a: SHIP THE WHOLE FILE. The measured saving is 1.09 MB → 0.42 MB at 3,000 characters, only 2.6x, and shipping the whole file deletes the entire 'walk the bank, emit codepoints, fail the build on a miss' risk class. On an offline-first PWA where a missing glyph is unrecoverable at a restaurant table with no signal, 670 KB is cheap insurance.
contested.side_b: SUBSET. At a 1,200-character bank the subset is 164.0 KB against 1.09 MB — a 925 KB saving on a 3 MB install budget that also has to hold the item bank, the app shell and a Latin face. Keep the CI gate and the risk is engineered away.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Final bank size and install budget. The crossover is around 2,000–2,500 characters (277.4 KB at 2,000, 418.6 KB at 3,000). Below ~1,500 characters subsetting is clearly worth it; above ~2,500 the insurance argument wins. EITHER WAY, if you subset, the CI gate is mandatory and non-negotiable — it is the only thing standing between you and tofu boxes on a customer's phone with no network to recover.
sources: Measured 2026-08-22 with fontTools/pyftsubset against @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0 — https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fontsource/noto-sans-sc

contested.question: Is 85% the right session accuracy target?
contested.side_a: Wilson, Shenhav, Straccia & Cohen (2019), Nature Communications 10:4646 derives an optimal training error rate of ≈15.87% (accuracy ≈84.13%, the normal point at one SD). The arithmetic identity checks out: Φ(−1) = 0.158655.
contested.side_b: The derivation covers gradient-descent-trained binary classifiers on two-alternative perceptual discrimination with a CONTINUOUSLY tunable difficulty parameter. Vocabulary recognition is discrete-item retrieval from declarative memory, where the governing quantity in every deployed system is desired retention — an economic trade-off between review cost and forgetting cost, not a learning-rate optimum. FSRS frames it exactly that way: minimise workload/knowledge, solved with Brent's method, 0.70–0.97 reasonable range, 0.90 default.
contested.what_it_turns_on: The paper itself, which NEITHER the sweep NOR the critique could open (nature.com and doi.org 403-blocked; the authors' replication repo did not resolve for the reviewer). Treat 15.87% as cited-from-record. The load-bearing part is the boundary condition, and it does not need the number: USE TWO SEPARATE KNOBS. FSRS desired retention stays at 0.90 and governs when an item returns across days; session pacing is a separate controller — and after the guessing correction it must be specified in RETRIEVABILITY, not in observed accuracy.
sources: Wilson, R. C. et al. (2019), The Eighty Five Percent Rule for optimal learning, Nature Communications 10:4646 — NOT RETRIEVED — https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-019-12552-4
Open Spaced Repetition, The-Optimal-Retention wiki, read in full — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/fsrs4anki/wiki/The-Optimal-Retention

contested.question: Is HSK band order frequency-ordered, and are the bands equal-sized?
contested.side_a: Band order IS strongly frequency-aligned and additionally corrects for concreteness: median frequency rank per band rises cleanly and monotonically (291, 479, 674, 872, 1302, 1702, 2637) with the share inside the top 1,000 falling 88%→79%→69%→57%→34%→13%→2%. And HSK BEATS raw frequency on travel vocabulary — 厕 is frequency rank 3,107 but sits in HSK 4; 禁 (947) and 止 (735) likewise. Band sizes are uneven: 246 / 125 / 284 / 441 / 431 / 413 / 1,148.
contested.side_b: The official lists are exactly 300 characters at each of levels 1–6 with zero duplicates, plus 1,200 at 七—九级 = 3,000 — parsed independently by two agents from the Pleco OCR of the official PDF and matching to the digit. And HSK is NOT frequency-optimal at any given size: HSK L1's 300 characters cover 43.3% of running characters versus 60.3% for a frequency-matched 300, and L1–3's 900 cover 79.4% versus 85.2%.
contested.what_it_turns_on: The band-size dispute resolves: side A's counts come from a community OCR (krmanik/HSK-3.0) that sums to ~3,088 against an official 3,000 and is self-flagged as ~3% noisy, while side B parsed the Pleco OCR of the official PDF and got exact totals with no duplicates. Use 300 per level. The frequency dispute does NOT resolve and both halves are true at once: HSK band order correlates monotonically with frequency AND is 6–17 points off frequency-optimal at any given size, because it deliberately front-loads concrete, sign-relevant characters that corpus frequency buries. So the practical answer is a BLENDED ordering — frequency × band × task relevance — not strict frequency bands and not HSK order.
sources: elkmovie/hsk30, parsed independently by two agents — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30
krmanik/HSK-3.0 hanzi lists, computed — https://github.com/krmanik/HSK-3.0
Coverage cross-tab computed over https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fxsjy/jieba/master/jieba/dict.txt

contested.question: Does an HSK level mean anything in CEFR terms, and should the UI say so?
contested.side_a: HSK-to-CEFR alignment is contested in the literature and should not appear anywhere in the product.
contested.side_b: The specific arithmetic argument originally offered for the criticism does not hold: HSK 3.0's cumulative word count through level 6 is 5,456, within ~9% of HSK 2.0's ~5,000 at level 6 — the apparent doubling is entirely the newly created 7–9 band (5,636 words) sitting above the old ceiling, and adding levels above an existing top level is not evidence that the old descriptors were inflated.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Nothing that changes the build decision. The recommendation stands on its own without the bad argument: put no CEFR letter in the UI, because you cannot compute or defend the equivalence. Express progress in the two ways you CAN compute — counts against the official lists, and domain coverage against your own corpus. Make the second one the hero number, because it is the promise the product actually makes.
sources: Cumulative level counts computed from GF0025-2021 — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30

contested.question: How confusable should a distractor be?
contested.side_a: Maximum confusability. Duolingo's failure mode is distractors that are too easy — three visually unrelated options let a learner shape-match without reading. Pick 2–3 distractors that share a component with the target (same radical, same phonetic, or same overall stroke silhouette) so the player must attend to the discriminating stroke.
contested.side_b: That is the opposite extreme, not the correct point. A learner who has never seen 请 will not learn it by being shown 请 清 情 晴 simultaneously; they will encode a fuzzy blend of all four. Make confusability a FUNCTION of the player's exposure state: distant distractors on the first correct encounter, component-sharing distractors unlocked only after the item has been answered correctly at least once.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Nothing in either sweep tested it — side B is an internal-contradiction argument, not a finding. But side B is free to implement and side A is not reversible after you have authored the sets. It also fits the deterministic-reducer constraint exactly: exposure_count is already per-player state, so distractor tier is a pure function of (item, exposure_count, seed) and every phone still derives an identical set. Ship side B, log the distractor set alongside the outcome, and settle it on your own data — which is currently the only way it will ever be settled.
sources: Internal-contradiction analysis of the landscape sweep against its own Duolingo criticism

contested.question: Should the gloss cost be public?
contested.side_a: Make the gloss cost something, in public. In a co-located game the currency already exists: revealing a gloss deducts from the current bid and the other players see that it happened. The social cost of asking for help is the mechanism, and a solitary app cannot charge it — that is precisely the advantage of building this co-located.
contested.side_b: Both cannot be right: the same sweep identifies public punishment of the weakest player as the fastest way to end a game night. The predictable failure is that a beginner stops requesting glosses and starts guessing, which converts a retrieval attempt into a coin flip and teaches nothing while the score still moves.
contested.what_it_turns_on: Separating two variables that were fused. Cost and visibility are independent. RULING FOR V1: cost yes, visibility no. Ship the public variant behind a flag, default OFF for any table containing a first-time player, and make it the first A/B once you have tables. This is the highest-risk unvalidated bet in the research and it was presented as its central design insight.
sources: Internal-contradiction analysis of the landscape sweep against its own co-operative-mode finding

myths.myth: 'Half-life regression improved Duolingo engagement 12% over the Leitner box system.' — the single most repeated claim in scheduling folklore.
myths.why_wrong: RETRACTED against the paper itself. Table 4: HLR vs Leitner, 6 weeks, just under 1M randomised students, gave Any activity +0.3 (n.s.), New lesson +0.3 (n.s.), Practice −7.3 (p<0.001) — no significant gain and a significant DROP. The +12.0% is Experiment II: HLR-lex versus HLR, i.e. the gain came from REMOVING the lexeme-tag features and making the model simpler. And the outcome measured throughout is next-day retention; no vocabulary gain was measured in either experiment.
sources: Settles & Meeder (2016), ACL 2016, §4.3–4.4, Tables 2 and 4 — https://github.com/duolingo/halflife-regression/blob/master/settles.acl16.pdf

myths.myth: 'FSRS delivers 20–30% fewer reviews than SM-2 for the same retention.'
myths.why_wrong: The FSRS project's own wiki carries the caveat inline: '(2026-02-12 update: the figure is based on simulation results)'. There is no A/B test and no user study behind the industry's most-cited efficiency number. Never put it, or any numeric efficiency claim, in the product, the store listing or the onboarding.
sources: Open Spaced Repetition wiki, ABC-of-FSRS.md line 19 — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/awesome-fsrs/wiki/ABC-of-FSRS

myths.myth: 'No experimental evidence exists that algorithmic scheduling or item selection improves learning.'
myths.why_wrong: FALSE, and it would be embarrassing in a design document. Upadhyay, Lancashire, Moser & Gomez-Rodriguez (2021), npj Science of Learning 6:26 is a large-scale randomised experiment on exactly the session-level item-selection layer, run in a live commercial app with released code and trial data. Nioche et al. (IUI '21) and Tabibian et al. (PNAS 2019) sit alongside it. All three are listed on a wiki page one click from the FSRS pages that were read.
sources: Networks-Learning/spaced-selection — https://github.com/Networks-Learning/spaced-selection
Open Spaced Repetition wiki, Research-resources — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/awesome-fsrs/wiki/Research-resources

myths.myth: 'Bayesian Knowledge Tracing cannot model forgetting.'
myths.why_wrong: FALSE of every maintained implementation. pyBKT exposes `forgets` as a first-class option, cross-validated in its own README examples, and documents the transition matrix as containing both learns and forgets. The claim is true only of Corbett & Anderson's 1995 canonical formulation. The recommendation not to ship BKT survives — for the right reason, which is that its latent state is binary while retrievability here is continuous and time-dependent.
sources: pyBKT README — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CAHLR/pyBKT/master/README.md

myths.myth: 'Deep knowledge tracing wins on datasets with long interaction sequences, so it is irrelevant to a short-session product.'
myths.why_wrong: The conclusion is right and the reason is backwards, refuted by the very table it cites. In Gervet et al.'s results the two LONGEST-sequence datasets — spanish (median length 1,924) and bridge_algebra06 (1,362) — both go to logistic regression, and the SHORTEST, assistments15 (median 20), is a DKT win. Justify 'no neural knowledge tracing' by the size of the gap (0.01–0.06 AUC) and the engineering cost, never by a sequence-length rule.
sources: Gervet et al. (2020), JEDM 12(3), results table and dataset statistics — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/theophilee/learner-performance-prediction/master/README.md

myths.myth: 'The head-to-head SM-2 versus FSRS comparison cannot be obtained from the benchmark.'
myths.why_wrong: It is one command away: the SM-2 rows are in the repository's git history at commit 45f61b2 (2025-07-24), on exactly the corpus the current README quotes. SM-2 Log Loss 0.722±0.017, Anki-SM-2 0.616±0.011, SM-2-short 0.653±0.015, SM-2-trainable 0.581±0.012, against FSRS-6's 0.3456. Declaring this unobtainable produced a chain of reasoning that budgeted the scheduler against the wrong alternative.
sources: srs-benchmark README @45f61b2182c27da83839383ec3b044fa5ae27b47 — https://github.com/open-spaced-repetition/srs-benchmark

myths.myth: 'CC-CEDICT is CC BY-SA 3.0.'
myths.why_wrong: Current distributions are CC BY-SA 4.0, confirmed on two builds (2023 and 2024). But do not call 3.0 a myth in the design document either: CC-CEDICT genuinely WAS 3.0 for years, so 3.0 is a STALE figure rather than a false one — and if you vendored a pre-switch copy, that copy is under 3.0 terms.
sources: CC-CEDICT headers, builds 2023-09-03 and 2024-12-06 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/huwd/learn_hanzi/main/spec/fixtures/cedict_ts.u8

myths.myth: 'Make Me a Hanzi is MIT licensed.'
myths.why_wrong: Neither half is. dictionary.txt is LGPL-3.0-or-later (from Unihan + CJKlib); graphics.txt and svgs.tar.gz are Arphic Public License (from AR PL KaitiM GB / AR PL UKai). Shipping dictionary.txt in a bundled PWA creates an LGPL relink obligation that is incoherent on a JSON blob and not obviously discharged. Do not ship it; regenerate the equivalent data from Unihan plus CC-CEDICT.
sources: skishore/makemeahanzi COPYING — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/skishore/makemeahanzi/master/COPYING

myths.myth: 'Noto Sans SC's Simplified Chinese subset is 4–5 MB over ~44,000 glyphs, and Fontsource ships it as one monolithic blob per weight.'
myths.why_wrong: Measured false on both halves. The named chinese-simplified woff2 at weight 400 is 1,142,552 B = 1.09 MB with 7,946 codepoints / 7,333 hanzi / 8,248 glyphs — about 4x smaller and 5x fewer glyphs than claimed. And @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0's DEFAULT index.css uses ~97 numbered unicode-range chunks, exactly the packaging it was said not to do. Every 'this dataset is N megabytes' claim in this space is answerable today with npm pack and fonttools, with no search budget.
sources: Measured 2026-08-22 with fontTools/pyftsubset against @fontsource/noto-sans-sc@5.3.0 — https://www.npmjs.com/package/@fontsource/noto-sans-sc

myths.myth: 'A menu game will reach for 焗 煲 涮 菌 藕 韭 — characters the font drops — so tofu boxes are a typeface risk.'
myths.why_wrong: All six are present in Noto Sans SC's chinese-simplified subset, as are all 3,000 HSK 3.0 characters and 笋 蒜 姜 葱 炝 烩 氽 煨 熘 腌 蕈 蚝 蛏 鲈 鳕 鳝. Tofu risk from the typeface is zero. The risk is created ENTIRELY by your own codepoint-extraction step if you subset — which is why the CI gate matters only in the subsetting branch, and matters absolutely there.
sources: fontTools cmap of noto-sans-sc-chinese-simplified-400-normal.woff2 intersected with the HSK 3.0 list, 2026-08-22

myths.myth: 'There is no published character-frequency corpus of Chinese urban signage, so we have to photograph one — and 5,000 captures makes it a dataset nobody has.'
myths.why_wrong: A character-level frequency corpus of Chinese text in the urban wild has existed since 2018/2019: CTW, 32,285 street-view images, 1,018,402 labelled character instances, 3,850 categories, with a STAT_FREQUENCY build target in the reference implementation. The absence claim came from searching linguistic-landscape sociolinguistics rather than computer vision. 5,000 captures is a rounding error against a million labelled instances. NOTE the offsetting fact: CTW's annotations are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, so the NC term still gates a commercial derivation.
sources: Yuan, T.-L. et al. (2019), JCST 34(3), 509–521 — https://ctwdataset.github.io/
ctw-baseline — https://github.com/yuantailing/ctw-baseline

myths.myth: 'HSK word lists are public domain' AND 'you cannot use HSK word lists'.
myths.why_wrong: Both are misreports. The standard's copyright position is genuinely unsettled — PRC Copyright Law Art. 5 excludes official documents of state organs, but national GB/GF standards sit in a contested category, and a bare word list is a thin-originality compilation of facts. Practically every product in the market uses them and enforcement is unheard of. The exposure that actually bites is TRADEMARK: the letters 'HSK', the logo, and 'HSK Level N' as a user-facing label or in store metadata.
sources: elkmovie/hsk30, MIT © 2021 Pleco Inc. — https://github.com/elkmovie/hsk30

myths.myth: 'SUBTLEX-CH is public domain / free to bundle.'
myths.why_wrong: Not established. It is safe only if you take the PLoS ONE Supporting Information copy, which inherits the article's CC BY; the lab-website and GitHub mirrors carry no licence text at all (leonsilicon/subtlex-ch-wf states none), and none of that was verifiable this session. Jun Da's MTSU list is research/education-only with no commercial grant despite being bundled commercially all over the ecosystem, and the circulating BCC bulk file has no licence statement.
sources: Cai & Brysbaert (2010), PLoS ONE 5(6):e10729 — article NOT accessed — https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0010729
https://github.com/leonsilicon/subtlex-ch-wf

myths.myth: 'This Chinese TTS model is open source, so we can use its voice.'
myths.why_wrong: That almost always refers to the CODE licence, not the corpus the weights were fitted on. CSMSC / 标贝 — the default single-speaker Mandarin corpus behind a large fraction of publicly released Chinese TTS checkpoints — is explicitly non-commercial and taints checkpoints trained on it. MagicData Mandarin is CC BY-ND 4.0, where ND arguably prohibits training a model on it at all. Common Voice is CC0 but is whole read sentences with no forced alignment, so it is not a pronunciation source.
sources: common-voice/common-voice README — https://github.com/common-voice/common-voice

myths.myth: 'Unihan kMandarin gives you a character's pinyin.'
myths.why_wrong: It gives ONE reading. 387 of HSK 3.0's 3,000 characters (12.9%) are 多音字, and they saturate this exact domain: 现磨 is mó not mò, 净含量 is liàng not liáng, 打折 is zhé, 行 is háng in 银行 but xíng in 人行道 and 行李寄存, 便 is biàn in 方便 but pián in 便宜, 地 is dì in 小心地滑 but de as an adverbial marker — and 菌 on a menu (菌菇, 野生菌) is jùn 'mushroom' while the default reading is jūn 'bacterium'. Choosing kMandarin to avoid a ShareAlike attribution line trades correctness for a line of text.
sources: 多音字 table (597 entries) intersected with the HSK 3.0 list, 2026-08-22 — https://github.com/jaywcjlove/table-of-general-standard-chinese-characters

myths.myth: 'Store traditional variants with Unihan kTraditionalVariant, or convert with OpenCC on export.'
myths.why_wrong: Simplified→traditional is 1:many and the collisions land on the highest-payoff items. 230 of HSK's 3,000 characters map to more than one traditional form, 89 of them inside the first 900. 干 — on every Sichuan menu in 干煸, 干锅, 豆干 — maps to both 乾 and 幹, and auto-picking 幹 yields a character that reads as an expletive in Taiwanese usage. 面 → 麵/麪, 发 → 發/髮, 只 → 隻/祗/衹, 台 → 臺/檯/颱. Never auto-convert; store both forms per string as a LIST, or ship simplified only.
sources: Computed by joining OpenCC STCharacters.txt against GF0025-2021, 2026-08-22 — https://github.com/BYVoid/OpenCC

myths.myth: '请 comes apart into 言 (speech) + 青 (qīng) — the flagship example for component teaching.'
myths.why_wrong: 言 + 青 is 請, the TRADITIONAL form. In simplified it is 讠 + 青 — verified by stroke decomposition: 请 10 strokes, 請 15, 讠 2, 言 7, 青 8. The same document also wrote 醬 (traditional) inside an argument about simplified; the simplified form is 酱 at 13 strokes, not the 15–17 claimed (蔬 is 15 and 藏 is 17, which do carry the density). If the flagship example of the component-teaching decision is script-confused, the authoring pipeline will be too.
sources: Stroke counts computed from hanzi-writer-data@2.0.1 per-character stroke arrays, 2026-08-22

myths.myth: 'A 60-item yes/no vocabulary check-in every ten sessions will show us whether players are learning.'
myths.why_wrong: Its minimum detectable change between two sittings is ≈27 percentage points (SE of a single corrected score ≈0.096, of a difference ≈0.136). Even at a flattering 0.90 hit / 0.05 false-alarm rate the MDC is ≈19 points. The number will move mostly at random, which is worse than no number because the team will read the noise. Resolving a 10-point change needs ~426 items (~10 minutes).
sources: Computed 2026-08-22 from the instrument's own specification, binomial sampling error

myths.myth: 'The 44px touch target is the accessibility requirement / an empirical finding.'
myths.why_wrong: It is a platform convention. WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) is 24×24 CSS px at Level AA; 44×44 is SC 2.5.5 at Level AAA; Apple HIG says 44×44 pt and Material says 48×48 dp — three numbers for three different things. The empirical anchor (Parhi et al. 2006, ~9.2 mm discrete / ~9.6 mm serial thumb targets) is in physical units and lands larger than 44 CSS px on most phones. Write down which number you are meeting and why.
sources: W3C WCAG 2.2 (October 2023), SC 2.5.5 and SC 2.5.8 — https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/
Parhi, Karlson & Bederson (2006), MobileHCI '06 — NOT RETRIEVED

directives.directive: Install ts-fsrs and run FSRS-6 in PRETRAIN-4 mode: ship the 21 default parameters, and fit only the four initial-stability parameters (one per grade) per player once that player has a few hundred reviews. Never write a per-user optimiser and never wire the WASM optimiser outside a dev flag. Budget: one npm dependency plus ~40 lines of glue.
directives.basis: Benchmark rows on the identical corpus: FSRS-6 default 0.3661, pretrain-4 0.3548, full 21-param 0.3456, MOVING-AVG 0.3369, SM-2 0.722. Pretrain-4 recovers most of the optimisation gain for a closed-form fit.

directives.directive: Implement the forgetting curve exactly as: decay = 0.1542; FACTOR = 0.9^(1/−0.1542) − 1 = 0.980346; R(t,S) = (1 + 0.980346·t/S)^(−0.1542); I(r,S) = S·(r^(1/−0.1542) − 1)/0.980346. Add a unit test asserting R(S) = 0.9 and R(10S) < 1.
directives.basis: Read from fsrs-rs inference.rs and ts-fsrs algorithm.ts. The sign convention and the 19/81 FACTOR are the two errors that ship as bugs; ts-fsrs's own docstring (t/9S) contradicts its code (t/S).

directives.directive: Per-(player, item, direction) state is 16 bytes: stability f32, difficulty f32, last_review f64. Compute R inline at selection time; NEVER persist a due-date. A 3,000-character + 3,000-word bank × 2 directions × 8 local players ≈ 96,000 rows ≈ 1.5 MB in IndexedDB.
directives.basis: FSRS-6 state definition read from source; storage arithmetic. Inline R means a device asleep three weeks needs no catch-up job on wake.

directives.directive: The learner model is a logistic regression over six integers per (player, item-skill): total attempts, total correct, attempts on this character/word, correct on this character/word, log1p(days since last attempt), item difficulty. ~24 bytes per player-item, SGD in milliseconds on-device, no ML dependency. Write 'no neural knowledge tracing, no BKT' into the architecture doc with the Gervet citation attached.
directives.basis: Gervet et al. 2020: 4–4 split with Best-LR, gaps 0.01–0.06 AUC, and the engineering cost of an RNN is not recoverable at ~30 responses per player per evening.

directives.directive: Store the standard review-log schema from day one: card_id, review_time (ms, UTC), review_rating {1,2,3,4}, review_state {0,1,2,3}, review_duration (ms), timezone (IANA), day_start = 4. Plus product columns: player_id, mode (solo|group), role (answered|co_committed|observed|exposure), format_tier, n_alternatives, eligible_for, render_variant, distractor_set, response_latency_ms, voluntarily_initiated, turns_since_last_public_failure.
directives.basis: FSRS Optimizer specification, explicitly a universal standard. review_duration is free to record now, impossible to reconstruct later, and is the only signal for 'was this player looking at the screen'.

directives.directive: Keep per-player scheduling state STRICTLY per-player and outside the signed shared event log. Two stores: the shared append-only game log (synced P2P), and a local per-player memory store (never synced to peers).
directives.basis: FSRS needs full per-item history; that history is private state, not game state. Merging them breaks both the privacy claim and the deterministic reducer.

directives.directive: Make group item selection a PURE, STATELESS function: pickItem(candidates, players[]) → item, taking each player's R for each candidate. Never collapse players into a single averaged learner — that discards the information the function exists to use. Because it is pure, you can swap the objective, log the counterfactual (what each alternative objective would have chosen) and A/B it later without touching storage.
directives.basis: No library, no benchmark, no on-point paper exists for N simultaneous learners on one stimulus. Purity is what makes the unknown cheap to change.

directives.directive: Score candidates by U(i) = −Σ_p w_p·(R_p(i) − 0.85)² and softmax-sample over the top 8 rather than taking the argmax, so the same evening never produces the same sequence twice. Persist per-player rounds_since_pivot and the chosen item's per-player R vector on the review rows so selection can be evaluated retrospectively. Cost: ~6,000 candidates × 8 players × one pow() ≈ 50k float ops per round, under 2 ms on a phone.
directives.basis: Reasoned from first principles, not from a located source. Explicitly a hand-rolled substitute for the single-learner objective in Tabibian et al. 2019 / Upadhyay et al. 2021 — read both before writing it.

directives.directive: Make the character-dependency constraint PER-PLAYER, not group-wide. A group whose weakest member knows 300 characters and whose strongest knows 1,200 has 1,451 eligible words rather than 7,330 under a group-wide constraint — 80% of the strong player's readable vocabulary excluded before the difficulty objective even runs. At 600 vs 1,800 it is still 62%. Log eligible_for per round so the floor effect is visible if it recurs.
directives.basis: Computed from the recomputed cumulative-character/decodable-word curve over GF0025-2021. Varying response format cannot recover this — a 4-choice over a trivial word is still trivial.

directives.directive: Core interaction loop: item appears → every player gets the SAME fixed commit window → each taps privately on their own phone with no feedback to others beyond an anonymous filled-dot count → window closes or all committed → simultaneous reveal with per-player correctness. Never award points for speed-to-buzz; if a speed dimension is wanted, make it a tiebreaker on an already-correct answer. Log one review row per player per round, always.
directives.basis: Collaborative inhibition: three players watching one player retrieve destroys the retrieval for all three. Blind simultaneous commit also produces a genuine independent outcome per player per round, which is what per-player scheduling requires.

directives.directive: Add a fourth beat after the reveal: ONE isomorphic item, answered individually, no discussion. Requires an isomorph_group_id field on the item bank so items are authored in pairs or triples (same radical family, or same confusable pair, different character).
directives.basis: Smith et al. 2009 (Science, n≈350): the transfer result lives in the second, independently-answered isomorphic question, not in the re-answer. This is the closest validated turn shape for one-item-many-learners.

directives.directive: Specify the pacing controller in RETRIEVABILITY, never in observed accuracy. To hit a common true R of 0.85: target observed 0.925 in 2AFC, 0.8875 in 4AFC, 0.85 in free entry. Keep FSRS desired retention at 0.90 as a separate knob that governs cross-day return; never let one drive the other.
directives.basis: P(correct) = R + (1−R)/k. Holding observed accuracy constant across formats puts the weakest players at the LOWEST true retrievability — the exact inverse of intent.

directives.directive: Do not feed 2-alternative (or fully-scaffolded) outcomes into stability updates at all. Log them role: exposure. Let scheduling state advance only on 4-alternative and free-entry responses. Grade mapping on the rest: free-recall correct → Good/Easy (3/4); 4-choice correct → Good (3); any incorrect → Again (1).
directives.basis: At an 85% operating point roughly half of 2AFC 'correct' responses are guesses, so tier-1 outcomes are ~50% noise regardless of which grade is assigned.

directives.directive: Four hard, non-tunable constraints in the selection function: (1) no item scored twice in one session — recurrences log role: exposure with no stability update; (2) no item advances out of LEARNING on same-session corrects, require a correct in a LATER session; (3) cap consecutive incorrect answers per player at 2 — on the third, force-inject an item where that player's R > 0.95 regardless of the group objective; (4) floor any item's per-player minimum interval at 1 day.
directives.basis: Documented Duolingo production failure (§4.4): over-short intervals on a feature-defined slice, user complaints, invisible in offline metrics because variants were 'virtually tied'.

directives.directive: Ship one monitoring query you actually look at: the per-item distribution of mean interval, so a slice of the bank collapsing to the floor is visible before players complain.
directives.basis: The Duolingo failure was invisible in aggregate offline metrics and surfaced only through user complaints.

directives.directive: Cold start: use FSRS pretrain-4 for the PLAYER side. Keep an Elo-style rating for the ITEM side only, where FSRS has no mechanism (its difficulty is per player-item from a global constant): two scalars per item (θ_i, n_i), update with K = 0.4/(1 + 0.05·n). Do NOT present these constants as literature-derived — they are reasonable starting values, not published ones. Store prior_difficulty and observed_difficulty in separate columns.
directives.basis: The Pelánek/Papoušek Elo deployment papers could not be retrieved by either agent; the K-form and constants are cited from record. FSRS pretrain-4 is benchmarked and is the better-evidenced player-side answer.

directives.directive: Demote the 60-item yes/no test to a PLACEMENT instrument at onboarding (where it also supplies the cold-start calibration a mixed-ability table needs) and a coarse band estimate. Take the actual outcome signal from the review log: accuracy on items whose interval has crossed a ≥7-day threshold, aggregated over hundreds of items per player.
directives.basis: MDC ≈ 27 percentage points between two sittings. The attempt log is free, continuous, and orders of magnitude better powered.

directives.directive: Ship a naked probe from v1: 10–15% of presentations render the target character alone, system face, plain ground. If a player's naked-probe accuracy trails their in-object accuracy by more than ~20 points, the app is teaching plates rather than characters — and it must say so internally from the first cohort, not at launch.
directives.basis: Every other in-app number is measured in the training context. This is the only cheap instrument that separates item learning from template learning.

directives.directive: Instrument learning and engagement as two separately-reported metric families and never conflate them. Learning: ≥7-day delayed accuracy from the log; transfer accuracy on a held-out set of real signage at d7 and d28; retrievals-to-stable-recall per item (measure it, do not assume 6–10). Engagement: sessions/week, retrievals/session, self-initiated vs notification opens. Guardrail: response_latency_ms, which inflates before accuracy drops.
directives.basis: Settles & Meeder measured next-day retention and never vocabulary gain, which is precisely how the field's most-cited engagement number came to be misread as a learning result.

directives.directive: Instrument sessions_per_week and days_between_sessions from the first cohort, split by mode. If median multiplayer gap exceeds ~7 days while solo sits under ~3, invert the architecture: solo daily becomes the primary path and multiplayer becomes the acquisition channel. This is the single cheapest falsification test of the whole product thesis.
directives.basis: Spacing operates on a days timescale; a party game is played when people happen to meet. If it is fortnightly, the scheduler never runs, ~6 well-spaced retrievals per item collapses to ~2, and the item bank and selection layer are all correct and all starved.

directives.directive: Never render a per-item mastery percentage or strength bar. Three coarse states, distinguished by shape and fill: NEW (outline chip), LEARNING (half-filled), SOLID (filled) — where SOLID can and does silently fall back to LEARNING when R decays below ~0.7, surfaced as '3 characters need a refresh'. Aggregate progress at deck level only.
directives.basis: Every published model discriminates item-level recall near chance in a real language product (all within 0.04 AUC of chance in Duolingo's own Table 2). A precise wrong number is a visible lie.

directives.directive: Put no CEFR letter anywhere in the UI and no HSK letters, logo or 'Level N' label anywhere user-facing or in store metadata. Express progress in the two ways you can compute and defend: counts against the official lists, and domain coverage against your own corpus. Make the second one the hero number.
directives.basis: CEFR alignment is contested and uncomputable; HSK exposure is trademark, not copyright. Both risks vanish for free.

directives.directive: Use 通用规范汉字表 tier as the character difficulty spine (MIT machine-readable copy: 8,105 characters in tiers 3,500/3,000/1,605) with HSK band as a secondary signal, and size the spine at ~1,500–1,800 characters, not 900. Take the 597-entry 多音字 table from the same repo directly.
directives.basis: TGH strictly contains HSK (2,967 of 3,000 in tier 1, 33 in tier 2, 0 outside) and adds the tier-1 characters HSK omits. HSK 1–3's 900 characters cover only 79.4% of running characters — one in five unknown on an unseen sign.

directives.directive: Split the v1 bank into two ITEM TYPES: character-acquisition items for the menu register (where the barrier is unknown characters — 0/10 cooking verbs and 0/7 ingredients are in HSK 1–3, and 焗 炝 烩 笋 藕 韭 are outside HSK 3.0 entirely), and compound-parsing/cloze items for transit, product-label and shopfront signage (where every character is already known — transit 12/12 in HSK 3.0, labels 13/13, shopfronts 7/7 — but 换乘, 末班, 净含量, 保质期 are opaque).
directives.basis: Measured per character against GF0025-2021. The 'HSK doesn't cover signage' argument is true for menus and false for the other three registers.

directives.directive: Item schema, mandatory and non-nullable: {string, gloss.nl, gloss.en, reading: [{char, pinyin}], has_variant_reading, semantic_component[], phonetic_component[], structure_enum, component_char_ids[] (SCRIPT-SCOPED), confusable_with[], interference_set[] (distinct from confusable_with), isomorph_group_id, trad: string[] (a LIST, never a scalar), tier, signage_frequency, explanation (≤20 words / 120 chars)}.
directives.basis: Every field here is forced by a measured failure: heteronyms (12.9% of HSK characters), 1:many traditional mapping (230 of 3,000), script-non-isomorphic dependency graphs, deterministic distractor derivation, and the isomorphic-transfer beat.

directives.directive: Build-time gates that fail CI: (1) any item-bank codepoint missing from the produced font subset; (2) any column in the emitted bank with no entry in the provenance manifest (column → dataset → licence); (3) any field traceable to makemeahanzi dictionary.txt; (4) any stored stroke_count disagreeing with Unihan kTotalStrokes; (5) any item containing a heteronym without an explicit per-character reading; (6) any item containing 面/干/发/后/里/松/只/几/表/系/术 with a scalar trad field; (7) any hanzi element without lang="zh-Hans" or gloss without a lang attribute; (8) the Latin face failing the ā á ǎ à ē é ě è ī í ǐ ì ō ó ǒ ò ū ú ǔ ù ǖ ǘ ǚ ǜ render assertion.
directives.basis: Each gate corresponds to a specific measured failure mode. Gates 2 and 3 are ten lines of script and are the difference between a defensible product and an undocumented one.

directives.directive: Ship glosses as a separate build artefact (/assets/gloss.cedict.json) under CC BY-SA 4.0 with LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt beside it, never inlined into the JS bundle. Publish the derived gloss file in the repo so the ShareAlike obligation is discharged once at build time. Add an in-app /licences route naming CC-CEDICT, MDBG, Denisowski 1997–98, Unicode, Pleco/MIT, the TGH transcriber, and OFL.
directives.basis: CC BY-SA 4.0 verified on two builds. The derived gloss table is an adaptation; the app code is mere aggregation. Keeping the boundary clean keeps SA off your source.

directives.directive: Stay a PWA, or serve the gloss and any stroke assets as separately-fetched, non-DRM'd files. Do not wrap the same bundle for the iOS App Store behind FairPlay while it contains CC BY-SA or Arphic-licensed data.
directives.basis: CC BY-SA 4.0 §2(a)(5)(B) forbids applying effective technological measures to the Licensed Material; Arphic PL §5 bars imposing further restrictions on recipients. This is the classic CC/App Store conflict and it is a distribution-channel decision, not a code decision.

directives.directive: Ship NO stroke graphics in v1. Measured: hanzi-writer-data@2.0.1 averages 3,368 B per character, so a 3,000-character bank is 9.64 MB raw / ≈3.9 MB gzip / ≈3.1 MB brotli, and even a 1,200-character bundle is 1.21 MB brotli — 40% of a 3 MB install budget for a skill this user will never perform. If a 'how is it written' affordance is wanted later, lazy-load one character's JSON from a separate APL-licensed static path, and if you only need order, ship the integer sequence (a standard, not an expressive work).
directives.basis: Measured over all 9,574 files. If you ever do ship reformatted Arphic data, publish the subset as a public repo with ARPHICPL.TXT and a CHANGES file — that repo is the 'designated place' and discharges §2(b) permanently.

directives.directive: Ship NO audio in v1. When it is added: pre-render at build time for the finite bank using a commercial TTS whose terms grant output rights (Azure, Google, ElevenLabs), Opus 24 kbps mono (~900 items × 1.5 s ≈ 4 MB) in Cache Storage with per-item eviction, autoplay at reveal only. Never the Web Speech API — zh-CN is frequently absent on iOS Safari and synthesis needs a user gesture, so it fails exactly at a table with mixed phones.
directives.basis: Common Voice has no forced alignment; Forvo forbids durable caching; CSMSC/标贝 is non-commercial and taints most public Chinese TTS checkpoints; MagicData is ND.

directives.directive: Use Noto Sans SC (no Reserved Font Name), not Source Han Sans (RFN 'Source'). Self-host. One weight (400) plus one heavier (500) for dark mode. Rename the subset family. Ship OFL.txt. Never a Google Fonts <link> — it needs network at render time and its hosts are unreachable in mainland China.
directives.basis: Both OFL files read verbatim; subsetting counts as modification, which is exactly what the RFN would constrain.

directives.directive: Decide the font branch by final bank size. Below ~1,500 characters: subset at build time from the item bank (measured: 1,200 hanzi → 164.0 KB woff2; 900 → 123.5 KB; 600 → 84.9 KB; 300 → 44.7 KB), with pyftsubset --text-file=bank-chars.txt --flavor=woff2 --layout-features= --no-hinting --desubroutinize, AND the CI gate. Above ~2,500 characters: ship the whole 1.09 MB chinese-simplified file and delete the missing-glyph risk class entirely.
directives.basis: All numbers measured with fonttools/pyftsubset this session. Near-linear at 109–137 bytes/glyph; the whole-file baseline is 1.09 MB / 7,946 codepoints, not the 4–5 MB widely assumed.

directives.directive: Transport: configure an EMPTY iceServers array explicitly (never inherit stun.l.google.com:19302), host candidates only, star topology with a QR join code, and ship a same-device pass-and-play fallback with a 'Hand to <name> — tap when ready' interstitial. Make the reducer transport-agnostic over {playerId, itemId, choice, elapsedMs} so same-device handoff, BroadcastChannel and WebRTC datachannel are swappable underneath. Take a Screen Wake Lock for the session. Test in aeroplane mode plus hotspot.
directives.basis: There is no browser API for local peer discovery on iPhones — Web Bluetooth is unimplemented in Safari on iOS and macOS at every current version. A co-located game needs no NAT traversal; pass-and-play is the only genuinely serverless option.

directives.directive: Prompt Add to Home Screen after the first successful session, and make explicit JSON export/import (or sync) the durable store with local as cache. Test the seven-day iOS storage-eviction case explicitly in QA. Resolve the tension with 'no server, no account' in the spec, not in production.
directives.basis: iOS Safari evicts IndexedDB, Cache API and service-worker caches after ~7 days of non-use for non-installed sites — which silently deletes exactly the returning-user history a fortnightly product depends on.

directives.directive: Use CTW internally as a research input only — to decide which characters to author — and ship no artefact derived from its annotations, unless a commercial grant is obtained from the authors. Its annotations are CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (the baseline code is MIT).
directives.basis: CTW is 1,018,402 labelled character instances over 32,285 street-view images with a STAT_FREQUENCY build target — it answers the signage-frequency question in an afternoon. The NC term is the gate, and it is the one open licensing item that has not been resolved.

directives.directive: Ship transcribed text set in your own licensed font; never ship a source photograph. If capture ships at all: on-device only, no GPS, no peer sync of images, no server-side pooling — store only the extracted character list. Drop the 'we photographed 200 real menus in Chengdu' provenance line.
directives.basis: Menu layout, dish photography, package artwork and shopfront logos are protected expression carrying live trademarks; GDPR engages the instant a person is in frame for a Dutch controller; PRC PIPL applies at collection and the Surveying and Mapping Law restricts geotagged collection by foreign nationals. Flagged for counsel, not asserted as settled.

directives.directive: Ship a 'no timers' setting, rem-relative sizing that survives 200% OS text scaling, a layout that tolerates text-spacing overrides, lang="zh-Hans" on every hanzi and lang="nl"/"en" on every gloss, 24×24 CSS px as the chrome target floor with answer rows at 60–64 px, and never colour as the sole carrier of information.
directives.basis: European Accessibility Act (Directive (EU) 2019/882) applicable since 28 June 2025 via EN 301 549 / WCAG 2.1 AA. The 45s/75s/120s bet timers engage SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable directly; this is a legal constraint, not a preference.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 1. The bet is how much scaffolding you give up: +1/-1 shows pinyin and English options; +5/-3 removes pinyin; +15/-10 also makes all four options Chinese signs.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: As a HANDICAPPING mechanic it is the right answer and it is already the best-argued call in the design: mixed ability at one table is the hardest problem in a co-located language game, board games solved it with bidding, and a bid that is invisible to the table is what makes the handicap socially acceptable. But it has three measurement consequences that are wrong as specified, and one structural conflict. (a) The +1/-1 tier shows pinyin AND English glosses on the options — that is not a character-reading retrieval, it is recognition with the answer supplied, and feeding it to FSRS as a 'correct' inflates stability on a skill that was never tested. (b) k stays at 4 across all three tiers, so the guessing floor is a constant 25% and none of the tiers is a genuinely free-recall event — any accuracy target must be converted through P(correct) = R + (1−R)/k before it means anything. (c) THE STRUCTURAL CONFLICT, which nobody has flagged: the bet is chosen BEFORE the item is seen and BY the player, so difficulty is self-selected. A pacing controller cannot target a retrievability through a channel the player owns, and a self-selected tier is not random assignment, so the outcomes are confounded with player confidence. You cannot have both a player-owned bet and a system-owned difficulty controller working through the same variable.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep the bet. Move all adaptive difficulty control to ITEM SELECTION, not to response format — the bet stays a player-owned points multiplier and scaffolding choice. Log +1/-1 answers with role: exposure and do not advance scheduling state on them; let stability advance only on the +5/-3 and +15/-10 tiers. Store format_tier and n_alternatives on every review row. Express any accuracy target in retrievability (observed 0.8875 at k=4 for a true R of 0.85). And scale each player's candidate pool by their own FSRS state so the beginner's +15/-10 item is not the expert's +15/-10 item: same tier, same points, different item, invisible to the table.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 2. Items render as the physical object they appear on — a station plate, a printed menu section with prices, a shopfront fascia, a shelf-edge price label, a hazard board. Two treatments are deliberately hard to read because real ones are.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: This cluster has nothing to say about whether object-realistic rendering helps or induces logo-style recognition — that is the memory/UI cluster's call, and it is genuinely contested there. What this cluster DOES rule on is implementation and measurement, and on one point it contradicts the obvious execution. Rendering the physical object with PHOTOGRAPHS is not shippable: menu layout and typography, dish photography, package artwork and shopfront logos are protected expression carrying live trademarks, and a Dutch controller collecting them engages GDPR and PIPL. Separately, the design has no instrument that can tell whether the templates are teaching characters or teaching plates — which is the whole risk of the decision. And CTW's annotation schema includes a 'wordart' attribute precisely because decorative display lettering is common enough in real street-view Chinese text to need its own class, which argues for typeface VARIABILITY across presentations rather than a fixed set of five templates.
verdicts_on_design.change: Build every template from type and CSS in your own licensed subset font — never from a source photograph. Add a naked probe from v1 (10–15% of presentations render the target alone, plain ground) and report the naked-probe-minus-in-object delta internally from the first cohort; over ~20 points means the app is teaching plates. Add a render_variant field and rotate each item across at least three fully legible faces (a Hei, a Song, and a display or handwritten form) so the 'deliberately hard' treatments are perceptual VARIABILITY, not perceptual DISFLUENCY — the first has a track record, the second is a documented failure. Keep the two hard treatments as a documented, deliberate accessibility exception with a non-timed alternative, since they will violate target-size guidance.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 3. The component breakdown is the main teaching surface, promoted to the body of the reveal, advanced only by an explicit tap. 牛肉 → 牛 ox + 肉 meat; swap the head for 猪肉/羊肉/鸡肉/鸭肉; then 肉 flattens to 月 on the left, so 肝 肠 肚 腰 脑.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: The worked example is clean and — unusually — is exactly the kind of decomposition that survives scrutiny. 牛肉 is semantic compounding, and 肉 → 月 is a radical-variant fact derivable from Unihan kRSUnicode (radical 130), which is permissively licensed with no attribution-in-UI burden. The 猪/羊/鸡/鸭 head-swap is a paradigm, not a mnemonic, and it makes no claim about pronunciation. Two constraints bind hard, though. FIRST, PROVENANCE: the obvious decomposition dataset, Make Me a Hanzi's dictionary.txt, is LGPL-3.0-or-later and must never be shipped — its data has to be regenerated from Unihan plus CC-CEDICT. SECOND, AND THIS LIMITS THE DECISION'S REACH: the PHONETIC half of component teaching is a design bet, not a finding. Measured over the top 1,000 characters, a phonetic component predicts the full reading (segments + tone) only ~17% of the time, predicts the syllable ignoring tone ~39%, and gives no cue at all ~35%; only ~53% of the top 1,000 are phono-semantic compounds at all, only ~45% are left-right, and only ~31% are both. So a two-slot meaning/sound card cannot be the default layout — it is a conditional selected off a stored structure enum. And the reveal must carry reading per (character, word-context), because 12.9% of HSK characters are heteronyms and a reveal that shows a character with 'its' pinyin will be wrong on roughly one item in eight.
verdicts_on_design.change: Derive semantic components from Unihan kRSUnicode; regenerate decomposition from Unihan + CC-CEDICT; CI-fail on any field traceable to dictionary.txt. Store a structure enum per character and select the reveal layout from it — never render a meaning/sound split for a character that is not a left-right phono-semantic compound. Add reading: [{char, pinyin}] and has_variant_reading, and CI-fail on any heteronym without an explicit per-character reading. Before committing content-authoring weeks to a phonetic-series table, run the three-way test (exact / segmental-only / no cue) over your own 1,200 characters and publish the proportions; if exact + segmental is below ~50%, that effort belongs in the semantic-component column instead.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 4. A confusable is shown beside the target on resolution: 入口 beside 出口, 公斤 beside 斤, 麻 beside 辣.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Whether simultaneous presentation of confusables aids discrimination or induces interference is the memory cluster's call and is contested there. From this cluster, three things bind. (a) DETERMINISM: the engine is a deterministic reducer over a shared event log, so confusable and distractor sets must be precomputed at build time and derived as a pure function of (item, exposure_count, seed). Generating them at runtime is too slow and non-deterministic, and phones will diverge. (b) READING COLLISIONS: the pairing logic must never pair two items that share a character with different readings as though they were the same item — 磨 mó against 磨 mò is a schema bug waiting to be authored, and 公斤/斤 is fine only because 斤 is monophonic. (c) SET CONTENT: the highest-value confusion pair for THIS product is missing from what the research proposed — 人 versus 入, since 入口 misread as 人口 is the canonical beginner error and sits at the centre of the flagship metro scene. 曰 and 犬 are effectively absent from modern travel signage and are low-value.
verdicts_on_design.change: Precompute confusable_with[] and a component-incidence index (component → characters, character → components) at build time from Unihan kRSUnicode plus your own decomposition table. Keep interference_set (items that must NOT be scheduled in the same acquisition block) as a SEPARATE field from confusable_with (items shown together at resolution) — they are opposite operations and fusing them is how you build an interference generator by accident. Gate component-sharing distractors on exposure_count ≥ 1: distant distractors on the first correct encounter. Priority pairs for a China travel reader: 人/入 (critical), 大/太, 千/干, 木/本/末/未, 己/已, 天/夭, 田/由/甲, 十/千. Log the distractor set alongside every outcome so this gets settled on your own data.

verdicts_on_design.decision: 5. Tone colour sits on the pinyin, never on the character.
verdicts_on_design.reasoning: Right call, and the half of it that says 'never on the character' is the more robust half. But the reason given is weaker than the reason available. Colour-coded tone has no controlled trial behind it in any product that uses it (Pleco, Hanping, Skritter, Dong Chinese all differ, and their palettes are mutually incompatible), and the standard four-tone palettes are red/green/blue/purple — red-green being the failing pair for roughly 8% of males of Northern European ancestry, i.e. a substantial share of a Dutch and English user base. Above both of those sits a legal constraint: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.1 Use of Colour, binding via EN 301 549 under the European Accessibility Act since 28 June 2025 for a Dutch-published consumer app, prohibits colour as the ONLY carrier of information — which means tone colour on pinyin is also non-conformant if colour is the only tone channel. And there is a transfer argument the design has not made: real signage carries no tone colour anywhere, so the cue is guaranteed to be absent at test, in a product whose criterion task is silent visual recognition.
verdicts_on_design.change: Keep colour off the character. If tone is displayed at all, carry it redundantly — a tone numeral or a contour mark alongside the colour, never colour alone. Then ask the prior question the decision skips: this is a reading product whose criterion task involves no tone at all, so consider shipping no tone channel in v1 and reclaiming the screen space. If tone stays, the separable segments/tone data model is worth keeping independently of any colour decision.
